lessons.title: Questions
lessons.notes_html:
1.1. Name several repetitive phenomena occurring in nature which could serve as reasonable time standards.

The rotation of the Earth on its axis (day and night), the revolution of the Earth around the Sun (a year), the phases of the Moon (a lunar month), the tides, the swinging of a pendulum, the vibration of a quartz crystal, the beating of the heart and the sunrise and sunset are all repetitive phenomena. Any phenomenon that repeats itself after a fixed, equal interval of time can serve as a time standard.

1.2. Give the drawbacks to use the period of a pendulum as a time standard.

The period of a pendulum depends on the value of g, which changes from place to place, and on the length of the pendulum, which changes with temperature. Friction at the support and air resistance also change the motion, and the period is not exactly the same for large swings. A pendulum is therefore not perfectly reproducible, is hard to carry from place to place, and its small errors add up over a long time.

1.3. Why do we find it useful to have two units for the amount of substance, the kilogram and the mole?

The kilogram measures mass, that is, how much matter a body contains. The mole measures the amount of substance, that is, how many particles (atoms or molecules) it contains. One mole contains 6.02 x 10^23 particles. Equal masses of different substances contain different numbers of particles, so in chemistry, where reactions depend on the number of particles, the mole is needed in addition to the kilogram.

1.4. Three students measured the length of a needle with a scale on which minimum division is 1 mm and recorded as (i) 0.2145 m (ii) 0.21 m (iii) 0.214 m. Which record is correct and why?

Record (iii) 0.214 m is correct. A scale with a minimum division of 1 mm = 0.001 m can be read reliably only up to three places of decimals in metres. Record (i) 0.2145 m claims a precision of 0.1 mm, which the scale cannot give. Record (ii) 0.21 m is less precise than the scale allows, because it drops a figure the scale can actually measure.

1.5. An old saying is that 'A chain is only as strong as its weakest link'. What analogous statement can you make regarding experimental data used in a computation?

A result obtained from experimental data is only as accurate as the least accurate measurement used in it. In a computation, the final answer cannot have more significant figures, or more decimal places in addition and subtraction, than the least precise measurement that went into it.

1.6. The period of simple pendulum is measured by a stop watch. What type of errors are possible in the time period?

Both systematic and random errors are possible. A systematic error comes from the stop watch itself, for example a zero error or a wrong calibration, which affects every reading in the same way. Random errors come from the observer, mainly the human reaction time in starting and stopping the watch, which is different at each trial, and from small variations in counting the vibrations.

1.7. Does a dimensional analysis give any information on constant of proportionality that may appear in an algebraic expression? Explain.

No. Dimensional analysis only fixes the powers of the quantities in a relation, because a constant of proportionality is dimensionless and does not change the dimensions of either side. The numerical value of the constant, for example 2 pi in T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g), cannot be found by dimensional analysis; it must be found by experiment or by a full theory.

1.8. Write the dimensions of (i) Pressure (ii) Density.

(i) Pressure = force / area. Dimensions = [M L T^-2] / [L^2] = [M L^-1 T^-2]. (ii) Density = mass / volume. Dimensions = [M] / [L^3] = [M L^-3].

1.9. The wavelength lambda of a wave depends on the speed v of the wave and its frequency f. Knowing that [lambda] = [L], [v] = [L T^-1] and [f] = [T^-1], decide which of the following is correct: f = v lambda or f = v / lambda.

Check f = v lambda: dimensions of v lambda = [L T^-1] x [L] = [L^2 T^-1], which is not [T^-1]. Check f = v / lambda: dimensions of v / lambda = [L T^-1] / [L] = [T^-1], which equals [f]. Therefore f = v / lambda is correct.

mcqs.q: Which of the following repetitive phenomena could serve as a reasonable time standard?
options: The vibration of a quartz crystal
The rusting of an iron nail
The melting of ice in summer
mcqs.why: Any phenomenon that repeats itself after a fixed, equal interval of time can serve as a time standard. The notes list the vibration of a quartz crystal, the swinging of a pendulum, the phases of the Moon and the rotation of the Earth as such repetitive phenomena.

mcqs.q: Why is the period of a pendulum not a perfectly reliable time standard?
options: Because a pendulum is too large to carry from place to place
Because its period depends on g, which changes from place to place, and on its length, which changes with temperature
Because a pendulum stops swinging after a few minutes
Because its period depends on the mass of the bob
mcqs.why: The notes give these drawbacks: the period depends on the value of g, which changes from place to place, and on the length, which changes with temperature; friction and air resistance also act, and the small errors add up over a long time.

mcqs.q: One mole of a substance contains how many particles?
mcqs.why: The mole measures the amount of substance, that is, the number of particles it contains. One mole contains 6.02 x 10^23 particles (atoms or molecules), which is why the mole is needed in chemistry in addition to the kilogram.

mcqs.why: A minimum division of 1 mm is 0.001 m, so the scale can be read reliably only up to three decimal places in metres. Record (iii) 0.214 m matches this; record (i) claims a precision of 0.1 mm the scale cannot give, and record (ii) drops a figure the scale can measure.

mcqs.q: What is the statement analogous to 'a chain is only as strong as its weakest link' for experimental data used in a computation?
options: A result is only as accurate as the least accurate measurement used in it
A result is only as accurate as the most accurate measurement used in it
A result is always more accurate than every measurement used in it
A result has the average accuracy of all the measurements used in it
mcqs.why: The notes state that a result obtained from experimental data is only as accurate as the least accurate measurement used in it: the final answer cannot have more significant figures than the least precise measurement that went into it.

mcqs.q: The period of a simple pendulum is measured with a stop watch. What types of error are possible in the measured period?
mcqs.why: Both types are possible. A systematic error comes from the stop watch itself, such as a zero error or wrong calibration. Random errors come from the observer, mainly the human reaction time in starting and stopping the watch, which differs at each trial.

mcqs.q: What information does dimensional analysis NOT give about an algebraic expression?
options: The powers of the quantities in the relation
The value of a dimensionless constant of proportionality, such as 2 pi in T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g)
Whether the dimensions of the two sides match
The dimensions of a derived quantity
mcqs.why: Dimensional analysis only fixes the powers of the quantities, because a constant of proportionality is dimensionless and does not change the dimensions of either side. Its numerical value, for example 2 pi in T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g), must be found by experiment or full theory.

mcqs.q: What are the dimensions of pressure?
mcqs.why: Pressure is force divided by area. Working: dimensions of force are [M L T^-2] and of area are [L^2], so pressure = [M L T^-2] / [L^2] = [M L^-1 T^-2], as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: What are the dimensions of density?
mcqs.why: Density is mass divided by volume. Working: dimensions of mass are [M] and of volume are [L^3], so density = [M] / [L^3] = [M L^-3], as given in the notes.

mcqs.q: The wavelength lambda of a wave depends on its speed v and frequency f. Given [lambda] = [L], [v] = [L T^-1] and [f] = [T^-1], which relation is dimensionally correct?
mcqs.why: Check f = v / lambda: dimensions are [L T^-1] / [L] = [T^-1], which equals [f]. Check f = v lambda: dimensions are [L T^-1] x [L] = [L^2 T^-1], which is not [T^-1]. So f = v / lambda is correct.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
1.1. A light year is the distance light travels in one year. How many metres are there in one light year? (speed of light = 3.0 x 10^8 ms^-1).

Step 1: Time in one year: t = 365 days x 24 hours/day x 3600 s/hour.

Step 2: t = 365 x 24 x 3600 s = 3.1536 x 10^7 s.

Step 3: Distance = speed x time: d = (3.0 x 10^8 ms^-1) x (3.1536 x 10^7 s).

Step 4: d = 9.4608 x 10^15 m, which to two significant figures is 9.5 x 10^15 m.

Answer: 9.5 x 10^15 m (as printed in the book).

1.2. (a) How many seconds are there in 1 year? (b) How many nanoseconds in 1 year? (c) How many years in 1 second?

Step 1: (a) Seconds in 1 year = 365 x 24 x 3600 = 3.1536 x 10^7 s.

Step 2: (b) 1 s = 10^9 ns, so nanoseconds in 1 year = 3.1536 x 10^7 x 10^9 = 3.1536 x 10^16 ns.

Step 3: (c) Years in 1 second = 1 / (3.1536 x 10^7) year = 3.17 x 10^-8 year.

Answer: (a) 3.1536 x 10^7 s, (b) 3.1536 x 10^16 ns, (c) 3.17 x 10^-8 year. Note: the book prints (c) as 3.1 x 10^-8 year, a rougher rounding; the value from 365 days is 3.17 x 10^-8 year.

1.3. The length and width of a rectangular plate are measured to be 15.3 cm and 12.80 cm, respectively. Find the area of the plate.

Step 1: Area = length x width = 15.3 cm x 12.80 cm.

Step 2: Area = 195.84 cm^2.

Step 3: The least precise measurement, 15.3 cm, has three significant figures, so the result is rounded to three significant figures.

Answer: 196 cm^2 (as printed in the book).

1.4. Add the following masses given in kg up to appropriate precision: 2.189, 0.089, 11.8 and 5.32.

Step 1: Add the masses: 2.189 + 0.089 + 11.8 + 5.32 = 19.398 kg.

Step 2: In addition, the result is rounded to the decimal place of the least precise measurement. The least precise value is 11.8 kg, which is known only to one place of decimals.

Step 3: 19.398 kg rounded to one place of decimals is 19.4 kg.

Answer: 19.4 kg (as printed in the book).

1.5. Find the value of 'g' and its uncertainty using T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g) from the following measurements: length of simple pendulum l = 100 cm; time for 20 vibrations = 40.2 s; length measured by a metre scale of accuracy up to 1 mm and time by stop watch of accuracy up to 0.1 s.

Step 1: Time period for one vibration: T = 40.2 s / 20 = 2.01 s.

Step 2: Length in metres: l = 100 cm = 1.00 m.

Step 3: From T = 2 pi sqrt(l/g), squaring both sides gives g = 4 pi^2 l / T^2.

Step 4: With pi = 3.14: g = 4 x (3.14)^2 x 1.00 / (2.01)^2 = 39.4384 / 4.0401 = 9.76 ms^-2.

Step 5: Uncertainty in length: delta l = 1 mm = 0.001 m, so delta l / l = 0.001 / 1.00 = 0.001.

Step 6: Uncertainty in one period: delta T = 0.1 s / 20 = 0.005 s, so delta T / T = 0.005 / 2.01 = 0.00249.

Step 7: Fractional uncertainty in g: delta g / g = delta l / l + 2 x (delta T / T) = 0.001 + 2 x 0.00249 = 0.00597.

Step 8: delta g = 9.76 x 0.00597 = 0.058 ms^-2, about 0.06 ms^-2.

Answer: g = 9.76 +- 0.06 ms^-2 (as printed in the book).

1.6. What are the dimensions and units of gravitational constant G in the formula F = G m1 m2 / r^2?

Step 1: Rearrange the formula: G = F r^2 / (m1 m2).

Step 2: Dimensions: [G] = [M L T^-2] x [L^2] / [M^2].

Step 3: [G] = [M^-1 L^3 T^-2].

Step 4: Unit: from F = G m1 m2 / r^2, the unit of G is N m^2 kg^-2.

Answer: [M^-1 L^3 T^-2], N m^2 kg^-2 (as printed in the book).

1.7. Show that the expression vf = vi + at is dimensionally correct, where vi is the velocity at t = 0, a is acceleration and vf is the velocity at time t.

Step 1: Dimensions of the left hand side: [vf] = [L T^-1].

Step 2: Dimensions of vi: [vi] = [L T^-1].

Step 3: Dimensions of at: [a] x [t] = [L T^-2] x [T] = [L T^-1].

Step 4: Both terms on the right hand side have the same dimensions, [L T^-1], and they equal the dimensions of the left hand side.

Answer: the expression is dimensionally correct (this shows consistency of dimensions, not that the equation is fully proved).

1.8. The speed v of sound waves through a medium may be assumed to depend on (a) the density rho of the medium and (b) its modulus of elasticity E which is the ratio of stress to strain. Deduce by the method of dimensions, the formula for the speed of sound.

Step 1: Assume v = Constant x rho^a x E^b, where a and b are to be found.

Step 2: Dimensions: [v] = [L T^-1], [rho] = [M L^-3], [E] = [M L^-1 T^-2] (the same dimensions as pressure).

Step 3: [L T^-1] = ([M L^-3])^a x ([M L^-1 T^-2])^b = [M^(a+b) L^(-3a-b) T^(-2b)].

Step 4: Equate the powers of M: a + b = 0.

Step 5: Equate the powers of T: -2b = -1, so b = 1/2.

Step 6: From a + b = 0, a = -1/2. Check the powers of L: -3a - b = -3(-1/2) - 1/2 = 1, as required.

Step 7: Therefore v = Constant x rho^(-1/2) x E^(1/2) = Constant x sqrt(E / rho).

Answer: v = Constant sqrt(E / rho) (as printed in the book).

1.9. Show that the famous 'Einstein equation' E = mc^2 is dimensionally consistent.

Step 1: Dimensions of energy E: [E] = [M L^2 T^-2].

Step 2: Dimensions of mc^2: [m] x [c]^2 = [M] x ([L T^-1])^2 = [M L^2 T^-2].

Step 3: Both sides have the same dimensions, [M L^2 T^-2].

Answer: E = mc^2 is dimensionally consistent.

1.10. Suppose, we are told that the acceleration of a particle moving in a circle of radius r with uniform speed v is proportional to some power of r, say r^n, and some power of v, say v^m, determine the powers of r and v.

Step 1: Write a = Constant x r^n x v^m.

Step 2: Dimensions: [a] = [L T^-2], [r]^n = [L^n], [v]^m = ([L T^-1])^m = [L^m T^-m].

Step 3: So [L T^-2] = [L^(n+m) T^-m].

Step 4: Equate the powers of T: -m = -2, so m = 2.

Step 5: Equate the powers of L: n + m = 1, so n = 1 - 2 = -1.

Answer: n = -1, m = 2 (as printed in the book), that is, a is proportional to v^2 / r.

mcqs.why: Working: time in one year t = 365 x 24 x 3600 = 31536000 s = 3.1536 x 10^7 s. Distance = speed x time = 3.0 x 10^8 x 3.1536 x 10^7 = 9.46 x 10^15 m, which to two significant figures is 9.5 x 10^15 m.

mcqs.q: How many years are there in 1 second?
mcqs.why: Working: 1 year contains 3.1536 x 10^7 s, so 1 second = 1 / 3.1536 x 10^7 years. Computing: 1 / 31536000 = 3.17 x 10^-8, so 1 second is 3.17 x 10^-8 years (the book prints the rougher rounding 3.1 x 10^-8 year).

mcqs.why: Working: area = 15.3 x 12.80 = 195.84 cm^2. The least precise measurement, 15.3 cm, has three significant figures, so the result is rounded to three significant figures: 196 cm^2.

mcqs.why: Working: the straight sum is 2.189 + 0.089 + 11.8 + 5.32 = 19.398 kg. In addition the result is rounded to the decimal place of the least precise measurement; 11.8 kg is known only to one decimal place, so the answer is 19.4 kg.

For the pendulum measurement above (length accurate to 1 mm, stop watch to 0.1 s), the uncertainty in g = 9.76 ms^-2 is about:

mcqs.why: Working: rearranging gives G = F r^2 / (m1 m2). Dimensions: [G] = [M L T^-2] x [L^2] / [M^2] = [M^-1 L^3 T^-2], as worked out in the notes.

mcqs.why: From F = G m1 m2 / r^2, the unit of G is the unit of F r^2 / (m1 m2), which is N m^2 kg^-2, matching its dimensions [M^-1 L^3 T^-2] found in the notes.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.notes_html:
2.1. Define the terms (i) unit vector (ii) Position vector and (iii) Components of a vector.

(i) A unit vector is a vector of magnitude one. It only shows a direction; for example, i, j and k are unit vectors along the x, y and z axes. (ii) A position vector is the vector drawn from the origin of a coordinate system to a point; it gives the position of that point. (iii) The components of a vector are its projections on the coordinate axes. For a vector A in three dimensions, Ax, Ay and Az are its rectangular components, and A = Ax i + Ay j + Az k.

2.2. The vector sum of three vectors gives a zero resultant. What can be the orientation of the vectors?

When the three vectors are placed head to tail, they form a closed triangle. This means the three vectors are coplanar and are arranged so that the head of the last vector meets the tail of the first, giving a zero resultant.

2.3. Vector A lies in the xy plane. For what orientation will both of its rectangular components be negative? For what orientation will its components have opposite signs?

Both components are negative when A lies in the third quadrant, that is, when it makes an angle between 180 degrees and 270 degrees with the positive x-axis. The components have opposite signs when A lies in the second quadrant (Ax negative, Ay positive) or in the fourth quadrant (Ax positive, Ay negative).

2.4. If one of the rectangular components of a vector is not zero, can its magnitude be zero? Explain.

No. The magnitude of a vector is the square root of the sum of the squares of its components, so it is at least as large as any one component. If even one component is not zero, the magnitude is greater than zero.

2.5. Can a vector have a component greater than the vector's magnitude?

No. A component is the magnitude multiplied by the cosine of an angle, and the cosine can never be greater than one in size. So no component can be greater than the magnitude of the vector itself.

2.6. Can the magnitude of a vector have a negative value?

No. The magnitude of a vector is a length, and a length is always zero or positive. It can never be negative.

2.7. If A + B = 0, what can you say about the components of the two vectors?

Then B = -A. The two vectors are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so their corresponding components are equal in size but opposite in sign: Bx = -Ax, By = -Ay and Bz = -Az.

2.8. Under what circumstances would a vector have components that are equal in magnitude?

When the vector makes equal angles with the axes, so that its direction cosines are equal in size. In two dimensions this happens when the vector makes an angle of 45 degrees with the x-axis, giving Ax = Ay.

2.9. Is it possible to add a vector quantity to a scalar quantity? Explain.

No. Only quantities of the same kind can be added. A vector has magnitude and direction, while a scalar has magnitude only, so adding them has no meaning in physics.

2.10. Can you add zero to a null vector?

A scalar zero cannot be added to a vector. But the null vector itself can be added to a null vector, and the result is still the null vector, because a null vector has zero magnitude.

2.11. Two vectors have unequal magnitudes. Can their sum be zero? Explain.

No. For the sum to be zero the two vectors must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, so that they cancel completely. With unequal magnitudes the smallest possible resultant is the difference of the two magnitudes, which is not zero.

2.12. Show that the sum and difference of two perpendicular vectors of equal lengths are also perpendicular and of the same length.

Let the vectors be A and B, perpendicular, each of length L. Their sum is A + B and their difference is A - B. Their dot product is (A + B).(A - B) = |A|^2 - |B|^2 = L^2 - L^2 = 0, so they are perpendicular. Their lengths are |A + B| = sqrt(L^2 + L^2) = L sqrt(2) and |A - B| = sqrt(L^2 + L^2) = L sqrt(2), so they are equal.

2.13. How would the two vectors of the same magnitude have to be oriented, if they were to be combined to give a resultant equal to a vector of the same magnitude?

They must be at an angle of 120 degrees to each other. If each vector has magnitude A, the resultant R satisfies R^2 = A^2 + A^2 + 2 A^2 cos(theta). Setting R = A gives cos(theta) = -1/2, so theta = 120 degrees.

2.14. The two vectors to be combined have magnitudes 60 N and 35 N. Pick the correct answer from those given below and tell why is it the only one of the three that is correct. (i) 100 N (ii) 70 N (iii) 20 N

The correct answer is (ii) 70 N. The magnitude of the resultant of two vectors must lie between the difference and the sum of their magnitudes, that is, between 60 - 35 = 25 N and 60 + 35 = 95 N. Only 70 N lies in this range; 100 N is greater than the sum and 20 N is less than the difference, so both are impossible.

2.15. Suppose the sides of a closed polygon represent vector arranged head to tail. What is the sum of these vectors?

The sum is zero (the null vector). Going around a closed polygon head to tail brings you back to the starting point, so there is no net displacement.

2.16. Identify the correct answer. (i) Two ships X and Y are travelling in different directions at equal speeds. The actual direction of motion of X is due north but to an observer on Y, the apparent direction of motion of X is north-east. The actual direction of motion of Y as observed from the shore will be (A) East (B) West (C) south-east (D) south-west. (ii) A horizontal force F is applied to a small object P of mass m at rest on a smooth plane inclined at an angle theta to the horizontal as shown in Fig. 2.21. The magnitude of the resultant force acting up and along the surface of the plane, on the object is (a) F cos(theta) - m g sin(theta) (b) F sin(theta) - m g cos(theta) (c) F cos(theta) + m g cos(theta) (d) F sin(theta) + m g sin(theta) (e) m g tan(theta).

(i) The correct answer is (B) West. The apparent velocity of X as seen from Y is the velocity of X minus the velocity of Y. X moves north and Y moves west at the same speed, so the apparent velocity points north-east, as given. (ii) The correct answer is (a) F cos(theta) - m g sin(theta). The component of the horizontal force F up the plane is F cos(theta), and the component of the weight down the plane is m g sin(theta). Their difference is the net force up the plane.

2.17. If all the components of the vectors, A1 and A2 were reversed, how would this alter A1 x A2?

It would not alter it at all. Reversing all components changes A1 to -A1 and A2 to -A2, and (-A1) x (-A2) = A1 x A2, because the two minus signs cancel.

2.18. Name the three different conditions that could make A1 x A2 = 0.

The cross product is zero if (1) A1 is the null vector, (2) A2 is the null vector, or (3) A1 and A2 are parallel or antiparallel to each other, so that the angle between them is 0 degrees or 180 degrees and sin(theta) = 0.

2.19. Identify true or false statements and explain the reason. (a) A body in equilibrium implies that it is not moving nor rotating. (b) If coplanar forces acting on a body form a closed polygon, then the body is said to be in equilibrium.

(a) False. Equilibrium means zero acceleration, not zero velocity. A body in equilibrium may be at rest, or it may move with a uniform velocity and rotate uniformly, because then its translational and angular accelerations are both zero. (b) True. If coplanar forces placed head to tail form a closed polygon, their vector sum is zero, which is the condition for translational equilibrium.

2.20. A picture is suspended from a wall by two strings. Show by diagram the configuration of the strings for which the tension in the strings will be minimum.

The tension is minimum when the two strings are vertical and parallel to each other. In that case each string carries half the weight of the picture, T = W/2. If the strings are spread apart, each string must also balance the sideways pull of the other, so the tension grows; it becomes very large when the strings are nearly horizontal.

2.21. Can a body rotate about its centre of gravity under the action of its weight?

No. The weight of a body acts at its centre of gravity, so the line of action of the weight passes through the centre of gravity itself. The moment arm about the centre of gravity is therefore zero, and the weight produces no torque about that point.

mcqs.q: What is a unit vector?
options: A vector of magnitude one that only shows a direction
A vector drawn from the origin to a point
A vector whose components are all equal
mcqs.why: A unit vector is a vector of magnitude one; it only shows a direction. For example, i, j and k are unit vectors along the x, y and z axes, as defined in the notes.

mcqs.q: The vector sum of three vectors is zero. How are the three vectors oriented?
options: They are all parallel to each other
Placed head to tail, they form a closed triangle and are coplanar
They must all have equal magnitudes
mcqs.why: When the three vectors are placed head to tail, they form a closed triangle: the head of the last vector meets the tail of the first, so the resultant is zero. The three vectors are coplanar.

mcqs.q: A vector A lies in the xy plane. For what orientation are both of its rectangular components negative?
options: When it lies in the first quadrant (0 to 90 degrees)
When it lies in the second quadrant (90 to 180 degrees)
When it lies in the fourth quadrant (270 to 360 degrees)
When it lies in the third quadrant (180 to 270 degrees)
mcqs.why: Both components are negative when A lies in the third quadrant, that is, when it makes an angle between 180 degrees and 270 degrees with the positive x-axis. In the second and fourth quadrants the components have opposite signs.

mcqs.q: Can a component of a vector be greater than the magnitude of the vector itself?
options: Yes, whenever the vector is at 45 degrees to the axis
No, because a component is the magnitude times a cosine, which can never exceed one
Yes, for vectors in three dimensions
Only if the other components are negative
mcqs.why: No. A component is the magnitude multiplied by the cosine of an angle, and the cosine can never be greater than one in size, so no component can be greater than the magnitude of the vector itself.

mcqs.q: Two vectors have unequal magnitudes. Can their sum be zero?
options: No, because for the sum to be zero they must be equal in magnitude and opposite in direction
Yes, if they are placed at 120 degrees to each other
Yes, if the smaller vector is reversed
mcqs.why: No. For the sum to be zero the two vectors must cancel completely, which needs equal magnitudes in opposite directions. With unequal magnitudes the smallest possible resultant is the difference of the two magnitudes, which is not zero.

mcqs.q: Two vectors of the same magnitude A are combined to give a resultant also of magnitude A. The angle between them must be:
mcqs.why: Working: R^2 = A^2 + A^2 + 2 A^2 cos(theta). Setting R = A gives cos(theta) = -1/2, so theta = 120 degrees, as derived in the notes.

mcqs.q: Two vectors have magnitudes 60 N and 35 N. Which of the following could be the magnitude of their resultant: (i) 100 N (ii) 70 N (iii) 20 N?
mcqs.why: Working: the resultant must lie between the difference and the sum of the magnitudes: 60 - 35 = 25 N and 60 + 35 = 95 N. Only 70 N lies between 25 N and 95 N; 100 N exceeds the sum and 20 N is less than the difference.

mcqs.q: The sides of a closed polygon represent vectors arranged head to tail. The sum of these vectors is:
options: Equal to the perimeter of the polygon
mcqs.why: Going around a closed polygon head to tail brings you back to the starting point, so there is no net displacement and the sum of the vectors is zero, the null vector.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a condition that can make A1 x A2 = 0?
options: A1 and A2 are perpendicular to each other
A1 and A2 are parallel or antiparallel
mcqs.why: The cross product is zero if A1 is the null vector, or A2 is the null vector, or the two are parallel or antiparallel (angle 0 or 180 degrees, so sin(theta) = 0). For perpendicular vectors the cross product is at its maximum, not zero.

mcqs.q: A picture of weight W hangs from two strings. For which arrangement is the tension in the strings minimum, and what is it?
options: Strings vertical and parallel, each with tension W/2
Strings nearly horizontal, each with tension W/2
Strings at 45 degrees, each with tension W
One string only, with tension W
mcqs.why: The tension is minimum when the two strings are vertical and parallel; then each string carries half the weight, T = W/2. If the strings are spread apart, each must also balance the sideways pull of the other, so the tension grows and becomes very large when the strings are nearly horizontal.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
2.1. Suppose, in a rectangular coordinate system, a vector A has its tail at the point P (-2, -3) and its tip at Q (3, 9). Determine the distance between these two points.

Step 1: Change in x: dx = 3 - (-2) = 5.

Step 2: Change in y: dy = 9 - (-3) = 12.

Step 3: Distance = sqrt(dx^2 + dy^2) = sqrt(25 + 144) = sqrt(169) = 13.

Answer: 13 units (as printed in the book).

2.2. A certain corner of a room is selected as the origin of a rectangular coordinate system. If an insect is sitting on an adjacent wall at a point having coordinates (2, 1), where the units are in metres, what is the distance of the insect from this corner of the room?

Step 1: Distance = sqrt(2^2 + 1^2) = sqrt(5).

Step 2: sqrt(5) = 2.236 m, about 2.2 m.

Answer: 2.2 m (as printed in the book).

2.3. What is the unit vector in the direction of the vector A = 4 i + 3 j?

Step 1: Magnitude of A: |A| = sqrt(4^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(25) = 5.

Step 2: Unit vector = A / |A| = (4 i + 3 j) / 5.

Answer: (4 i + 3 j) / 5 (as printed in the book).

2.4. Two particles are located at r1 = 3 i + 7 j and r2 = -2 i + 3 j respectively. Find both the magnitude of the vector r2 - r1 and its orientation with respect to the x-axis.

Step 1: r2 - r1 = (-2 - 3) i + (3 - 7) j = -5 i - 4 j.

Step 2: Magnitude = sqrt((-5)^2 + (-4)^2) = sqrt(41) = 6.4.

Step 3: The vector lies in the third quadrant. tan(phi) = (-4)/(-5) = 0.8, so phi = 38.7 degrees.

Step 4: Angle with the positive x-axis = 180 degrees + 38.7 degrees = 218.7 degrees, about 219 degrees.

Answer: 6.4, 219 degrees (as printed in the book).

2.5. If a vector B is added to vector A, the result is 6 i + j. If B is subtracted from A, the result is -4 i + 7 j. What is the magnitude of vector A?

Step 1: A + B = 6 i + j and A - B = -4 i + 7 j.

Step 2: Add the two equations: 2A = (6 - 4) i + (1 + 7) j = 2 i + 8 j.

Step 3: So A = i + 4 j.

Step 4: Magnitude of A = sqrt(1^2 + 4^2) = sqrt(17) = 4.1.

Answer: 4.1 (as printed in the book).

2.6. Given that A = 2 i + 3 j and B = 3 i - 4 j, find the magnitude and angle of (a) C = A + B, and (b) D = 3A - 2B.

Step 1: (a) C = A + B = (2 + 3) i + (3 - 4) j = 5 i - j.

Step 2: Magnitude of C = sqrt(25 + 1) = sqrt(26) = 5.1.

Step 3: Angle of C: tan(theta) = -1/5, so theta = -11.3 degrees, which is 360 - 11.3 = 349 degrees from the positive x-axis.

Step 4: (b) D = 3A - 2B = (6 - 6) i + (9 + 8) j = 17 j.

Step 5: Magnitude of D = 17, and its angle with the positive x-axis is 90 degrees.

Answer: 5.1, 349 degrees; 17, 90 degrees (as printed in the book).

2.7. Find the angle between the two vectors, A = 5 i + j and B = 2 i + 4 j.

Step 1: Dot product: A.B = (5 x 2) + (1 x 4) = 14.

Step 2: |A| = sqrt(25 + 1) = sqrt(26) = 5.10.

Step 3: |B| = sqrt(4 + 16) = sqrt(20) = 4.47.

Step 4: cos(theta) = (A.B) / (|A| |B|) = 14 / (5.10 x 4.47) = 14 / 22.80 = 0.614.

Step 5: theta = cos^-1(0.614) = 52 degrees.

Answer: 52 degrees (as printed in the book).

2.8. Find the work done when the point of application of the force 3 i + 2 j moves in a straight line from the point (2, -1) to the point (6, 4).

Step 1: Displacement = (6 - 2) i + (4 - (-1)) j = 4 i + 5 j.

Step 2: Work = F.d = (3 x 4) + (2 x 5) = 12 + 10 = 22.

Answer: 22 units (as printed in the book).

2.9. Show that the three vectors i + j + k, 2 i - 3 j + k and 4 i + j - 5 k are mutually perpendicular.

Step 1: Dot product of the first and second: (1 x 2) + (1 x -3) + (1 x 1) = 2 - 3 + 1 = 0.

Step 2: Dot product of the first and third: (1 x 4) + (1 x 1) + (1 x -5) = 4 + 1 - 5 = 0.

Step 3: Dot product of the second and third: (2 x 4) + (-3 x 1) + (1 x -5) = 8 - 3 - 5 = 0.

Step 4: All three dot products are zero, so each pair is perpendicular.

Answer: the three vectors are mutually perpendicular.

2.10. Given that A = i - 2 j + 3 k and B = 3 i - 4 k, find the projection of A on B.

Step 1: Dot product: A.B = (1 x 3) + (-2 x 0) + (3 x -4) = 3 - 12 = -9.

Step 2: Magnitude of B: |B| = sqrt(9 + 16) = 5.

Step 3: Scalar projection of A on B = (A.B) / |B| = -9 / 5.

Answer: -9/5 (as printed in the book). The negative sign means the projection points opposite to B.

2.11. Vectors A, B and C are 4 units north, 3 units west and 8 units east, respectively. Describe carefully (a) A x B (b) A x C (c) B x C.

Step 1: Take north as j and east as i. Then A = 4 j, B = -3 i, C = 8 i.

Step 2: (a) A x B = 4 j x (-3 i) = -12 (j x i) = -12 (-k) = 12 k. Magnitude 12 units, direction vertically up.

Step 3: (b) A x C = 4 j x 8 i = 32 (j x i) = -32 k. Magnitude 32 units, direction vertically down.

Step 4: (c) B x C = (-3 i) x (8 i) = 0, because the vectors are parallel (both along the east-west line).

Answer: (a) 12 units vertically up (b) 32 units vertically down (c) Zero (as printed in the book).

2.12. The torque or turning effect of force about a given point is given by r x F where r is the vector from the given point to the point of application of F. Consider a force F = -3 i + j + 5 k (newton) acting on the point 7 i + 3 j + k (m). What is the torque in N m about the origin?

Step 1: Torque = r x F, with r = 7 i + 3 j + k and F = -3 i + j + 5 k.

Step 2: i-component: (3 x 5) - (1 x 1) = 15 - 1 = 14.

Step 3: j-component: -[(7 x 5) - (1 x -3)] = -(35 + 3) = -38.

Step 4: k-component: (7 x 1) - (3 x -3) = 7 + 9 = 16.

Answer: 14 i - 38 j + 16 k N m (as printed in the book).

2.13. The line of action of force, F = i - 2 j, passes through a point whose position vector is (-j + k). Find (a) the moment of F about the origin, (b) the moment of F about the point of which the position vector is i + k.

Step 1: (a) Moment about the origin = r x F with r = -j + k and F = i - 2 j.

Step 2: i-component: (-1 x 0) - (1 x -2) = 2.

Step 3: j-component: -[(0 x 0) - (1 x 1)] = 1.

Step 4: k-component: (0 x -2) - (-1 x 1) = 1. So the moment about the origin is 2 i + j + k.

Step 5: (b) Vector from the new point to the point on the line of action: (-j + k) - (i + k) = -i - j.

Step 6: Moment = (-i - j) x (i - 2 j) = (-i) x (-2 j) + (-j) x (i) = 2 k + k = 3 k.

Answer: (a) 2 i + j + k, (b) 3 k (as printed in the book).

2.14. The magnitude of dot and cross products of two vectors are 6 sqrt(3) and 6 respectively. Find the angle between the vectors.

Step 1: |A x B| = A B sin(theta) = 6 and A.B = A B cos(theta) = 6 sqrt(3).

Step 2: Divide: tan(theta) = |A x B| / (A.B) = 6 / (6 sqrt(3)) = 1 / sqrt(3).

Step 3: theta = tan^-1(1 / sqrt(3)) = 30 degrees.

Answer: 30 degrees (as printed in the book).

2.15. A load of 10.0 N is suspended from a clothes line. This distorts the line so that it makes an angle of 15 degrees with the horizontal at each end. Find the tension in the clothes line.

Step 1: At the load, the two halves of the line pull up and outwards, each with tension T at 15 degrees to the horizontal.

Step 2: Vertical equilibrium: the upward components balance the weight: 2 T sin(15 degrees) = 10.0 N.

Step 3: sin(15 degrees) = 0.2588, so 2 T x 0.2588 = 10.0.

Step 4: T = 10.0 / 0.5176 = 19.3 N.

Answer: 19.3 N (as printed in the book).

2.16. A tractor of weight 15,000 N crosses a single span bridge of weight 8000 N and of length 21.0 m. The bridge span is supported half a metre from either end. The tractor's front wheels take 1/3 of the total weight of the tractor, and the rear wheels are 3 m behind the front wheels. Calculate the force on the bridge supports when the rear wheels are at the middle of the bridge span.

Step 1: Supports are 0.5 m from each end, so the distance between the supports is 21.0 - 0.5 - 0.5 = 20.0 m. Call the left support A and the right support B.

Step 2: Rear wheels at the middle of the span: 10.5 m from the left end, carrying 2/3 x 15,000 = 10,000 N. Front wheels 3 m ahead: 13.5 m from the left end, carrying 1/3 x 15,000 = 5,000 N.

Step 3: Bridge weight 8,000 N acts at its centre, 10.5 m from the left end. Total downward force = 10,000 + 5,000 + 8,000 = 23,000 N.

Step 4: Take moments about A (0.5 m from the left end). Distances from A: rear wheels 10.0 m, front wheels 13.0 m, bridge centre 10.0 m.

Step 5: R_B x 20.0 = (10,000 x 10.0) + (5,000 x 13.0) + (8,000 x 10.0) = 100,000 + 65,000 + 80,000 = 245,000.

Step 6: R_B = 245,000 / 20.0 = 12,250 N = 12.25 kN.

Step 7: R_A = 23,000 - 12,250 = 10,750 N = 10.75 kN.

Answer: 12.25 kN and 10.75 kN (as printed in the book; the larger force is on the right support, nearer the front wheels).

2.17. A spherical ball of weight 50 N is to be lifted over the step as shown in the Fig. 2.23. Calculate the minimum force needed just to lift it above the floor. (Fig. 2.23: ball radius 20 cm, step height 5 cm, horizontal force F whose line of action is 10 cm above the centre of the ball.)

Step 1: Take the corner of the step as the pivot. Just as the ball starts to lift, it turns about this corner.

Step 2: Radius R = 20 cm, step height h = 5 cm. The centre of the ball is R - h = 15 cm above the pivot level.

Step 3: Horizontal distance from the pivot to the vertical line through the centre: sqrt(R^2 - (R - h)^2) = sqrt(20^2 - 15^2) = sqrt(400 - 225) = sqrt(175) = 13.23 cm.

Step 4: Moment of the weight about the pivot: 50 N x 13.23 cm (this resists the lift).

Step 5: The line of action of F is 10 cm above the centre, so its height above the pivot level is 10 + 15 = 25 cm. Moment of F about the pivot: F x 25 cm.

Step 6: For just lifting, the moments balance: F x 25 = 50 x 13.23, so F = 661.5 / 25 = 26.5 N, about 26 N.

Answer: 26 N (as printed in the book).

2.18. A uniform sphere of weight 10.0 N is held by a string attached to a frictionless wall so that the string makes an angle of 30 degrees with the wall as shown in Fig. 2.24. Find the tension in the string and the force exerted on the sphere by the wall.

Step 1: Forces on the sphere: weight 10.0 N downwards, tension T along the string, and the normal force N from the wall, horizontal.

Step 2: The string makes 30 degrees with the wall (the vertical), so the vertical component of T is T cos(30 degrees) and the horizontal component is T sin(30 degrees).

Step 3: Vertical equilibrium: T cos(30 degrees) = 10.0 N, so T = 10.0 / 0.8660 = 11.55 N, about 11.6 N.

Step 4: Horizontal equilibrium: N = T sin(30 degrees) = 11.55 x 0.5 = 5.77 N.

Answer: 11.6 N, 5.77 N (as printed in the book).

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.notes_html:
3.1. What is the difference between uniform and variable velocity? From the explanation of variable velocity, define acceleration. Give SI units of velocity and acceleration.

Uniform velocity means a body covers equal displacements in equal intervals of time, in the same direction. Variable velocity means the velocity changes, either in magnitude or in direction or both. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity, a = change in velocity / time taken. The SI unit of velocity is metre per second (ms^-1) and of acceleration is metre per second squared (ms^-2).

3.2. An object is thrown vertically upward. Discuss the sign of acceleration due to gravity, relative to velocity, while the object is in air.

Take the upward direction as positive. The acceleration due to gravity is always downwards, so it is always negative, -g, throughout the flight. While the object rises, its velocity is positive and decreasing, so acceleration is opposite to velocity. At the highest point the velocity is zero for an instant, but the acceleration is still -g. While the object falls, its velocity is negative and growing in size, so acceleration is in the same direction as velocity.

3.3. Can the velocity of an object reverse the direction when acceleration is constant? If so, give an example.

Yes. A ball thrown vertically upward is an example: its acceleration is the constant acceleration due to gravity, downwards, yet its velocity is first upward, becomes zero at the top, and then becomes downward. The velocity reverses its direction while the acceleration stays constant.

3.4. Specify the correct statements: (a) An object can have a constant velocity even its speed is changing. (b) An object can have a constant speed even its velocity is changing. (c) An object can have a zero velocity even its acceleration is not zero. (d) An object subjected to a constant acceleration can reverse its velocity.

(a) False. Constant velocity means both magnitude and direction are unchanged, so the speed, which is the magnitude of velocity, cannot change. (b) True. In uniform circular motion the speed stays constant while the direction of velocity changes all the time. (c) True. At the highest point of a vertical throw the velocity is zero for an instant, but the acceleration due to gravity is still acting. (d) True. An object thrown upward under constant acceleration due to gravity rises, stops, and then falls back, so its velocity reverses.

3.5. A man standing on the top of a tower throws a ball straight up with initial velocity vi, and at the same time throws a second ball straight downward with the same speed. Which ball will have larger speed when it strikes the ground? Ignore air friction.

Both balls strike the ground with the same speed. The ball thrown upward returns to the level of the tower top with the same speed vi, now directed downward, which is exactly the starting condition of the ball thrown downward. From there both fall through the same height under the same gravity, so both reach the ground with speed sqrt(vi^2 + 2 g h). Air friction is ignored.

3.6. Explain the circumstances in which the velocity v and acceleration a of a car are (i) Parallel (ii) Anti-parallel (iii) Perpendicular to one another (iv) v is zero but a is not zero (v) a is zero but v is not zero.

(i) Parallel: velocity and acceleration point in the same direction, for example a car speeding up on a straight road. (ii) Anti-parallel: acceleration points opposite to velocity, for example a car braking on a straight road. (iii) Perpendicular to one another: acceleration is at right angles to velocity, for example a car going round a bend at constant speed, where the acceleration is centripetal. (iv) v is zero but a is not zero: at the instant a ball thrown upward reaches its highest point, or at the instant a car starts from rest. (v) a is zero but v is not zero: a car moving with uniform velocity on a straight road, with no net force acting.

3.7. Motion with constant velocity is a special case of motion with constant acceleration. Is this statement true? Discuss.

True. Motion with constant velocity is motion with a constant acceleration of zero. Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity; if the velocity does not change, its rate of change is zero, which is a constant value. All the equations of uniformly accelerated motion then reduce to the uniform-motion results, for example distance = velocity x time.

3.8. Find the change in momentum for an object subjected to a given force for a given time and state law of motion in terms of momentum.

The change in momentum is the product of the force and the time for which it acts: change in momentum = F x t. This is the impulse of the force. Newton's second law of motion in terms of momentum states that the force acting on a body is equal to the rate of change of its momentum: F = change in momentum / time taken.

3.9. Define impulse and show that how it is related to linear momentum?

Impulse is the product of a force and the time for which it acts: Impulse = F x t. By Newton's second law, F = m a = m (vf - vi) / t, so F x t = m vf - m vi, which is the change in linear momentum. Impulse is therefore equal to the change in linear momentum, and its unit is N s, the same as kg ms^-1.

3.10. State the law of conservation of linear momentum, pointing out the importance of isolated system. Explain, why under certain conditions, the law is useful even though the system is not completely isolated?

The law of conservation of linear momentum states that the total linear momentum of an isolated system remains constant, provided no external force acts on the system. An isolated system is important because only then is the total external impulse zero, so the total momentum cannot change. The law is still useful for systems that are not completely isolated when the external forces are negligible during a very short interaction, such as a collision or an explosion, where the large internal forces act for such a short time that the external impulse is negligibly small, or when the external forces cancel out in the direction being considered.

3.11. Explain the difference between elastic and inelastic collisions. Explain how would a bouncing ball behave in each case? Give plausible reasons for the fact that K.E is not conserved in most cases?

In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved, and the colliding bodies separate without permanent change. In an inelastic collision momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not conserved; part of it is changed into heat, sound and energy of deformation. A bouncing ball in a nearly elastic bounce returns almost to its original height each time, while in an inelastic bounce it returns to a lower height each time and soon stops bouncing. Kinetic energy is not conserved in most real collisions because real bodies deform, vibrate and warm up on impact, so kinetic energy is converted into internal energy, sound and heat.

3.12. Explain what is meant by projectile motion. Derive expressions for (a) the time of flight (b) the range of projectile. Show that the range of projectile is maximum when projectile is thrown at an angle of 45 degrees with the horizontal.

Projectile motion is the motion of a body thrown into the air which then moves under the action of gravity alone, following a parabolic path. (a) Time of flight: the vertical motion gives T = 2 vi sin(theta) / g, where vi is the initial speed and theta the angle of projection. (b) Range of projectile: the horizontal distance covered in this time is R = vi cos(theta) x T = vi^2 sin(2 theta) / g. The range is maximum when sin(2 theta) is maximum, that is, when sin(2 theta) = 1, which gives 2 theta = 90 degrees, so theta = 45 degrees.

3.13. At what point or points in its path does a projectile have its minimum speed, its maximum speed?

The speed of a projectile is minimum at the highest point of its path, because there its vertical component of velocity is zero and only the horizontal component, vi cos(theta), remains. The speed is maximum at the points of projection and of landing (at the same level), where the speed is the full initial speed vi, because the vertical component is largest there in size.

3.14. Each of the following questions is followed by four answers, one of which is correct answer. Identify that answer. (i) What is meant by a ballistic trajectory? (a) The paths followed by an un-powered and unguided projectile. (b) The path followed by the powered and unguided projectile. (c) The path followed by un-powered but guided projectile. (d) The path followed by powered and guided projectile. (ii) What happens when a system of two bodies undergoes an elastic collision? (a) The momentum of the system changes. (b) The momentum of the system does not change. (c) The bodies come to rest after collision. (d) The energy conservation law is violated.

(i) The correct answer is (a): a ballistic trajectory is the path followed by an un-powered and unguided projectile, which moves under gravity alone after launch. (ii) The correct answer is (b): when a system of two bodies undergoes an elastic collision, the momentum of the system does not change; in fact both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved, so the bodies do not have to come to rest and no conservation law is violated.

Its velocity is zero but its acceleration is still -g

An object can have constant speed while its velocity is changing
An object under constant acceleration can never reverse its velocity

mcqs.q: In which situation are the velocity v and acceleration a of a car perpendicular to one another?
options: A car speeding up on a straight road
A car going round a bend at constant speed
A car braking on a straight road
mcqs.why: Going round a bend at constant speed, the acceleration is centripetal, directed towards the centre of the bend, at right angles to the velocity. Speeding up gives a parallel to v, and braking gives a anti-parallel to v.
