mcqs.q: The law of conservation of linear momentum applies to an isolated system. Why is an isolated system important?
options: Because only then is the total external impulse zero, so the total momentum cannot change
Because internal forces disappear in an isolated system
Because the masses stay constant only in an isolated system
Because kinetic energy is conserved only in an isolated system
mcqs.why: The law states that the total linear momentum of an isolated system remains constant provided no external force acts. Only in an isolated system is the total external impulse zero, so the total momentum cannot change.

mcqs.q: In an inelastic collision, which quantity is NOT conserved?
mcqs.why: In an inelastic collision momentum is conserved but kinetic energy is not; part of it changes into heat, sound and energy of deformation. In an elastic collision both momentum and kinetic energy are conserved.

mcqs.q: The range of a projectile is maximum when it is thrown at what angle with the horizontal?
mcqs.why: The range is R = vi^2 sin(2 theta) / g. It is maximum when sin(2 theta) is maximum, that is sin(2 theta) = 1, which gives 2 theta = 90 degrees, so theta = 45 degrees.

mcqs.q: At which point of its path does a projectile have its minimum speed?
options: At the highest point of its path
Halfway down from the highest point
mcqs.why: The speed is minimum at the highest point, because there the vertical component of velocity is zero and only the horizontal component, vi cos(theta), remains. The speed is maximum at projection and at landing at the same level.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
3.1. A helicopter is ascending vertically at the rate of 19.6 ms^-1. When it is at a height of 156.8 m above the ground, a stone is dropped. How long does the stone take to reach the ground?

Step 1: The stone starts with the helicopter's upward velocity, 19.6 ms^-1 upward. Take downward as positive: initial velocity u = -19.6 ms^-1, acceleration a = +9.8 ms^-2, distance s = 156.8 m.

Step 2: Use s = u t + (1/2) a t^2: 156.8 = -19.6 t + 4.9 t^2.

Step 3: Divide by 4.9: 32 = -4 t + t^2, so t^2 - 4 t - 32 = 0.

Step 4: Factorise: (t - 8)(t + 4) = 0. The positive root is t = 8 s.

Answer: 8.0 s (as printed in the book).

3.2. Using the following data, draw a velocity-time graph for a short journey on a straight road of a motorbike. Velocity (ms^-1): 0, 10, 20, 20, 20, 20, 0 at Time (s): 0, 30, 60, 90, 120, 150, 180. Use the graph to calculate (a) the initial acceleration (b) the final acceleration and (c) the total distance travelled by the motorcyclist.

Step 1: Graph instruction: plot velocity on the vertical axis against time on the horizontal axis, join the points (0,0), (30,10), (60,20), (90,20), (120,20), (150,20), (180,0) with straight lines. The graph rises steadily to 20 ms^-1, stays level, then falls to zero.

Step 2: (a) Initial acceleration = slope of the rising part = (20 - 0) / (60 - 0) = 20 / 60 = 0.33 ms^-2.

Step 3: (b) Final acceleration = slope of the falling part = (0 - 20) / (180 - 150) = -20 / 30 = -0.67 ms^-2.

Step 4: (c) Total distance = area under the velocity-time graph. From 0 to 30 s: (1/2) x 30 x 10 = 150 m. From 30 to 60 s: (1/2) x (10 + 20) x 30 = 450 m.

Step 5: From 60 to 150 s: 20 x 90 = 1800 m. From 150 to 180 s: (1/2) x 20 x 30 = 300 m.

Step 6: Total = 150 + 450 + 1800 + 300 = 2700 m = 2.7 km.

Answer: (a) 0.33 ms^-2, (b) -0.67 ms^-2, (c) 2.7 km (as printed in the book).

3.3. A proton moving with speed of 1.0 x 10^7 ms^-1 passes through a 0.020 cm thick sheet of paper and emerges with a speed of 2.0 x 10^6 ms^-1. Assuming uniform deceleration, find retardation and time taken to pass through the paper.

Step 1: Thickness in metres: s = 0.020 cm = 2.0 x 10^-4 m.

Step 2: Use vf^2 - vi^2 = 2 a s: (2.0 x 10^6)^2 - (1.0 x 10^7)^2 = 2 a x (2.0 x 10^-4).

Step 3: Left side: 4.0 x 10^12 - 1.0 x 10^14 = -9.6 x 10^13.

Step 4: So a = (-9.6 x 10^13) / (4.0 x 10^-4) = -2.4 x 10^17 ms^-2. The retardation is 2.4 x 10^17 ms^-2.

Step 5: Time: t = (vf - vi) / a = (2.0 x 10^6 - 1.0 x 10^7) / (-2.4 x 10^17) = (-8.0 x 10^6) / (-2.4 x 10^17) = 3.3 x 10^-11 s.

Answer: 2.4 x 10^17 ms^-2, 3.3 x 10^-11 s (as printed in the book).

3.4. Two masses m1 and m2 are initially at rest with a spring compressed between them. What is the ratio of the magnitude of their velocities after the spring has been released?

Step 1: Initially the total momentum is zero, and no external force acts while the spring pushes the masses apart, so total momentum stays zero.

Step 2: After release: m1 v1 + m2 v2 = 0 (with opposite signs for opposite directions).

Step 3: In magnitudes: m1 v1 = m2 v2, so v1 / v2 = m2 / m1.

Answer: v1 / v2 = m2 / m1 (as printed in the book).

3.5. An amoeba of mass 1.0 x 10^-12 kg propels itself through water by blowing a jet of water through a tiny orifice. The amoeba ejects water with a speed of 1.0 x 10^-4 ms^-1 and at a rate of 1.0 x 10^-13 kgs^-1. Assume that the water is being continuously replenished so that the mass of the amoeba remains the same. (a) If there were no force on amoeba other than the reaction force caused by the emerging jet, what would be the acceleration of the amoeba? (b) If amoeba moves with constant velocity through water, what is force of surrounding water (exclusively of jet) on the amoeba?

Step 1: Thrust of the jet = rate of mass ejection x ejection speed = (1.0 x 10^-13 kgs^-1) x (1.0 x 10^-4 ms^-1) = 1.0 x 10^-17 N.

Step 2: (a) Acceleration = force / mass = (1.0 x 10^-17) / (1.0 x 10^-12) = 1.0 x 10^-5 ms^-2.

Step 3: (b) At constant velocity the net force is zero, so the resistance of the surrounding water must exactly balance the thrust: 1.0 x 10^-17 N, opposite to the thrust.

Answer: (a) 1.0 x 10^-5 ms^-2 (b) 1.0 x 10^-17 N (as printed in the book).

3.6. A boy places a fire cracker of negligible mass in an empty can of 40 g mass. He plugs the end with a wooden block of mass 200 g. After igniting the firecracker, he throws the can straight up. It explodes at the top of its path. If the block shoots out with a speed of 3.0 ms^-1, how fast will the can be going?

Step 1: At the top of its path the can and block are momentarily at rest, so the total momentum just before the explosion is zero.

Step 2: After the explosion, momentum is conserved: (0.200 kg x 3.0 ms^-1) + (0.040 kg x v) = 0.

Step 3: So 0.040 v = -0.600, giving v = -15 ms^-1. The minus sign means the can moves in the opposite direction to the block.

Answer: 15 ms^-1 (as printed in the book).

3.7. An electron (m = 9.1 x 10^-31 kg) travelling at 2.0 x 10^7 ms^-1 undergoes a head on collision with a hydrogen atom (m = 1.67 x 10^-27 kg) which is initially at rest. Assuming the collision to be perfectly elastic and a motion to be along a straight line, find the velocity of hydrogen atom.

Step 1: For a perfectly elastic head-on collision with the target at rest, the velocity of the target is v2 = [2 m1 / (m1 + m2)] x u1.

Step 2: v2 = [2 x 9.1 x 10^-31 / (9.1 x 10^-31 + 1.67 x 10^-27)] x 2.0 x 10^7.

Step 3: The denominator is about 1.671 x 10^-27, so the bracket is (1.82 x 10^-30) / (1.671 x 10^-27) = 1.089 x 10^-3.

Step 4: v2 = 1.089 x 10^-3 x 2.0 x 10^7 = 2.18 x 10^4 ms^-1, about 2.2 x 10^4 ms^-1.

Answer: 2.2 x 10^4 ms^-1 (as printed in the book).

3.8. A truck weighing 2500 kg and moving with a velocity of 21 ms^-1 collides with stationary car weighing 1000 kg. The truck and the car move together after the impact. Calculate their common velocity.

Step 1: This is a completely inelastic collision, so momentum is conserved but the bodies move together afterwards.

Step 2: Initial momentum = 2500 x 21 + 1000 x 0 = 52,500 kg ms^-1.

Step 3: Total mass afterwards = 2500 + 1000 = 3500 kg.

Step 4: Common velocity = 52,500 / 3500 = 15 ms^-1.

Answer: 15 ms^-1 (as printed in the book).

3.9. Two blocks of masses 2.0 kg and 0.50 kg are attached at the two ends of a compressed spring. The elastic potential energy stored in the spring is 10 J. Find the velocities of the blocks if the spring delivers its energy to the blocks when released.

Step 1: Momentum is conserved and starts at zero: 2.0 v1 + 0.50 v2 = 0, so v2 = -4 v1.

Step 2: Energy is conserved: (1/2) x 2.0 x v1^2 + (1/2) x 0.50 x v2^2 = 10 J.

Step 3: Substitute v2 = -4 v1: v1^2 + 0.25 x 16 v1^2 = 10, so 5 v1^2 = 10 and v1^2 = 2.

Step 4: v1 = 1.4 ms^-1 and v2 = -4 x 1.4 = -5.6 ms^-1. The opposite signs show the blocks move in opposite directions.

Answer: 1.4 ms^-1, -5.6 ms^-1 (as printed in the book).

3.10. A foot ball is thrown upward with an angle of 30 degrees with respect to the horizontal. To throw a 40 m pass what must be the initial speed of the ball?

Step 1: Range R = vi^2 sin(2 theta) / g, with R = 40 m and theta = 30 degrees, so sin(2 theta) = sin(60 degrees) = 0.866.

Step 2: vi^2 = R g / sin(2 theta) = (40 x 9.8) / 0.866 = 392 / 0.866 = 452.7.

Step 3: vi = sqrt(452.7) = 21.3 ms^-1, about 21 ms^-1.

Answer: 21 ms^-1 (as printed in the book).

3.11. A ball is thrown horizontally from a height of 10 m with velocity of 21 ms^-1. How far off it hit the ground and with what velocity?

Step 1: Time to fall: vertical motion starts from rest, h = (1/2) g t^2, so t = sqrt(2 h / g) = sqrt(20 / 9.8) = sqrt(2.04) = 1.43 s.

Step 2: Horizontal distance = horizontal speed x time = 21 x 1.43 = 30.0 m.

Step 3: Vertical speed at the ground: vy = g t = 9.8 x 1.43 = 14.0 ms^-1. Horizontal speed is still 21 ms^-1.

Step 4: Resultant speed = sqrt(21^2 + 14.0^2) = sqrt(441 + 196) = sqrt(637) = 25.2 ms^-1, about 25 ms^-1.

Answer: 30 m, 25 ms^-1 (as printed in the book).

3.12. A bomber dropped a bomb at a height of 490 m when its velocity along the horizontal was 300 kmh^-1. (a) How long was it in air? (b) At what distance from the point vertically below the bomber at the instant the bomb was dropped, did it strike the ground?

Step 1: Horizontal speed in ms^-1: 300 kmh^-1 = 300 x 1000 / 3600 = 83.33 ms^-1.

Step 2: (a) Time in air from vertical fall: t = sqrt(2 h / g) = sqrt(980 / 9.8) = sqrt(100) = 10 s.

Step 3: (b) Horizontal distance = 83.33 x 10 = 833 m.

Answer: 10 s, 833 m (as printed in the book).

3.13. Find the angle of projection of a projectile for which its maximum height and horizontal range are equal.

Step 1: Maximum height H = vi^2 sin^2(theta) / (2 g). Horizontal range R = vi^2 sin(2 theta) / g = 2 vi^2 sin(theta) cos(theta) / g.

Step 2: Set H = R: vi^2 sin^2(theta) / (2 g) = 2 vi^2 sin(theta) cos(theta) / g.

Step 3: Cancel vi^2, sin(theta) and g: sin(theta) / 2 = 2 cos(theta), so sin(theta) = 4 cos(theta).

Step 4: tan(theta) = 4, so theta = tan^-1(4) = 76 degrees.

Answer: 76 degrees (as printed in the book).

3.14. Prove that for angles of projection, which exceed or fall short of 45 degrees by equal amounts, the ranges are equal.

Step 1: Range at angle theta: R = vi^2 sin(2 theta) / g.

Step 2: For the angle 45 degrees + alpha: sin(2 theta) = sin(90 degrees + 2 alpha) = cos(2 alpha).

Step 3: For the angle 45 degrees - alpha: sin(2 theta) = sin(90 degrees - 2 alpha) = cos(2 alpha).

Step 4: Both angles give the same value of sin(2 theta), so both give the same range, R = vi^2 cos(2 alpha) / g.

Answer: the ranges are equal.

3.15. A SLBM (submarine launched ballistic missile) is fired from a distance of 3000 km. If the Earth is considered flat and the angle of launch is 45 degrees with horizontal, find the velocity with which the missile is fired and the time taken by SLBM to hit the target.

Step 1: Range R = 3000 km = 3.0 x 10^6 m, angle theta = 45 degrees, so sin(2 theta) = sin(90 degrees) = 1.

Step 2: R = vi^2 / g, so vi^2 = R g = 3.0 x 10^6 x 9.8 = 2.94 x 10^7.

Step 3: vi = sqrt(2.94 x 10^7) = 5422 ms^-1 = 5.42 kms^-1.

Step 4: Time of flight T = 2 vi sin(theta) / g = 2 x 5422 x 0.7071 / 9.8 = 7668 / 9.8 = 782 s.

Step 5: 782 s = 13.0 minutes, about 13 min.

Answer: 5.42 kms^-1, 13 min (as printed in the book).

mcqs.q: A helicopter ascends vertically at 19.6 ms^-1. At a height of 156.8 m a stone is dropped from it. How long does the stone take to reach the ground?
mcqs.why: Working: the stone starts with the upward velocity 19.6 ms^-1. Taking downward as positive: 156.8 = -19.6 t + 4.9 t^2. Dividing by 4.9: t^2 - 4 t - 32 = 0, which factorises as (t - 8)(t + 4) = 0. The positive root is t = 8.0 s.

mcqs.q: A motorbike's velocity-time graph rises to 20 ms^-1 in 60 s, stays level until 150 s, then falls to zero at 180 s. The total distance travelled is:
mcqs.why: Working: distance is the area under the graph. Parts: (1/2) x 30 x 10 = 150 m; (1/2) x (10 + 20) x 30 = 450 m; 20 x 90 = 1800 m; (1/2) x 20 x 30 = 300 m. Total = 150 + 450 + 1800 + 300 = 2700 m = 2.7 km.

mcqs.q: A proton moving at 1.0 x 10^7 ms^-1 passes through a 0.020 cm thick sheet of paper and emerges at 2.0 x 10^6 ms^-1. Its retardation, assuming uniform deceleration, is:
A fire cracker in a can of mass 40 g explodes at the top of its path, shooting out a wooden block of mass 200 g at 3.0 ms^-1. How fast does the can move?
options: 15 ms^-1, in the opposite direction to the block
mcqs.why: Working: at the top the total momentum is zero, and it stays zero after the explosion: 0.200 x 3.0 + 0.040 x v = 0. Now 0.200 x 3.0 = 0.600, so v = -0.600 / 0.040 = -15 ms^-1. The minus sign shows the can moves opposite to the block, at 15 ms^-1.

mcqs.q: An electron (9.1 x 10^-31 kg) travelling at 2.0 x 10^7 ms^-1 makes a perfectly elastic head-on collision with a hydrogen atom (1.67 x 10^-27 kg) at rest. The velocity of the hydrogen atom after the collision is about:
mcqs.why: Working: for an elastic head-on collision with the target at rest, v2 = [2 m1 / (m1 + m2)] x u1. The bracket is (2 x 9.1 x 10^-31) / (1.671 x 10^-27) = 1.089 x 10^-3. Then v2 = 1.089 x 10^-3 x 2.0 x 10^7 = 2.18 x 10^4 ms^-1, about 2.2 x 10^4 ms^-1.

mcqs.q: A truck of 2500 kg moving at 21 ms^-1 collides with a stationary car of 1000 kg and the two move together. Their common velocity is:
mcqs.why: Working: initial momentum = 2500 x 21 = 52500 kg ms^-1. Total mass afterwards = 2500 + 1000 = 3500 kg. Common velocity = 52500 / 3500 = 15 ms^-1.

mcqs.q: Blocks of 2.0 kg and 0.50 kg at the ends of a compressed spring are released; the spring stores 10 J. The speeds of the blocks are:
options: 1.4 ms^-1 and 5.6 ms^-1, in opposite directions
5.6 ms^-1 and 1.4 ms^-1, in the same direction
mcqs.why: Working: momentum stays zero: 2.0 v1 + 0.50 v2 = 0, so v2 = -4 v1. Energy: v1^2 + 0.25 x 16 v1^2 = 10, that is 5 v1^2 = 10, so v1^2 = 2 and v1 = 1.4 ms^-1. Then v2 = -4 x 1.4 = -5.6 ms^-1; the blocks move oppositely at 1.4 and 5.6 ms^-1.

mcqs.q: To throw a 40 m pass at an angle of 30 degrees to the horizontal, a football must be thrown with initial speed:
mcqs.why: Working: R = vi^2 sin(2 theta) / g with sin(60 degrees) = 0.866. So vi^2 = 40 x 9.8 / 0.866 = 392 / 0.866 = 452.7. Then vi = sqrt(452.7) = 21.3 ms^-1, about 21 ms^-1.

mcqs.q: A bomber flying horizontally at 300 km h^-1 drops a bomb from a height of 490 m. How long is the bomb in the air?
mcqs.why: Working: the time depends only on the vertical fall: t = sqrt(2 h / g) = sqrt(980 / 9.8) = sqrt(100) = 10 s. In this time the bomb travels 83.33 x 10 = 833 m horizontally.

mcqs.q: For which angle of projection are the maximum height and the horizontal range of a projectile equal?
mcqs.why: Working: setting H = vi^2 sin^2(theta) / (2 g) equal to R = 2 vi^2 sin(theta) cos(theta) / g gives sin(theta) / 2 = 2 cos(theta), so tan(theta) = 4 and theta = 76 degrees.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.notes_html:
4.1. A person holds a bag of groceries while standing still, talking to a friend. A car is stationary with its engine running. From the stand point of work, how are these two situations similar?

In both cases no work is done in the physics sense. The person holds the bag still, so the upward force acts through zero displacement, and work = force x displacement = 0. The stationary car also has zero displacement, so the engine does no work on the car, even though it burns fuel and gives out heat. The similarity is that energy is being spent (by muscles, by fuel) but no mechanical work is done because nothing moves.

4.2. Calculate the work done in kilo joules in lifting a mass of 10 kg (at a steady velocity) through a vertical height of 10 m.

Work done against gravity = m g h = 10 kg x 9.8 ms^-2 x 10 m = 980 J. In kilo joules this is 0.98 kJ, about 1.0 kJ. At a steady velocity the lifting force equals the weight, so no extra work is done in accelerating the mass.

4.3. A force F acts through a distance L. The force is then increased to 3 F, and then acts through a further distance of 2 L. Draw the work diagram to scale.

Draw a force-distance graph with distance on the horizontal axis and force on the vertical axis. From distance 0 to L the force is F, giving a rectangle of area F x L. From distance L to 3L the force is 3F, giving a rectangle of area 3F x 2L = 6 F L. The total work is the total area under the graph: F L + 6 F L = 7 F L. The second rectangle is three times as high and twice as wide as the first.

4.4. In which case is more work done? When a 50 kg bag of books is lifted through 50 cm, or when a 50 kg crate is pushed through 2 m across the floor with a force of 50 N?

More work is done in lifting the bag. Lifting: work = weight x height = 50 x 9.8 x 0.50 = 245 J. Pushing: work = force x distance = 50 N x 2 m = 100 J. Although the pushing distance is larger, the lifting force (the weight, 490 N) is much larger than the pushing force, so the work done in lifting, 245 J, is greater than the 100 J done in pushing.

4.5. An object has 1 J of potential energy. Explain what does it mean?

It means the body has the capacity to do 1 joule of work by virtue of its position, for example by falling back to the chosen reference level. One joule of potential energy is stored energy that can be converted into kinetic energy or used to do work.

4.6. A ball of mass m is held at a height h1 above a table. The table top is at a height h2 above the floor. One student says that the ball has potential energy mgh1 but another says that it is mg (h1 + h2). Who is correct?

Both students can be correct, because potential energy is measured from an arbitrary reference level. Measured from the table top, the ball is at height h1, so its potential energy is m g h1. Measured from the floor, the ball is at height h1 + h2, so its potential energy is m g (h1 + h2). Only differences of potential energy have physical meaning; the zero level can be chosen freely.

4.7. When a rocket re-enters the atmosphere, its nose cone becomes very hot. Where does this heat energy come from?

The heat energy comes from the mechanical energy of the rocket itself. As the rocket rushes through the air, air friction (drag) does negative work on it, converting its kinetic energy, and some of its potential energy, into heat energy, which warms the nose cone and the air around it.

4.8. What sort of energy is in the following: (a) Compressed spring (b) Water in a high dam (c) A moving car

(a) Compressed spring: elastic potential energy, stored by the deformation of the spring. (b) Water in a high dam: gravitational potential energy, stored by virtue of its height above the turbines. (c) A moving car: kinetic energy, possessed by virtue of its motion.

4.9. A girl drops a cup from a certain height, which breaks into pieces. What energy changes are involved?

First the cup has gravitational potential energy. As it falls, this changes into kinetic energy. On hitting the ground, the kinetic energy changes into sound energy, heat energy, and the energy needed to break the bonds of the material, that is, the energy of fracture and deformation of the pieces, with a little kinetic energy left in the flying pieces.

4.10. A boy uses a catapult to throw a stone which accidentally smashes a green house window. List the possible energy changes.

The boy's muscles do work to stretch the rubber of the catapult, storing elastic potential energy in it. On release, this changes into kinetic energy of the stone. As the stone flies, kinetic energy changes partly into gravitational potential energy. On striking the window, the kinetic energy changes into sound energy, heat energy, and the work done in breaking the glass, with kinetic energy carried away by the glass pieces.

mcqs.q: A person holds a bag of groceries while standing still, and a car stands stationary with its engine running. From the standpoint of work, how are the two situations similar?
options: In both, a large force does a large amount of work
In both, no mechanical work is done because the displacement is zero, even though energy is being spent
In both, work is done against gravity only
In both, the work done equals the fuel or food energy used
mcqs.why: In both cases no work is done in the physics sense: work = force x displacement, and the displacement is zero. The person's muscles spend energy holding the bag, and the car's engine burns fuel, but with nothing moving, no mechanical work is done.

mcqs.q: Calculate the work done in lifting a mass of 10 kg at a steady velocity through a vertical height of 10 m.
mcqs.why: Working: at a steady velocity the lifting force equals the weight, so work done against gravity = m g h = 10 x 9.8 x 10 = 980 J. In kilojoules this is 0.98 kJ, about 1.0 kJ.

mcqs.q: A force F acts through a distance L. The force is then increased to 3F and acts through a further distance of 2L. The total work done, from the work diagram, is:
mcqs.why: Working: the work is the area under the force-distance graph. First rectangle: F x L. Second rectangle: 3F x 2L = 6 F L. Total work = F L + 6 F L = 7 F L.

mcqs.q: In which case is more work done: lifting a 50 kg bag of books through 50 cm, or pushing a 50 kg crate through 2 m across the floor with a force of 50 N?
options: Pushing the crate, because the distance is larger
Lifting the bag: 245 J against 100 J
Pushing the crate: 250 J against 100 J
mcqs.why: Working: lifting work = weight x height = 50 x 9.8 x 0.50 = 245 J. Pushing work = force x distance = 50 x 2 = 100 J. Although the pushing distance is larger, the lifting force (the weight, 490 N) is much larger, so more work is done in lifting.

mcqs.q: An object has 1 J of potential energy. What does this mean?
options: It is moving with a kinetic energy of 1 J
It has used up 1 J of energy
It can fall a distance of 1 m
It has the capacity to do 1 joule of work by virtue of its position
mcqs.why: Potential energy is stored energy. One joule of potential energy means the body has the capacity to do 1 joule of work by virtue of its position, for example by falling back to the chosen reference level, converting the stored energy into kinetic energy or work.

mcqs.q: A ball of mass m is held at height h1 above a table whose top is h2 above the floor. One student says its potential energy is m g h1, another says m g (h1 + h2). Who is correct?
options: Both can be correct, because potential energy is measured from an arbitrary reference level
Neither; potential energy cannot be measured from a table
mcqs.why: Measured from the table top the ball is at height h1, giving m g h1; measured from the floor it is at height h1 + h2, giving m g (h1 + h2). Only differences of potential energy have physical meaning, and the zero level can be chosen freely, so both students can be correct.

mcqs.q: When a rocket re-enters the atmosphere, its nose cone becomes very hot. Where does this heat energy come from?
options: From the rocket's fuel burning in the atmosphere
From the Sun heating the nose cone
From the mechanical energy of the rocket itself, converted by air friction
From the heat of the upper atmosphere
mcqs.why: The heat energy comes from the mechanical energy of the rocket itself. As it rushes through the air, air friction (drag) does negative work on it, converting its kinetic energy, and some of its potential energy, into heat energy in the nose cone and the surrounding air.

mcqs.q: What sort of energy is stored in the water of a high dam?
mcqs.why: Water in a high dam has gravitational potential energy, stored by virtue of its height above the turbines. By comparison, a compressed spring stores elastic potential energy, and a moving car has kinetic energy.

mcqs.q: A girl drops a cup, which breaks into pieces on the ground. What energy changes are involved?
options: Kinetic energy changes into potential energy, then into sound
Potential energy stays constant and kinetic energy becomes heat only
Chemical energy changes directly into sound energy
Gravitational potential energy changes into kinetic energy, which on impact becomes sound, heat and the energy of breaking the material
mcqs.why: First the cup has gravitational potential energy. As it falls this becomes kinetic energy. On hitting the ground the kinetic energy changes into sound energy, heat energy and the energy needed to break the bonds of the material, with a little kinetic energy left in the flying pieces.

mcqs.q: A boy stretches a catapult and throws a stone. The elastic potential energy stored in the stretched rubber changes into:
options: Gravitational potential energy of the rubber
mcqs.why: The boy's muscles do work to stretch the rubber, storing elastic potential energy in it. On release this changes into kinetic energy of the stone; as the stone flies, some kinetic energy becomes gravitational potential energy, and on striking a window it becomes sound, heat and the work of breaking glass.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
4.1. A man pushes a lawn mower with a 40 N force directed at an angle of 20 degrees downward from the horizontal. Find the work done by the man as he cuts a strip of grass 20 m long.

Step 1: Only the horizontal component of the force does work along the strip: F cos(theta) = 40 x cos(20 degrees).

Step 2: cos(20 degrees) = 0.9397, so the horizontal component is 40 x 0.9397 = 37.59 N.

Step 3: Work = component along displacement x distance = 37.59 x 20 = 751.8 J.

Answer: 7.5 x 10^2 J (as printed in the book).

4.2. A rain drop (m = 3.35 x 10^-5 kg) falls vertically at a constant speed under the influence of the forces of gravity and friction. In falling through 100 m, how much work is done by (a) gravity and (b) friction.

Step 1: (a) Work by gravity = weight x distance fallen = m g h = 3.35 x 10^-5 x 9.8 x 100.

Step 2: Work by gravity = 0.03283 J, about 0.0328 J. Gravity acts in the direction of motion, so this work is positive.

Step 3: (b) At constant speed the net work is zero, so the work by friction must cancel the work by gravity.

Step 4: Work by friction = -0.0328 J. Friction acts opposite to the motion, so its work is negative.

Answer: (a) 0.0328 J (b) -0.0328 J (as printed in the book).

4.3. Ten bricks, each 6.0 cm thick and mass 1.5 kg, lie flat on a table. How much work is required to stack them one on the top of another?

Step 1: The first brick stays on the table and needs no lifting. The second brick is lifted by one thickness, the third by two thicknesses, and so on up to the tenth brick, lifted by nine thicknesses.

Step 2: Total height lifted, summed over bricks = 6.0 cm x (1 + 2 + ... + 9) = 0.06 m x 45 = 2.70 m.

Step 3: Work = m g x total height = 1.5 kg x 9.8 ms^-2 x 2.70 m = 39.7 J.

Answer: 40 J (as printed in the book).

4.4. A car of mass 800 kg travelling at 54 kmh^-1 is brought to rest in 60 metres. Find the average retarding force on the car. What has happened to original kinetic energy?

Step 1: Speed in ms^-1: 54 kmh^-1 = 54 x 1000 / 3600 = 15 ms^-1.

Step 2: By the work-energy principle, work done by the retarding force = loss of kinetic energy: F x s = (1/2) m v^2.

Step 3: F x 60 = (1/2) x 800 x 15^2 = 90,000 J.

Step 4: F = 90,000 / 60 = 1500 N.

Step 5: The original kinetic energy is converted into heat energy in the brakes, tyres and road, with a little sound energy.

Answer: 1500 N (as printed in the book).

4.5. A 1000 kg automobile at the top of an incline 10 metre high and 100 m long is released and rolls down the hill. What is its speed at the bottom of the incline if the average retarding force due to friction is 480 N?

Step 1: Potential energy at the top = m g h = 1000 x 9.8 x 10 = 98,000 J.

Step 2: Work done against friction along the incline = force x distance = 480 x 100 = 48,000 J.

Step 3: Kinetic energy at the bottom = 98,000 - 48,000 = 50,000 J.

Step 4: (1/2) m v^2 = 50,000, so v^2 = 2 x 50,000 / 1000 = 100.

Step 5: v = 10 ms^-1.

Answer: 10 ms^-1 (as printed in the book).

4.6. 100 m^3 of water is pumped from a reservoir into a tank, 10 m higher than the reservoir, in 20 minutes. If density of water is 1000 kg m^-3, find (a) the increase in P.E. (b) the power delivered by the pump.

Step 1: Mass of water = volume x density = 100 x 1000 = 100,000 kg.

Step 2: (a) Increase in potential energy = m g h = 100,000 x 9.8 x 10 = 9.8 x 10^6 J.

Step 3: (b) Time = 20 minutes = 1200 s. Power = energy / time = 9.8 x 10^6 / 1200 = 8167 W.

Step 4: In kilowatts this is 8.2 kW.

Answer: (a) 9.8 x 10^6 J (b) 8.2 kW (as printed in the book).

4.7. A force (thrust) of 400 N is required to overcome road friction and air resistance in propelling an automobile at 80 kmh^-1. What power (kW) must the engine develop?

Step 1: Speed in ms^-1: 80 kmh^-1 = 80 x 1000 / 3600 = 22.22 ms^-1.

Step 2: Power = force x velocity = 400 x 22.22 = 8889 W.

Step 3: In kilowatts: 8.9 kW.

Answer: 8.9 kW (as printed in the book).

4.8. How large a force is required to accelerate an electron (m = 9.1 x 10^-31 kg) from rest to a speed of 2.0 x 10^7 ms^-1 through a distance of 5.0 cm?

Step 1: By the work-energy principle: F x s = (1/2) m v^2.

Step 2: (1/2) m v^2 = (1/2) x 9.1 x 10^-31 x (2.0 x 10^7)^2 = (1/2) x 9.1 x 10^-31 x 4.0 x 10^14 = 1.82 x 10^-16 J.

Step 3: Distance s = 5.0 cm = 0.050 m, so F = 1.82 x 10^-16 / 0.050 = 3.64 x 10^-15 N.

Answer: 3.6 x 10^-15 N (as printed in the book).

4.9. A diver weighing 750 N dives from a board 10 m above the surface of a pool of water. Use the conservation of mechanical energy to find his speed at a point 5.0 m above the water surface, neglecting air friction.

Step 1: Take the point 5.0 m above the water as the level to find the speed. The diver has fallen 10 - 5.0 = 5.0 m from the board.

Step 2: Loss of potential energy = gain of kinetic energy: m g x 5.0 = (1/2) m v^2.

Step 3: The mass cancels: v^2 = 2 x 9.8 x 5.0 = 98.

Step 4: v = sqrt(98) = 9.9 ms^-1.

Answer: 9.9 ms^-1 (as printed in the book).

4.10. A child starts from rest at the top of a slide of height 4.0 m. (a) What is his speed at the bottom if the slide is frictionless? (b) If he reaches the bottom, with a speed of 6 ms^-1, what percentage of his total energy at the top of the slide is lost as a result of friction?

Step 1: (a) Without friction, potential energy at the top becomes kinetic energy at the bottom: (1/2) m v^2 = m g h.

Step 2: v^2 = 2 x 9.8 x 4.0 = 78.4, so v = sqrt(78.4) = 8.85 ms^-1, about 8.8 ms^-1.

Step 3: (b) With friction the speed at the bottom is 6 ms^-1. Kinetic energy at the bottom is proportional to v^2, so the fraction remaining is (6 / 8.85)^2 = 36 / 78.4 = 0.459.

Step 4: Fraction lost = 1 - 0.459 = 0.541, that is, 54 percent.

Answer: (a) 8.8 ms^-1 (b) 54% (as printed in the book).

mcqs.q: A man pushes a lawn mower with a 40 N force directed at 20 degrees downward from the horizontal, along a strip 20 m long. The work done by the man is:
mcqs.why: Working: only the horizontal component does work along the strip: F cos(20 degrees) = 40 x 0.9397 = 37.59 N. Work = 37.59 x 20 = 751.8 J, that is 7.5 x 10^2 J.

mcqs.q: A raindrop (m = 3.35 x 10^-5 kg) falls vertically at constant speed through 100 m. The work done by gravity is:
mcqs.why: Working: work by gravity = m g h = 3.35 x 10^-5 x 9.8 x 100 = 0.0328 J, positive because gravity acts along the motion. Since the speed is constant, the net work is zero, so the work done by friction is -0.0328 J.

mcqs.q: Ten bricks, each 6.0 cm thick and of mass 1.5 kg, lie flat on a table. The work required to stack them one on top of another is about:
mcqs.why: Working: the first brick needs no lifting; the others are lifted by 1, 2, ... 9 thicknesses. Total height summed = 0.06 x 45 = 2.70 m. Work = 1.5 x 9.8 x 2.70 = 39.7 J, about 40 J.

mcqs.q: A car of mass 800 kg travelling at 54 km h^-1 is brought to rest in 60 m. The average retarding force on the car is:
mcqs.why: Working: 54 km h^-1 = 15 ms^-1. Loss of kinetic energy = (1/2) x 800 x 225 = 90000 J. By the work-energy principle, F x 60 = 90000, so F = 90000 / 60 = 1500 N. The kinetic energy becomes heat in the brakes, tyres and road.

mcqs.q: A 1000 kg automobile rolls from rest down an incline 10 m high and 100 m long against an average friction force of 480 N. Its speed at the bottom is:
mcqs.why: Working: potential energy at the top = 1000 x 9.8 x 10 = 98000 J. Work against friction = 480 x 100 = 48000 J. Kinetic energy at the bottom = 98000 - 48000 = 50000 J. Then v^2 = 2 x 50000 / 1000 = 100, so v = 10 ms^-1.

mcqs.q: 100 m^3 of water is pumped into a tank 10 m higher in 20 minutes (density of water 1000 kg m^-3). The power delivered by the pump is:
mcqs.why: Working: mass of water = 100 x 1000 = 100000 kg. Increase in potential energy = 100000 x 9.8 x 10 = 9.8 x 10^6 J. Time = 20 x 60 = 1200 s. Power = 9.8 x 10^6 / 1200 = 8167 W, about 8.2 kW.

mcqs.q: A thrust of 400 N overcomes friction and air resistance to propel an automobile at 80 km h^-1. The power the engine must develop is:
mcqs.why: Working: speed = 80 x 1000 / 3600 = 22.22 ms^-1. Power = force x velocity = 400 x 22.22 = 8889 W, which is 8.9 kW.

mcqs.q: How large a force is required to accelerate an electron (m = 9.1 x 10^-31 kg) from rest to 2.0 x 10^7 ms^-1 through a distance of 5.0 cm?
mcqs.why: Working: kinetic energy gained = (1/2) x 9.1 x 10^-31 x 4.0 x 10^14 = 1.82 x 10^-16 J. By the work-energy principle, F = 1.82 x 10^-16 / 0.050 = 3.64 x 10^-15 N, about 3.6 x 10^-15 N.

mcqs.q: A diver weighing 750 N dives from a board 10 m above a pool. Neglecting air friction, his speed at a point 5.0 m above the water surface is:
mcqs.why: Working: he has fallen 10 - 5.0 = 5.0 m, so loss of potential energy equals gain of kinetic energy and the mass cancels: v^2 = 2 x 9.8 x 5.0 = 98. Then v = sqrt(98) = 9.9 ms^-1.

mcqs.q: A child starts from rest at the top of a frictionless slide 4.0 m high but, with friction, reaches the bottom at 6 ms^-1 instead of the frictionless value. The percentage of his total energy lost to friction is:
mcqs.why: Working: without friction v^2 = 2 x 9.8 x 4.0 = 78.4, so v = 8.85 ms^-1. With friction the fraction of energy remaining is 36 / 78.4 = 0.459. Fraction lost = 1 - 0.459 = 0.541, that is 54 percent.

lessons.notes_html:
5.1. Explain the difference between tangential velocity and the angular velocity. If one of these is given for a wheel of known radius, how will you find the other?

Tangential velocity is the linear velocity of a point on a rotating body, directed along the tangent to its circular path; it is different for points at different distances from the axis. Angular velocity is the rate at which the body turns, the angle swept per unit time; it is the same for every point of the body. They are related by v = r x omega, where r is the distance from the axis. So if v is given for a wheel of known radius, omega = v / r; if omega is given, v = r x omega.

5.2. Explain what is meant by centripetal force and why it must be furnished to an object if the object is to follow a circular path?

Centripetal force is the net force directed towards the centre of a circular path, which is needed to keep a body moving in a circle. A body in circular motion is constantly changing the direction of its velocity, so it has an acceleration towards the centre, a = v^2 / r. By Newton's second law this acceleration needs a force, F = m v^2 / r, towards the centre. Without such a force the body would move off in a straight line along the tangent, by Newton's first law. The centripetal force can be supplied by tension in a string, gravity, friction, or the normal reaction, depending on the situation.

5.3. What is meant by moment of inertia? Explain its significance.

Moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass. It measures how much a body resists a change in its state of rotation, and it depends not only on the mass of the body but also on how that mass is distributed about the axis of rotation: I = sum of m r^2 over the body. Its significance is that, just as a larger mass needs a larger force for the same linear acceleration, a larger moment of inertia needs a larger torque for the same angular acceleration, since torque = I x angular acceleration.

5.4. What is meant by angular momentum? Explain the law of conservation of angular momentum.

Angular momentum is the rotational analogue of linear momentum. For a body rotating about an axis it is L = I x omega, where I is the moment of inertia and omega the angular velocity; it is a vector along the axis of rotation. The law of conservation of angular momentum states that if no external torque acts on a system, its total angular momentum remains constant, because torque is the rate of change of angular momentum, so zero torque means zero change in angular momentum.

5.5. Show that orbital angular momentum L_o = m v r.

For a particle moving in a circle, the moment of inertia about the centre is I = m r^2, where m is its mass and r the radius of its path. Its angular velocity is omega = v / r, where v is its tangential speed. The orbital angular momentum is L = I x omega = m r^2 x (v / r) = m v r. This is also the magnitude of r cross p, since the radius and the momentum are perpendicular.

5.6. Describe what should be the minimum velocity, for a satellite, to orbit close to the Earth around it.

For a satellite in a low orbit close to the Earth, the gravitational force supplies the centripetal force: m v^2 / R = m g, where R is the radius of the Earth and g the acceleration due to gravity at its surface. So v = sqrt(g R) = sqrt(9.8 x 6.4 x 10^6) = 7.9 x 10^3 ms^-1, about 7.9 kms^-1. This is the minimum speed, the first cosmic velocity, for a satellite to stay in orbit just above the Earth.

5.7. State the direction of the following vectors in simple situations; angular momentum and angular velocity.

Angular velocity and angular momentum are vectors along the axis of rotation, in the direction given by the right-hand rule: curl the fingers of the right hand in the sense of rotation, and the thumb points along the vector. For example, a wheel rotating anticlockwise when seen from above has its angular velocity and angular momentum pointing upward; rotating clockwise, they point downward. For the Earth spinning from west to east, they point towards the north pole; for a satellite orbiting eastward above the equator, they also point north.

5.8. Explain why an object, orbiting the Earth, is said to be freely falling. Use your explanation to point out why objects appear weightless under certain circumstances.

A satellite in orbit is continuously falling towards the Earth under gravity, but it also has a large tangential velocity, so as it falls it keeps missing the Earth and follows a curved path around it. This is free fall, like a projectile that never lands. Objects inside the satellite appear weightless because they too are falling with the same acceleration as the satellite, so there is no contact force between them and the floor of the satellite to register as weight. The same happens in a freely falling lift: everything inside falls together, so apparent weight becomes zero.

5.9. When mud flies off the tyre of a moving bicycle, in what direction does it fly? Explain.

The mud flies off along the tangent to the tyre at the point where it leaves the surface. While it is on the tyre, the tyre supplies the centripetal force that keeps it moving in a circle. Once it comes off, no such force acts on it, so by Newton's first law it continues in a straight line in the direction of its velocity at that instant, which is the tangent to the tyre.

5.10. A disc and a hoop start moving down from the top of an inclined plane at the same time. Which one will be moving faster on reaching the bottom?

The disc will be moving faster on reaching the bottom. Both start with the same potential energy, but part of it goes into rotational kinetic energy. The hoop has a larger moment of inertia for the same mass and radius (I = m r^2, against I = (1/2) m r^2 for the disc), so more of its energy goes into rotation and less remains for translation. The acceleration down the plane is g sin(theta) / (1 + I / (m r^2)), which is (2/3) g sin(theta) for the disc but only (1/2) g sin(theta) for the hoop, so the disc accelerates more and arrives first.

5.11. Why does a diver change his body positions before and after diving in the pool?

A diver changes his body position to change his moment of inertia, and therefore his rate of rotation, while his angular momentum stays nearly constant in the air. Leaving the board he is stretched out, with a large moment of inertia and a slow rotation. In the air he tucks into a ball, reducing his moment of inertia, so his angular velocity increases and he somersaults quickly. Before entering the water he stretches out again, increasing his moment of inertia and slowing his rotation, so that he enters the water vertically.

5.12. A student holds two dumb-bells with stretched arms while sitting on a turn table. He is given a push until he is rotating at certain angular velocity. The student then pulls the dumb-bells towards his chest (Fig. 5.25). What will be the effect on rate of rotation?

The rate of rotation will increase. Pulling the dumb-bells towards his chest reduces the moment of inertia of the student about the vertical axis. Since no external torque acts, his angular momentum L = I x omega stays constant, so a smaller I must be balanced by a larger omega. The student therefore spins faster, as shown in Fig. 5.25, where the final angular velocity omega_f is greater than the initial omega_i.

5.13. Explain how many minimum number of geo-stationary satellites are required for global coverage of T.V transmission.

A single geo-stationary satellite, high above the equator, can see about one third of the Earth's surface, roughly 120 degrees of longitude. Three such satellites, spaced 120 degrees apart around the equator, are therefore the minimum number needed to cover the whole Earth (except the polar regions) for global television transmission, with each satellite handing over to the next as the Earth turns.

mcqs.q: How are the tangential velocity v and angular velocity omega of a point on a rotating wheel of radius r related, and how does each behave for different points of the wheel?
options: v = r omega; omega is the same for every point of the wheel, while v grows with r
v = omega / r; v is the same for every point
v = r / omega; both change from point to point
v = r omega^2; omega changes from point to point
mcqs.why: Tangential velocity is the linear velocity of a point, directed along the tangent; it differs for points at different distances from the axis. Angular velocity, the angle swept per unit time, is the same for every point of the body. They are related by v = r omega, so omega = v / r and v = r omega.

mcqs.q: Why must a centripetal force be furnished to an object moving in a circular path, and in which direction does it act?
options: To speed the object up; along the tangent
Because the direction of velocity keeps changing, giving an acceleration towards the centre; the force F = m v^2 / r acts towards the centre
Because the object tends to fly inward; away from the centre
mcqs.why: A body in circular motion constantly changes the direction of its velocity, so it has an acceleration a = v^2 / r towards the centre. By Newton's second law this needs a force F = m v^2 / r towards the centre, supplied by tension, gravity, friction or normal reaction as the case may be.

mcqs.q: What is meant by the moment of inertia of a body?
options: The product of its mass and velocity
The rotational analogue of mass: I = sum of m r^2, depending on the mass and its distribution about the axis
The torque needed to stop the body in one second
The angular momentum per unit mass
mcqs.why: Moment of inertia measures how much a body resists a change in its state of rotation. It depends not only on the mass but on how the mass is distributed about the axis: I = sum of m r^2. Just as a larger mass needs a larger force, a larger I needs a larger torque for the same angular acceleration.

mcqs.q: Show the result for the orbital angular momentum of a particle of mass m moving in a circle of radius r with speed v.
mcqs.why: Working: the moment of inertia about the centre is I = m r^2 and the angular velocity is omega = v / r. So L = I x omega = m r^2 x (v / r) = m v r, which is also the magnitude of r cross p since radius and momentum are perpendicular.

mcqs.q: What is the minimum speed for a satellite to orbit close to the Earth?
mcqs.why: Working: gravity supplies the centripetal force: m v^2 / R = m g, so v = sqrt(g R) = sqrt(9.8 x 6.4 x 10^6) = 7.9 x 10^3 ms^-1, about 7.9 km s^-1. This first cosmic velocity is the minimum speed to stay in a low orbit.

mcqs.q: Why do objects inside an orbiting satellite appear weightless?
options: Because there is no gravity in orbit
Because the satellite shields them from gravity
Because they are too far from the Earth for gravity to act
Because they are freely falling with the same acceleration as the satellite, so no contact force registers as weight
mcqs.why: A satellite in orbit is continuously falling towards the Earth but keeps missing it, following a curved path: it is in free fall. Objects inside fall with the same acceleration as the satellite, so there is no contact force between them and the floor to register as weight, just as in a freely falling lift.

mcqs.q: When mud flies off the tyre of a moving bicycle, in what direction does it fly?
options: Along the tangent to the tyre at the point where it leaves
Opposite to the motion of the bicycle
mcqs.why: While on the tyre, the mud is kept in a circle by the centripetal force from the tyre. Once it comes off, no such force acts, so by Newton's first law it continues in a straight line in the direction of its velocity at that instant, which is the tangent to the tyre.

mcqs.q: A disc and a hoop of the same mass and radius start together down an inclined plane. Which reaches the bottom faster, and why?
options: The hoop, because its moment of inertia is larger
They arrive together, having the same potential energy
The disc, because its smaller moment of inertia leaves more energy for translation
The hoop, because all its mass is at the rim
mcqs.why: Both start with the same potential energy, but part goes into rotation. The hoop has I = m r^2 against (1/2) m r^2 for the disc, so more of its energy goes into rotation. The disc's acceleration is (2/3) g sin(theta) against (1/2) g sin(theta) for the hoop, so the disc moves faster and arrives first.

mcqs.q: A diver tucks into a ball in mid-air and then stretches out before entering the water. Why?
options: Tucking increases his angular momentum so he spins faster
Tucking reduces his moment of inertia, so with angular momentum nearly constant his angular velocity increases; stretching out again slows the rotation
Stretching out increases his angular momentum for a vertical entry
Tucking reduces air resistance so he falls faster
mcqs.why: In the air the diver's angular momentum stays nearly constant. Tucking reduces his moment of inertia, so his angular velocity increases and he somersaults quickly. Stretching out before entry increases the moment of inertia again, slowing the rotation so he enters the water vertically.

mcqs.q: How many geo-stationary satellites are the minimum required for global coverage of TV transmission?
options: Three, spaced 120 degrees apart around the equator
mcqs.why: A single geo-stationary satellite above the equator can see about one third of the Earth's surface, roughly 120 degrees of longitude. Three such satellites, spaced 120 degrees apart around the equator, are therefore the minimum needed to cover the whole Earth except the polar regions.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
5.1. A tiny laser beam is directed from the Earth to the Moon. If the beam is to have a diameter of 2.50 m at the Moon, how small must divergence angle be for the beam? The distance of Moon from the Earth is 3.8 x 10^8 m.

Step 1: For a small angle, angle in radians = arc length / radius = diameter at the Moon / distance to the Moon.

Step 2: Angle = 2.50 / (3.8 x 10^8) = 6.58 x 10^-9 rad.

Answer: 6.6 x 10^-9 rad (as printed in the book).

5.2. A gramophone record turntable accelerates from rest to an angular velocity of 45.0 rev min^-1 in 1.60 s. What is its average angular acceleration?

Step 1: Final angular velocity in rad s^-1: 45.0 rev min^-1 = 45.0 x 2 pi / 60 = 4.712 rad s^-1.

Step 2: Average angular acceleration = change in angular velocity / time = (4.712 - 0) / 1.60 = 2.945 rad s^-2.

Answer: 2.95 rad s^-2 (as printed in the book).

5.3. A body of moment of inertia I = 0.80 kg m^2 about a fixed axis, rotates with a constant angular velocity of 100 rad s^-1. Calculate its angular momentum L and the torque to sustain this motion.

Step 1: Angular momentum L = I x omega = 0.80 x 100 = 80 J s.

Step 2: The angular velocity is constant, so the angular acceleration is zero.

Step 3: Torque = I x angular acceleration = 0.80 x 0 = 0. No torque is needed to sustain uniform rotation.

Answer: 80 J s, 0 (as printed in the book).

5.4. Consider the rotating cylinder shown in Fig. 5.26. Suppose that m = 5.0 kg, F = 0.60 N and r = 0.20 m. Calculate (a) the torque acting on the cylinder, (b) the angular acceleration of the cylinder. (Moment of inertia of cylinder = (1/2) m r^2.)

Step 1: (a) Torque = force x radius = 0.60 x 0.20 = 0.12 N m.

Step 2: Moment of inertia of the cylinder = (1/2) m r^2 = (1/2) x 5.0 x (0.20)^2 = 0.10 kg m^2.

Step 3: (b) Angular acceleration = torque / moment of inertia = 0.12 / 0.10 = 1.2 rad s^-2.

Answer: 0.12 N m, 1.2 rad s^-2 (as printed in the book).

5.5. Calculate the angular momentum of a star of mass 2.0 x 10^30 kg and radius 7.0 x 10^5 km. If it makes one complete rotation about its axis once in 20 days, what is its kinetic energy?

Step 1: Radius in metres: 7.0 x 10^5 km = 7.0 x 10^8 m. Period T = 20 days = 20 x 24 x 3600 = 1.728 x 10^6 s.

Step 2: Angular velocity omega = 2 pi / T = 6.283 / (1.728 x 10^6) = 3.636 x 10^-6 rad s^-1.

Step 3: Moment of inertia (sphere) I = (2/5) M R^2 = 0.4 x 2.0 x 10^30 x (7.0 x 10^8)^2 = 3.92 x 10^47 kg m^2.

Step 4: Angular momentum L = I x omega = 3.92 x 10^47 x 3.636 x 10^-6 = 1.4 x 10^42 J s.

Step 5: Rotational kinetic energy = (1/2) I omega^2 = (1/2) x 3.92 x 10^47 x (3.636 x 10^-6)^2 = 2.6 x 10^36 J, about 2.5 x 10^36 J.

Answer: 1.4 x 10^42 J s, 2.5 x 10^36 J (as printed in the book).

5.6. A 1000 kg car travelling with a speed of 144 km h^-1 round a curve of radius 100 m. Find the necessary centripetal force.

Step 1: Speed in ms^-1: 144 km h^-1 = 144 x 1000 / 3600 = 40 ms^-1.

Step 2: Centripetal force = m v^2 / r = 1000 x 40^2 / 100 = 1000 x 1600 / 100 = 16,000 N.

Answer: 1.60 x 10^4 N (as printed in the book).

5.7. What is the least speed at which an aeroplane can execute a vertical loop of 1.0 km radius so that there will be no tendency for the pilot to fall down at the highest point?

Step 1: At the highest point, the pilot's weight supplies the centripetal force when the seat just stops pushing on him: m g = m v^2 / r.

Step 2: The mass cancels: v^2 = g r = 9.8 x 1000 = 9800.

Step 3: v = sqrt(9800) = 99 ms^-1. Any slower, and the pilot would tend to fall away from his seat at the top.

Answer: 99 ms^-1 (as printed in the book).

5.8. The Moon orbits the Earth so that the same side always faces the Earth. Determine the ratio of its spin angular momentum (about its own axis) and its orbital angular momentum. (In this case, treat the Moon as a particle orbiting the Earth). Distance between the Earth and the Moon is 3.85 x 10^8 m. Radius of Moon is 1.74 x 10^6 m.

Step 1: The Moon spins once per orbit, so its spin angular velocity equals its orbital angular velocity, omega.

Step 2: Spin angular momentum = I x omega = (2/5) M R^2 x omega, with R = 1.74 x 10^6 m.

Step 3: Orbital angular momentum (particle) = M x v x D = M x omega x D^2, with D = 3.85 x 10^8 m.

Step 4: Ratio = [(2/5) M R^2 omega] / [M D^2 omega] = (2/5) x (R / D)^2 = 0.4 x (1.74 x 10^6 / 3.85 x 10^8)^2.

Step 5: R / D = 4.519 x 10^-3. Its square is 2.042 x 10^-5. Ratio = 0.4 x 2.042 x 10^-5 = 8.2 x 10^-6.

Answer: 8.2 x 10^-6 (as printed in the book).

5.9. The Earth rotates on its axis once a day. Suppose, by some process the Earth contracts so that its radius is only half as large as at present. How fast will it be rotating then? (For sphere I = 2/5 M R^2.)

Step 1: Moment of inertia of a sphere is proportional to R^2. Halving the radius reduces I to one quarter: I' = I / 4.

Step 2: No external torque acts, so angular momentum is conserved: I' x omega' = I x omega.

Step 3: omega' = omega x (I / I') = 4 omega. The Earth spins four times as fast.

Step 4: New period = 24 hours / 4 = 6 hours.

Answer: The Earth would complete its rotation in 6 hours (as printed in the book).

5.10. What should be the orbiting speed to launch a satellite in a circular orbit 900 km above the surface of the Earth? (Take mass of the Earth as 6.0 x 10^24 kg and its radius as 6400 km).

Step 1: Orbital radius from the Earth's centre: r = 6400 + 900 = 7300 km = 7.3 x 10^6 m.

Step 2: Orbital speed v = sqrt(G M / r), with G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2 and M = 6.0 x 10^24 kg.

Step 3: G M = 6.67 x 10^-11 x 6.0 x 10^24 = 4.00 x 10^14.

Step 4: v = sqrt(4.00 x 10^14 / 7.3 x 10^6) = sqrt(5.48 x 10^7) = 7400 ms^-1 = 7.4 kms^-1.

Answer: 7.4 km s^-1 (as printed in the book).

mcqs.q: A laser beam directed from the Earth to the Moon (distance 3.8 x 10^8 m) is to have a diameter of 2.50 m at the Moon. The divergence angle of the beam must be:
mcqs.why: Working: for a small angle, angle in radians = arc length / radius = diameter at the Moon / distance to the Moon = 2.50 / 3.8 x 10^8 = 6.58 x 10^-9 rad, about 6.6 x 10^-9 rad.

mcqs.q: A gramophone turntable accelerates from rest to 45.0 rev min^-1 in 1.60 s. Its average angular acceleration is:
mcqs.why: Working: final angular velocity = 45.0 x 2 pi / 60 = 4.712 rad s^-1. Average angular acceleration = change in angular velocity / time = 4.712 / 1.60 = 2.945 rad s^-2, about 2.95 rad s^-2.

mcqs.q: A body of moment of inertia 0.80 kg m^2 rotates about a fixed axis with constant angular velocity 100 rad s^-1. Its angular momentum is:
options: 80 J s, and no torque is needed to sustain the uniform rotation
mcqs.why: Working: angular momentum L = I x omega = 0.80 x 100 = 80 J s. The angular velocity is constant, so the angular acceleration is zero and the torque = I x 0 = 0; no torque is needed to sustain uniform rotation.

mcqs.q: A cylinder (m = 5.0 kg, r = 0.20 m, I = (1/2) m r^2) is acted on by a tangential force F = 0.60 N at its rim. Its angular acceleration is:
mcqs.why: Working: torque = F x r = 0.60 x 0.20 = 0.12 N m. Moment of inertia = (1/2) x 5.0 x 0.04 = 0.10 kg m^2. Angular acceleration = torque / I = 0.12 / 0.10 = 1.2 rad s^-2.

mcqs.q: A star of mass 2.0 x 10^30 kg and radius 7.0 x 10^5 km rotates once in 20 days. Its angular momentum is about:
mcqs.why: Working: omega = 2 pi / T = 6.283 / 1.728 x 10^6 = 3.636 x 10^-6 rad s^-1. Moment of inertia I = (2/5) M R^2 = 3.92 x 10^47 kg m^2. Angular momentum L = I x omega = 3.92 x 10^47 x 3.636 x 10^-6 = 1.4 x 10^42 J s. Its rotational kinetic energy is about 2.5 x 10^36 J.

mcqs.q: A 1000 kg car travels at 144 km h^-1 round a curve of radius 100 m. The necessary centripetal force is:
mcqs.why: Working: speed = 144 x 1000 / 3600 = 40 ms^-1. Centripetal force = m v^2 / r = 1000 x 1600 / 100 = 16000 N = 1.60 x 10^4 N.

mcqs.q: What is the least speed at which an aeroplane can execute a vertical loop of radius 1.0 km without the pilot tending to fall at the highest point?
mcqs.why: Working: at the highest point the pilot's weight just supplies the centripetal force: m g = m v^2 / r, so v^2 = g r = 9.8 x 1000 = 9800. Then v = sqrt(9800) = 99 ms^-1. Any slower and the pilot would tend to fall away from his seat.

mcqs.q: The Moon always shows the same face to the Earth. Treating the Moon as a particle for its orbit (R = 1.74 x 10^6 m, D = 3.85 x 10^8 m), the ratio of its spin angular momentum to its orbital angular momentum is:
mcqs.why: Working: the Moon spins once per orbit, so both motions share the same omega. Ratio = (2/5) x (R / D)^2. Now R / D = 1.74 x 10^6 / 3.85 x 10^8 = 4.519 x 10^-3, whose square is 2.042 x 10^-5. Ratio = 0.4 x 2.042 x 10^-5 = 8.2 x 10^-6.

mcqs.q: Suppose the Earth contracts so that its radius is only half as large as at present (I proportional to R^2, no external torque). How fast will it rotate then?
mcqs.why: Working: halving the radius reduces the moment of inertia to one quarter, I' = I / 4. Angular momentum is conserved: I' omega' = I omega, so omega' = 4 omega; the Earth spins four times as fast. New period = 24 / 4 = 6 hours.

mcqs.q: What orbiting speed is needed for a satellite in a circular orbit 900 km above the Earth? (M = 6.0 x 10^24 kg, radius of Earth 6400 km, G = 6.67 x 10^-11 N m^2 kg^-2)

lessons.notes_html:
6.1. Explain what do you understand by the term viscosity?

Viscosity is the internal friction of a fluid. It is the property by which one layer of a fluid resists motion relative to a neighbouring layer, so that a tangential force is needed to maintain flow. The coefficient of viscosity, eta, is defined as the tangential stress divided by the velocity gradient between layers. Its SI unit is N s m^-2, also called pascal second. Thick fluids like honey have a high viscosity, while water has a low viscosity.

6.2. What is meant by drag force? What are the factors upon which drag force acting upon a small sphere of radius r, moving down through a liquid, depend?

Drag force is the retarding force exerted by a fluid on a body moving through it, acting opposite to the direction of motion. For a small sphere of radius r moving slowly through a liquid, Stokes' law gives the drag force as F = 6 pi eta r v. The drag force therefore depends on the viscosity eta of the liquid, the radius r of the sphere, and the speed v of the sphere. In general it also depends on the shape of the body and, at higher speeds, on the density of the fluid.

6.3. Why fog droplets appear to be suspended in air?

Fog droplets are extremely small, so their terminal velocity in air is extremely small. By Stokes' law the terminal velocity is proportional to the square of the radius, so a tiny droplet falls very slowly, only a fraction of a millimetre per second. The slightest upward currents of air, and even the random motion of air molecules, are enough to keep the droplets floating, so they appear to be suspended in the air.

6.4. Explain the difference between laminar flow and turbulent flow.

In laminar (streamline) flow, the fluid moves in smooth, orderly layers, each layer sliding past its neighbours without mixing, and the velocity at any point does not change with time. In turbulent flow, the motion is disorderly, with eddies and swirls, the velocity at a point keeps changing, and layers mix. Laminar flow occurs at low speeds; above a critical speed the flow becomes turbulent.

6.5. State Bernoulli's relation for a liquid in motion and describe some of its applications.

Bernoulli's relation for a liquid in steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow states that along a streamline, the sum of pressure energy, kinetic energy and potential energy per unit volume is constant: P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant, where P is pressure, rho density, v speed and h height. Its applications include the lift on an aeroplane wing, the Venturi meter for measuring flow speed, the carburettor of a motorcar, the filter pump and atomiser, the swing of a spinning cricket ball, and the design of chimneys and roofs in strong winds.

6.6. A person is standing near a fast moving train. Is there any danger that he will fall towards it?

Yes, there is a real danger. The fast train drags air with it, so the air between the person and the train moves fast, and by Bernoulli's principle its pressure falls. The air behind the person is nearly still, at normal atmospheric pressure, so the pressure difference pushes the person towards the train. That is why passengers must stand well back from the edge of a platform.

6.7. Identify the correct answer. What do you infer from Bernoulli's theorem? (i) Where the speed of the fluid is high the pressure will be low. (ii) Where the speed of the fluid is high the pressure is also high. (iii) This theorem is valid only for turbulent flow of the liquid.

The correct answer is (i): where the speed of the fluid is high the pressure will be low. Statement (ii) is the opposite of Bernoulli's principle and is false. Statement (iii) is also false: Bernoulli's theorem applies to steady, streamline (laminar) flow of an incompressible, non-viscous fluid, not to turbulent flow, where energy is lost in eddies.

6.8. Two row boats moving parallel in the same direction are pulled towards each other. Explain.

The water between the two boats is confined to a narrow channel, and the boats drag it along, so it moves faster than the water on the outer sides. By Bernoulli's principle the pressure between the boats is therefore lower than the pressure outside them, and the higher outside pressure pushes the boats towards each other.

6.9. Explain, how the swing is produced in a fast moving cricket ball.

A cricket ball swings because the air flows differently on its two sides. One side of the ball is kept smooth and shiny, while the other becomes rough, and the seam is held at an angle. The boundary layer of air separates later on the smooth side, so the air speeds up more on one side than on the other. By Bernoulli's principle the pressure is lower on the faster side, and this sideways pressure difference pushes the ball sideways, making it swing in the air.

6.10. Explain the working of a carburetor of a motorcar using by Bernoulli's principle.

In a carburettor, air from outside is drawn through a narrow throat, a Venturi. As the air passes the narrow part its speed increases and, by Bernoulli's principle, its pressure falls. A small jet opens into this low-pressure region, and the higher pressure on the petrol in the float chamber pushes petrol out of the jet as a fine spray. The spray mixes with the fast-moving air to form the combustible mixture that goes into the engine cylinders.

6.11. For which position will the maximum blood pressure in the body have the smallest value. (a) Standing up right (b) Sitting (c) Lying horizontally (d) Standing on one's head?

(c) Lying horizontally. When a person stands upright, the blood pressure in the feet is the heart pressure plus the hydrostatic pressure of the column of blood, rho g h, from the heart down to the feet, so the maximum pressure in the body is large. When the person lies horizontally, the heart, head and feet are all at nearly the same level, so there is almost no hydrostatic difference, and the maximum blood pressure in the body is at its smallest. Standing on one's head would make the pressure in the head the largest of all.

6.12. In an orbiting space station, would the blood pressure in major arteries in the leg ever be greater than the blood pressure in major arteries in the neck?

No. In an orbiting space station everything is in free fall, so there is no weight and no hydrostatic pressure difference due to gravity. On Earth the blood pressure in the legs is greater than in the neck because of the weight of the column of blood between them. In orbit that column has no weight, so the pressure in the major arteries of the legs will not be greater than in the neck; apart from the pumping of the heart, the pressures will be nearly equal.

options: N s m^-2, also called the pascal second
mcqs.why: Viscosity is the internal friction of a fluid. The coefficient of viscosity eta is defined as the tangential stress divided by the velocity gradient between layers, and its SI unit is N s m^-2, also called the pascal second. Honey has a high viscosity and water a low one.

options: The density of the sphere only
The viscosity of the liquid, the radius of the sphere and its speed
The depth of the liquid and the weight of the sphere
The surface tension of the liquid only
mcqs.why: Drag force is the retarding force exerted by a fluid on a body moving through it, opposite to the motion. For a small sphere moving slowly, Stokes' law gives F = 6 pi eta r v, so the drag depends on the viscosity eta, the radius r and the speed v (in general also on the shape of the body).

Because their terminal velocity is extremely small, being proportional to the square of their tiny radius
Because the air is perfectly still everywhere

options: The fluid moves in smooth, orderly layers and the velocity at any point does not change with time
The motion is disorderly, with eddies and swirls
The velocity at a point keeps changing and the layers mix
It occurs only at very high speeds
mcqs.why: In laminar flow the fluid moves in smooth, orderly layers, each sliding past its neighbours without mixing, and the velocity at any point does not change with time. Turbulent flow is the disorderly one with eddies; laminar flow occurs at low speeds and becomes turbulent above a critical speed.

mcqs.q: Bernoulli's relation for a liquid in steady, incompressible, non-viscous flow states that along a streamline:
options: P + (1/2) rho v^2 + rho g h = constant
(1/2) rho v^2 - rho g h = constant

mcqs.q: A person standing near a fast-moving train is in danger of falling towards it because:
options: The train pushes air outwards at high pressure
The air between the person and the train moves fast, so its pressure falls, and the still air behind pushes the person towards the train
The train's weight attracts the person gravitationally
The train creates a vacuum behind it only
mcqs.why: The fast train drags air with it, so the air between the person and the train moves fast and, by Bernoulli's principle, its pressure falls. The nearly still air behind the person is at normal atmospheric pressure, so the pressure difference pushes the person towards the train.

options: Where the speed of the fluid is high, the pressure is also high
The theorem is valid only for turbulent flow
Where the speed of the fluid is high, the pressure will be low
Pressure is the same at all points of a moving fluid
mcqs.why: The correct inference is (i): where the speed of the fluid is high the pressure will be low. The opposite statement is false, and the theorem applies to steady, streamline flow of an incompressible, non-viscous fluid, not to turbulent flow.

mcqs.q: Two row boats moving parallel in the same direction are pulled towards each other because:
options: The water between them moves faster, so the pressure between them is lower than the pressure outside
The boats attract each other through the water
The water between them is shallower
mcqs.why: The water between the boats is confined to a narrow channel and is dragged along faster than the water on the outer sides. By Bernoulli's principle the pressure between the boats is lower, and the higher outside pressure pushes the boats towards each other.

mcqs.q: For which position will the maximum blood pressure in the body have the smallest value?
mcqs.why: When a person stands upright, the pressure in the feet is the heart pressure plus the hydrostatic pressure rho g h of the column of blood, so the maximum is large. Lying horizontally, the heart, head and feet are at nearly the same level, so there is almost no hydrostatic difference and the maximum blood pressure is at its smallest.

options: Yes, because the heart pumps downwards
No, because in free fall there is no weight and so no hydrostatic pressure difference due to gravity
No, because there is no blood pressure in space
mcqs.why: In an orbiting station everything is in free fall, so there is no weight and no hydrostatic pressure difference due to gravity. On Earth the leg pressure exceeds the neck pressure because of the weight of the blood column between them; in orbit that column has no weight, so the pressures are nearly equal apart from the heart's pumping.

lessons.notes_html:
6.1. Certain globular protein particle has a density of 1246 kg m^-3. It falls through pure water (eta = 8.0 x 10^-4 Nsm^-2) with a terminal speed of 3.0 cm h^-1. Find the radius of the particle.

Step 1: Terminal speed in ms^-1: 3.0 cm h^-1 = 0.030 m / 3600 s = 8.33 x 10^-6 ms^-1.

Step 2: At terminal speed the viscous drag balances the weight minus the upthrust: 6 pi eta r v = (4/3) pi r^3 (rho - sigma) g, where sigma = 1000 kg m^-3 is the density of water.

Step 3: This gives Stokes' terminal velocity: v = (2/9) x (rho - sigma) x g x r^2 / eta, so r^2 = 9 eta v / [2 (rho - sigma) g].

Step 4: r^2 = 9 x 8.0 x 10^-4 x 8.33 x 10^-6 / [2 x (1246 - 1000) x 9.8] = 6.0 x 10^-8 / 4822 = 1.24 x 10^-11.

Step 5: r = sqrt(1.24 x 10^-11) = 3.5 x 10^-6 m. Note: the book prints the answer as 1.6 x 10^-6 m. That value follows if the upthrust of the water is left out, using the particle density alone: r^2 = 9 eta v / (2 rho g) = 6.0 x 10^-8 / 24422 = 2.46 x 10^-12, giving r = 1.6 x 10^-6 m. The physically complete Stokes result, with upthrust, is 3.5 x 10^-6 m; the book's printed answer is recorded here as printed.

6.2. Water flows through a hose, whose internal diameter is 1 cm at a speed of 1 ms^-1. What should be the diameter of the nozzle if the water is to emerge at 21 ms^-1?

Step 1: By the equation of continuity, A1 v1 = A2 v2, and area is proportional to the square of the diameter.

Step 2: So (d2 / d1)^2 = v1 / v2 = 1 / 21.

Step 3: d2 = d1 x sqrt(1/21) = 1 cm x 0.218 = 0.218 cm, about 0.2 cm.

Answer: 0.2 cm (as printed in the book).

6.3. The pipe near the lower end of a large water storage tank develops a small leak and a stream of water shoots from it. The top of water in the tank is 15 m above the point of leak. (a) With what speed does the water rush from the hole? (b) If the hole has an area of 0.060 cm^2, how much water flows out in one second?

Step 1: (a) By Torricelli's theorem, the speed of efflux is v = sqrt(2 g h) = sqrt(2 x 9.8 x 15) = sqrt(294) = 17.1 ms^-1.

Step 2: (b) Volume flow rate = area x speed = 0.060 cm^2 x 1710 cm s^-1 (since 17.1 ms^-1 = 1710 cm s^-1).

Step 3: Volume per second = 0.060 x 1710 = 102.6 cm^3, about 102 cm^3.

Answer: (a) 17 ms^-1, (b) 102 cm^3 (as printed in the book).

6.4. Water is flowing smoothly through a closed pipe system. At one point the speed of water is 3.0 ms^-1, while at another point 3.0 m higher, the speed is 4.0 ms^-1. If the pressure is 80 kPa at the lower point, what is pressure at the upper point?

Step 1: Bernoulli's equation: P1 + (1/2) rho v1^2 + rho g h1 = P2 + (1/2) rho v2^2 + rho g h2. Take the lower point as h1 = 0, so h2 = 3.0 m.

Step 2: P2 = P1 + (1/2) rho (v1^2 - v2^2) - rho g h2 = 80,000 + (1/2) x 1000 x (9 - 16) - 1000 x 9.8 x 3.0.

Step 3: P2 = 80,000 - 3,500 - 29,400 = 47,100 Pa = 47.1 kPa.

Answer: 47 kPa (as printed in the book).

6.5. An airplane wing is designed so that when the speed of the air across the top of wing is 450 ms^-1, the speed of air below the wing is 410 ms^-1. What is the pressure difference between the top and bottom of the wings? (Density of air = 1.29 kgm^-3.)

Step 1: Pressure difference = (1/2) rho (v_top^2 - v_bottom^2) = (1/2) x 1.29 x (450^2 - 410^2).

Step 2: 450^2 - 410^2 = 202,500 - 168,100 = 34,400.

Step 3: Pressure difference = 0.645 x 34,400 = 22,188 Pa, about 22 kPa. The pressure below the wing is higher, giving lift.

Answer: 22 kPa (as printed in the book).

6.6. The radius of the aorta is about 1.0 cm and the blood flowing through it has a speed of about 30 cms^-1. Calculate the average speed of the blood in the capillaries using the fact that although each capillary has a diameter of about 8 x 10^-4 cm, there are literally millions of them so that their total cross section is about 2000 cm^2.

Step 1: Cross section of the aorta = pi r^2 = 3.14 x (1.0)^2 = 3.14 cm^2.

Step 2: Volume flow rate = area x speed = 3.14 x 30 = 94.2 cm^3 s^-1.

Step 3: By continuity, the same flow passes through the capillaries: speed in capillaries = flow rate / total capillary area = 94.2 / 2000 = 0.0471 cm s^-1.

Step 4: In ms^-1 this is 4.71 x 10^-4 ms^-1, about 5 x 10^-4 ms^-1.

Answer: 5 x 10^-4 ms^-1 (as printed in the book).

6.7. How large must a heating duct be if air moving 3.0 ms^-1 along it can replenish the air in a room of 300 m^3 volume every 15 min? Assume the air's density remains constant.

Step 1: Volume flow rate needed = 300 m^3 / (15 x 60 s) = 300 / 900 = 0.333 m^3 s^-1.

Step 2: Area of duct = flow rate / speed = 0.333 / 3.0 = 0.111 m^2.

Step 3: For a circular duct, area = pi r^2, so r = sqrt(0.111 / 3.14) = sqrt(0.0354) = 0.188 m, about 19 cm.

Answer: Radius = 19 cm (as printed in the book).

6.8. An airplane design calls for a 'lift' due to the net force of the moving air on the wing of about 1000 Nm^-2 of wing area. Assume that air flows past the wing of an aircraft with streamline flow. If the speed of flow past the lower wing surface is 160 ms^-1, what is the required speed over the upper surface to give a 'lift' of 1000 Nm^-2? The density of air is 1.29 kgm^-3 and assume maximum thickness of wing to be one metre.

Step 1: Lift per unit area = pressure difference = (1/2) rho (v_top^2 - v_bottom^2). The height term rho g x 1 m is only about 13 Pa and is negligible beside 1000 Pa, so it is left out.

Step 2: 1000 = (1/2) x 1.29 x (v_top^2 - 160^2), so v_top^2 - 25,600 = 2000 / 1.29 = 1550.

Step 3: v_top^2 = 25,600 + 1550 = 27,150, so v_top = sqrt(27,150) = 164.8 ms^-1, about 165 ms^-1.

Answer: 165 ms^-1 (as printed in the book).

6.9. What gauge pressure is required in the city mains for a stream from a fire hose connected to the mains to reach a vertical height of 15.0 m?

Step 1: The gauge pressure must supply the potential energy of the water column: P = rho g h.

Step 2: P = 1000 x 9.8 x 15.0 = 147,000 Pa = 1.47 x 10^5 Pa.

Answer: 1.47 x 10^5 Pa (as printed in the book).
