lessons.title: Questions
lessons.notes_html:
7.1. Name two characteristics of simple harmonic motion.

Two characteristics of simple harmonic motion are: (1) the acceleration is directly proportional to the displacement from the mean position and is always directed towards the mean position, a = -omega^2 x; and (2) the motion is periodic, repeating itself after a fixed time, the time period, with the velocity greatest at the mean position and zero at the extreme positions.

7.2. Does frequency depends on amplitude for harmonic oscillators?

No. For a harmonic oscillator the frequency is fixed by the properties of the system, not by the amplitude. For a mass-spring system f = (1 / 2 pi) sqrt(k / m), and for a simple pendulum f = (1 / 2 pi) sqrt(g / l). As long as the motion remains simple harmonic, a larger amplitude only makes the body move faster, it does not change the time period. This independence of period from amplitude is called isochronism.

7.3. Can we realize an ideal simple pendulum?

An ideal simple pendulum is a point mass hanging from a light, inextensible string, swinging through small angles with no friction and no air resistance. It cannot be realised exactly in practice, because a real bob has a finite size, a real string has some mass and can stretch slightly, the support has friction, and air resistance always acts. A small, dense bob on a long, light thread swinging through a small angle is a good approximation to it.

7.4. What is the total distance travelled by an object moving with SHM in a time equal to its period, if its amplitude is A?

In one complete period the body travels four times the amplitude. Starting from the mean position it goes to one extreme (distance A), back to the mean position (distance A), on to the other extreme (distance A), and back to the mean position (distance A). The total distance is A + A + A + A = 4 A.

7.5. What happens to the period of a simple pendulum if its length is doubled? What happens if the suspended mass is doubled?

The period of a simple pendulum is T = 2 pi sqrt(l / g). If the length is doubled, the period becomes sqrt(2) times larger, about 1.41 times the original period. If the suspended mass is doubled, the period does not change at all, because the period of a simple pendulum does not depend on the mass.

7.6. Does the acceleration of a simple harmonic oscillator remain constant during its motion? Is the acceleration ever zero? Explain.

No, the acceleration does not remain constant, because a = -omega^2 x, so it changes with the displacement x: it is greatest at the extreme positions and changes sign on either side of the mean position. Yes, the acceleration is zero at the mean position, where x = 0, so the restoring force is zero there and the body momentarily has no acceleration, even though its velocity is greatest.

7.7. What is meant by phase angle? Does it define angle between maximum displacement and the driving force?

The phase angle is the quantity (omega t + phi) in the displacement equation y = A sin(omega t + phi). It tells the state of vibration of the body at any time, that is, how far through its cycle it has gone, and the initial phase phi is its value at t = 0. No, it does not by itself define the angle between the maximum displacement and the driving force; that phase difference belongs to forced vibrations, where the displacement lags behind the driving force by an amount that depends on the driving frequency and the damping.

7.8. Under what conditions does the addition of two simple harmonic motions produce a resultant, which is also simple harmonic?

The addition of two simple harmonic motions gives a resultant that is also simple harmonic when the two motions have the same frequency (the same period) and act along the same straight line. The resultant is then a simple harmonic motion of the same frequency, whose amplitude depends on the phase difference between the two motions: it is greatest when they are in phase and smallest when they are exactly out of phase. If the frequencies differ, beats are produced, and if the motions are perpendicular, the path is a Lissajous figure, not a straight-line SHM.

7.9. Show that in SHM the acceleration is zero when the velocity is greatest and the velocity is zero when the acceleration is greatest?

In SHM the velocity is v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2) and the acceleration is a = -omega^2 x. At the mean position x = 0, so a = 0, while v = omega A, its greatest value. At an extreme position x = plus or minus A, so v = 0, while a = minus or plus omega^2 A, its greatest value in size. The acceleration is therefore zero exactly when the velocity is greatest, and the velocity is zero exactly when the acceleration is greatest.

7.10. In relation to SHM, explain the equations: (i) y = A sin (omega t + phi) (ii) a = -omega^2 x

(i) y = A sin(omega t + phi) gives the displacement y of the oscillator at time t. A is the amplitude, the maximum displacement; omega is the angular frequency, 2 pi times the frequency; and phi is the initial phase, the phase at t = 0, which fixes where in its cycle the body starts. (ii) a = -omega^2 x is the defining equation of SHM: the acceleration a is proportional to the displacement x, and the minus sign shows that it is directed opposite to the displacement, that is, always towards the mean position.

7.11. Explain the relation between total energy, potential energy and kinetic energy for a body oscillating with SHM.

The total energy of a body in SHM is constant: E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2, where m is the mass, omega the angular frequency and A the amplitude. The potential energy is P.E. = (1/2) k x^2 = (1/2) m omega^2 x^2, which is greatest at the extremes and zero at the mean position. The kinetic energy is K.E. = (1/2) m v^2 = (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2), which is greatest at the mean position and zero at the extremes. At every point, K.E. + P.E. = E, so energy continuously changes between kinetic and potential forms while the total stays the same.

7.12. Describe some common phenomena in which resonance plays an important role.

Resonance is important in many common phenomena: a child on a swing goes higher when pushed at the swing's natural frequency; a radio or television set is tuned by making its circuit resonate with the frequency of the wanted station; musical instruments sound loudly because their strings or air columns resonate; a bridge can be damaged when soldiers march across it in step at its natural frequency, or when wind gusts match it, as in the collapse of the Tacoma Narrows bridge; buildings can suffer in an earthquake when the ground vibrations match their natural frequency; and a singer can shatter a glass by singing its resonant note.

7.13. If a mass spring system is hung vertically and set into oscillations, why does the motion eventually stop?

Because the motion is damped. Friction at the support, air resistance on the mass, and internal friction in the spring all oppose the motion and dissipate its energy as heat. The amplitude therefore decreases with every swing, and the oscillations gradually die away until the mass comes to rest at its equilibrium position.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a defining characteristic of simple harmonic motion?
options: The acceleration is constant in magnitude and direction
The acceleration is directly proportional to the displacement from the mean position and always directed towards it, a = -omega^2 x
The velocity is greatest at the extreme positions
mcqs.why: Two characteristics of SHM are: (1) the acceleration is directly proportional to the displacement from the mean position and always directed towards the mean position, a = -omega^2 x; and (2) the motion is periodic, with the velocity greatest at the mean position and zero at the extreme positions.

mcqs.q: Does the frequency of a harmonic oscillator depend on its amplitude?
options: Yes, larger amplitude gives higher frequency
Yes, larger amplitude gives lower frequency
No, the frequency is fixed by the properties of the system, such as sqrt(k/m) or sqrt(g/l); this independence is called isochronism
Only for a pendulum, not for a mass-spring system
mcqs.why: No. For a mass-spring system f = (1 / 2 pi) sqrt(k / m) and for a simple pendulum f = (1 / 2 pi) sqrt(g / l); neither contains the amplitude. A larger amplitude only makes the body move faster; the period is unchanged as long as the motion stays simple harmonic.

mcqs.q: An object moves with SHM of amplitude A. The total distance it travels in a time equal to one period is:
options: Zero, because it returns to its start
mcqs.why: In one complete period the body goes from the mean position to one extreme (distance A), back to the mean (A), on to the other extreme (A) and back to the mean (A). The total distance is A + A + A + A = 4 A, even though the net displacement is zero.

mcqs.q: What happens to the period of a simple pendulum if its length is doubled, and if the suspended mass is doubled?
options: Doubling the length multiplies the period by sqrt(2), about 1.41; doubling the mass leaves the period unchanged
Doubling the length doubles the period; doubling the mass halves it
mcqs.why: The period is T = 2 pi sqrt(l / g). If the length is doubled the period becomes sqrt(2) times larger, about 1.41 times the original. The period does not depend on the mass at all, so doubling the suspended mass changes nothing.

mcqs.q: In SHM, the acceleration is zero when:
options: The body is at an extreme position
The body is at the mean position, where the velocity is greatest
The body is halfway to an extreme
mcqs.why: Since a = -omega^2 x, the acceleration changes with displacement: it is greatest at the extremes and zero at the mean position, where x = 0 and the restoring force vanishes. At that same mean position the velocity v = omega A is at its greatest.

mcqs.q: What does the phase angle (omega t + phi) in y = A sin(omega t + phi) tell us?
options: The state of vibration of the body at time t, that is, how far through its cycle it has gone
The angle between the maximum displacement and the driving force
The direction of the restoring force
mcqs.why: The phase angle (omega t + phi) tells the state of vibration of the body at any time; the initial phase phi is its value at t = 0 and fixes where in its cycle the body starts. It does not by itself define an angle between displacement and a driving force; that phase difference belongs to forced vibrations.

mcqs.q: Under what conditions does the addition of two simple harmonic motions give a resultant that is also simple harmonic?
options: When the two motions are perpendicular to each other
When the two motions have different frequencies
When the two motions have the same frequency and act along the same straight line
For any two simple harmonic motions whatever
mcqs.why: The resultant is also simple harmonic, of the same frequency, when the two motions have the same frequency (the same period) and act along the same straight line; its amplitude depends on the phase difference. Different frequencies give beats, and perpendicular motions give Lissajous figures.

mcqs.q: For a body oscillating with SHM, which statement about its energies is correct?
options: The total energy E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 stays constant; potential energy is greatest at the extremes and kinetic energy greatest at the mean position
The total energy grows with time
Kinetic energy is greatest at the extremes
Potential energy is zero at the extremes
mcqs.why: The total energy E = (1/2) m omega^2 A^2 is constant. Potential energy (1/2) m omega^2 x^2 is greatest at the extremes and zero at the mean position; kinetic energy (1/2) m omega^2 (A^2 - x^2) is greatest at the mean position and zero at the extremes. At every point K.E. + P.E. = E.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is an example of resonance?
options: A radio set tuned so its circuit resonates with the frequency of the wanted station
A pendulum swinging freely with decreasing amplitude
A ball rolling to rest on a rough floor
Sound spreading out through a room
mcqs.why: Resonance occurs when a system is driven at its natural frequency. Examples in the notes include tuning a radio or television circuit to a station, a child on a swing pushed at the swing's natural frequency, and a bridge endangered when soldiers march across it in step at its natural frequency.

mcqs.q: A vertically hung mass-spring system is set oscillating. Why does the motion eventually stop?
options: Because gravity slowly removes the energy
Because the spring constant decreases to zero
Because the motion is damped: friction and air resistance dissipate the energy as heat, so the amplitude dies away
Because the mass reaches its final equilibrium weight
mcqs.why: Because the motion is damped. Friction at the support, air resistance on the mass and internal friction in the spring all oppose the motion and dissipate its energy as heat. The amplitude therefore decreases with every swing until the mass comes to rest at its equilibrium position.

7.1. A 100.0 g body hung on a spring elongates the spring by 4.0 cm. When a certain object is hung on the spring and set vibrating, its period is 0.568 s. What is the mass of the object pulling the spring?

Step 1: Spring constant from the known body: k = m g / x = 0.100 x 9.8 / 0.040 = 24.5 N m^-1.

Step 2: Period of a mass-spring system: T = 2 pi sqrt(m / k), so m = k x (T / 2 pi)^2.

Step 3: m = 24.5 x (0.568 / 6.283)^2 = 24.5 x (0.0904)^2 = 24.5 x 0.00817 = 0.200 kg.

Answer: 0.20 kg (as printed in the book).

7.2. A load of 15.0 g elongates a spring by 2.00 cm. If body of mass 294 g is attached to the spring and is set into vibration with an amplitude of 10.0 cm, what will be its (i) period (ii) spring constant (iii) maximum speed of its vibration.

Step 1: (ii) Spring constant: k = m g / x = 0.015 x 9.8 / 0.020 = 7.35 N m^-1.

Step 2: (i) Period: T = 2 pi sqrt(m / k) = 2 pi sqrt(0.294 / 7.35) = 2 pi sqrt(0.040) = 2 pi x 0.20 = 1.26 s.

Step 3: (iii) Angular frequency omega = sqrt(k / m) = sqrt(7.35 / 0.294) = sqrt(25) = 5.0 rad s^-1.

Step 4: Maximum speed = omega x amplitude = 5.0 x 0.10 = 0.50 m s^-1 = 50 cm s^-1.

Answer: (i) 1.26 s, (ii) 7.35 N m^-1, (iii) 50 cm s^-1. Note: the book prints (iii) as 49.0 cm s^-1, a small difference from rounding the angular frequency from the rounded period; the direct value is 50 cm s^-1.

7.3. An 8.0 kg body executes SHM with amplitude 30 cm. The restoring force is 60 N when the displacement is 30 cm. Find (i) Period (ii) Acceleration, speed, kinetic energy and potential energy when the displacement is 12 cm.

Step 1: Spring constant: k = F / x = 60 / 0.30 = 200 N m^-1.

Step 2: (i) Period: T = 2 pi sqrt(m / k) = 2 pi sqrt(8 / 200) = 2 pi x 0.20 = 1.26 s, about 1.3 s.

Step 3: Angular frequency omega = 2 pi / T = 5.0 rad s^-1.

Step 4: (ii) Acceleration at x = 0.12 m: a = k x / m in size = 200 x 0.12 / 8 = 3.0 m s^-2, directed towards the mean position.

Step 5: Speed at x = 0.12 m: v = omega sqrt(A^2 - x^2) = 5.0 x sqrt(0.30^2 - 0.12^2) = 5.0 x sqrt(0.0756) = 5.0 x 0.275 = 1.4 m s^-1.

Step 6: Kinetic energy = (1/2) m v^2 = (1/2) x 8 x 1.4^2 = 7.6 J (using the unrounded speed 1.375 m s^-1 gives 7.56 J).

Step 7: Potential energy = (1/2) k x^2 = (1/2) x 200 x (0.12)^2 = 100 x 0.0144 = 1.44 J.

Answer: (i) 1.3 s, (ii) 3.0 m s^-2, 1.4 m s^-1, 7.6 J, 1.44 J (as printed in the book).

7.4. A block of mass 4.0 kg is dropped from a height of 0.80 m on to a spring of spring constant k = 1960 Nm^-1. Find the maximum distance through which the spring will be compressed.

Step 1: Let the maximum compression be x. The block falls a total distance (0.80 + x), so the loss of gravitational potential energy is m g (0.80 + x).

Step 2: This equals the elastic potential energy stored at maximum compression: (1/2) k x^2. So 4.0 x 9.8 x (0.80 + x) = (1/2) x 1960 x x^2.

Step 3: 39.2 (0.80 + x) = 980 x^2, that is, 980 x^2 - 39.2 x - 31.36 = 0.

Step 4: Divide by 39.2: 25 x^2 - x - 0.80 = 0. Solving, x = [1 + sqrt(1 + 80)] / 50 = (1 + 9) / 50 = 0.20 m. Note: the book prints 0.18 m. That value follows if the small extra fall x during compression is left out, using m g x 0.80 = (1/2) k x^2, which gives x = sqrt(2 x 39.2 x 0.80 / 1960) = 0.18 m. The complete energy result is 0.20 m; the book's printed answer is recorded here as printed.

7.5. A simple pendulum is 50.0 cm long. What will be its frequency of vibration at a place where g = 9.8 ms^-2?

Step 1: Period T = 2 pi sqrt(l / g) = 2 pi sqrt(0.50 / 9.8) = 2 pi x 0.2259 = 1.42 s.

Step 2: Frequency f = 1 / T = 1 / 1.42 = 0.705 Hz, about 0.70 Hz.

Answer: 0.70 Hz (as printed in the book).

7.6. A block of mass 1.6 kg is attached to a spring with spring constant 1000 Nm^-1, as shown in Fig. 7.14. The spring is compressed through a distance of 2.0 cm and the block is released from rest. Calculate the velocity of the block as it passes through the equilibrium position, x = 0, if the surface is frictionless.

Step 1: Elastic potential energy at release = (1/2) k x^2 = (1/2) x 1000 x (0.020)^2 = 0.20 J.

Step 2: At the equilibrium position all of this has become kinetic energy: (1/2) m v^2 = 0.20 J.

Step 3: v^2 = 2 x 0.20 / 1.6 = 0.25, so v = 0.50 m s^-1.

Answer: 0.50 ms^-1 (as printed in the book).

7.7. A car of mass 1300 kg is constructed using a frame supported by four springs. Each spring has a spring constant 20,000 Nm^-1. If two people riding in the car have a combined mass of 160 kg, find the frequency of vibration of the car, when it is driven over a pot hole in the road. Assume the weight is evenly distributed.

Step 1: Total mass = 1300 + 160 = 1460 kg. The four springs act in parallel, so the total spring constant is 4 x 20,000 = 80,000 N m^-1.

Step 2: Frequency f = (1 / 2 pi) sqrt(k / m) = (1 / 6.283) x sqrt(80,000 / 1460).

Step 3: sqrt(80,000 / 1460) = sqrt(54.79) = 7.40. So f = 7.40 / 6.283 = 1.18 Hz.

Answer: 1.18 Hz (as printed in the book).

7.8. Find the amplitude, frequency and period of an object vibrating at the end of a spring, if the equation for its position, as a function of time, is x = 0.25 cos ((pi / 8) t). What is the displacement of the object after 2.0 s?

Step 1: Compare with x = A cos(omega t): amplitude A = 0.25 m and angular frequency omega = pi / 8 rad s^-1.

Step 2: Frequency f = omega / (2 pi) = (pi / 8) / (2 pi) = 1 / 16 Hz.

Step 3: Period T = 1 / f = 16 s.

Step 4: Displacement after 2.0 s: x = 0.25 x cos((pi / 8) x 2.0) = 0.25 x cos(pi / 4) = 0.25 x 0.7071 = 0.177 m, about 0.18 m.

Answer: 0.25 m, (1/16) Hz, 16 s, x = 0.18 m (as printed in the book).

mcqs.why: Working: spring constant k = m g / x = 0.100 x 9.8 / 0.040 = 24.5 N m^-1. From T = 2 pi sqrt(m / k), m = k x (T / 2 pi)^2 = 24.5 x 0.00817 = 0.200 kg, that is 0.20 kg.

mcqs.q: A load of 15.0 g elongates a spring by 2.00 cm. A 294 g body on the same spring vibrates with amplitude 10.0 cm. Its maximum speed is:

mcqs.q: An 8.0 kg body executes SHM with amplitude 30 cm; the restoring force is 60 N at a displacement of 30 cm. At a displacement of 12 cm, the acceleration is:

mcqs.q: For the same 8.0 kg body (k = 200 N m^-1), the potential energy at a displacement of 12 cm is:
mcqs.why: Working: potential energy = (1/2) k x^2 = (1/2) x 200 x 0.0144 = 1.44 J. At the same displacement the speed is 1.4 m s^-1 and the kinetic energy is 7.6 J, the two adding to the total energy of the oscillation.

mcqs.q: A block of mass 4.0 kg is dropped from 0.80 m onto a spring of k = 1960 N m^-1. Counting the extra fall during compression, the maximum compression of the spring is:
mcqs.why: Working: the block falls (0.80 + x), so m g (0.80 + x) = (1/2) k x^2, giving 980 x^2 - 39.2 x - 31.36 = 0, or 25 x^2 - x - 0.80 = 0. Solving, x = (1 + 9) / 50 = 0.20 m. The book's printed 0.18 m leaves out the small extra fall x during compression.

mcqs.q: A 1.6 kg block attached to a spring (k = 1000 N m^-1) is released from rest with the spring compressed by 2.0 cm on a frictionless surface. Its velocity at the equilibrium position is:

mcqs.why: Working: total mass = 1300 + 160 = 1460 kg; the four springs in parallel give k = 4 x 20000 = 80000 N m^-1. Frequency f = (1 / 2 pi) sqrt(k / m) = (1 / 6.283) x sqrt(54.79). Now sqrt(54.79) = 7.40, so f = 7.40 / 6.283 = 1.18 Hz.
