lessons.notes_html:
8.1. What features do longitudinal waves have in common with transverse waves?

Both longitudinal and transverse waves carry energy from one place to another without any net transport of the medium itself. Both can be described by the same quantities: amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period, with wave speed v = f lambda. Both obey the principle of superposition, and both show reflection, refraction, diffraction and interference. The difference is only in the direction of vibration of the particles relative to the direction of propagation.

8.2. The five possible waveforms obtained, when the output from a microphone is fed into the Y-input of cathode ray oscilloscope, with the time base on, are shown in Fig. 8.23. These waveforms are obtained under the same adjustment of the cathode ray oscilloscope controls. Indicate the waveform (a) which trace represents the loudest note? (b) which trace represents the highest frequency?

The loudness of a note depends on the amplitude of the waveform, and the frequency on the number of cycles in a given time, since the time base is the same for all traces. (a) The loudest note is trace D, which has the greatest amplitude, the tallest peaks. (b) The highest frequency is trace B, which shows the most complete cycles in the same time, so it has the most vibrations per second.

8.3. Is it possible for two identical waves travelling in the same direction along a string to give rise to a stationary wave?

No. A stationary wave is formed by the superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions along the same string, so that the incident wave and its reflection combine to give fixed nodes and antinodes. Two identical waves travelling in the same direction simply add together to give a larger travelling wave, not a stationary wave.

8.4. A wave is produced along a stretched string but some of its particles permanently show zero displacement. What type of wave is it?

It is a stationary (standing) wave. In a stationary wave, some points, the nodes, are permanently at rest and always show zero displacement, while points between them vibrate with maximum amplitude at the antinodes.

8.5. Explain the terms crest, trough, node and antinode.

A crest is the highest point of a transverse wave, where the displacement is maximum in one direction. A trough is the lowest point, where the displacement is maximum in the opposite direction. A node is a point in a stationary wave where the particles are permanently at rest, with zero amplitude. An antinode is a point in a stationary wave midway between two nodes, where the particles vibrate with maximum amplitude.

8.6. Why does sound travel faster in solids than in gases?

The speed of sound in a medium depends on its elasticity and its density: v = sqrt(E / rho), where E is the elastic modulus. Solids are far more elastic than gases, and their particles are closely packed and strongly linked, so a disturbance is passed on very quickly from particle to particle. The much greater elasticity of solids more than makes up for their greater density, so sound travels faster in solids than in gases.

8.7. How are beats useful in tuning musical instruments?

When two notes of nearly the same frequency are sounded together, beats are heard, and the beat frequency equals the difference of the two frequencies. To tune an instrument, its note is sounded together with a standard note, such as a tuning fork of known frequency. The tension or length of the string is adjusted until the beats slow down and finally disappear, which shows that the two frequencies are now equal and the instrument is in tune.

8.8. When two notes of frequencies f1 and f2 are sounded together, beats are formed. If f1 > f2, what will be the frequency of beats? (i) f1 + f2 (ii) (1/2)(f1 + f2) (iii) f1 - f2 (iv) (1/2)(f1 - f2)

(iii) f1 - f2. The beat frequency is the difference between the two frequencies. Since f1 is greater than f2, the number of beats per second is f1 - f2.

8.9. As a result of a distant explosion, an observer senses a ground tremor and then hears the explosion. Explain the time difference.

The ground tremor is carried by seismic waves travelling through the Earth, which move much faster than sound waves travelling through the air. The observer therefore feels the tremor from the explosion before the sound of the explosion reaches his ears, and the time difference is due to the different speeds of the two kinds of wave over the same distance.

8.10. Explain why sound travels faster in warm air than in cold air.

The speed of sound in a gas increases with temperature, v being proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature. In warm air the molecules move faster and collide more often, so a disturbance is handed on more quickly from molecule to molecule. The speed of sound in air is given by v = v0 + 0.61 t, increasing by about 0.61 m s^-1 for every degree Celsius rise in temperature.

8.11. How should a sound source move with respect to an observer so that the frequency of its sound does not change?

The change in frequency, the Doppler effect, depends on the component of the relative motion along the line joining the source and the observer. If the source moves at right angles to that line, or moves with exactly the same velocity as the observer so that there is no relative motion towards or away from the observer, the apparent frequency does not change.

mcqs.q: What do longitudinal and transverse waves have in common?
options: Both need a material medium in all cases, including light
Both form nodes and antinodes as they travel
Their particles vibrate perpendicular to the direction of propagation
Both carry energy from place to place without net transport of the medium, and both are described by amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period with v = f lambda
mcqs.why: Both longitudinal and transverse waves carry energy from one place to another without any net transport of the medium itself. Both are described by amplitude, wavelength, frequency and period, with wave speed v = f lambda, and both show superposition, reflection, refraction, diffraction and interference. They differ only in the direction of vibration relative to propagation.

mcqs.q: Can two identical waves travelling in the same direction along a string give rise to a stationary wave?
options: Yes, if their amplitudes are equal
Yes, if their frequencies are high enough
No; a stationary wave needs two identical waves travelling in opposite directions, such as a wave and its reflection
Yes, whenever two waves meet on a string
mcqs.why: No. A stationary wave is formed by the superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions along the same string, so that the incident wave and its reflection combine to give fixed nodes and antinodes. Two waves travelling in the same direction simply add to give a larger travelling wave.

mcqs.q: A wave is produced along a stretched string, but some of its particles permanently show zero displacement. What type of wave is it?
options: A stationary (standing) wave, the points of zero displacement being its nodes
A progressive wave of very small amplitude
mcqs.why: It is a stationary (standing) wave. In a stationary wave some points, the nodes, are permanently at rest and always show zero displacement, while points between them vibrate with maximum amplitude at the antinodes.

mcqs.q: What is a node in a stationary wave?
options: A point where the particles are permanently at rest, with zero amplitude
A point midway between two crests
The lowest point of the wave
The highest point of the wave
mcqs.why: A node is a point in a stationary wave where the particles are permanently at rest, with zero amplitude. An antinode is a point midway between two nodes where the particles vibrate with maximum amplitude. A crest and a trough are the highest and lowest points of a transverse wave.

mcqs.q: Why does sound travel faster in solids than in gases?
options: Because solids are denser than gases
Because the particles of a solid are heavier
Because solids are far more elastic, and v = sqrt(E / rho), so their greater elasticity more than makes up for their greater density
Because gases absorb the sound energy
mcqs.why: The speed of sound depends on elasticity and density: v = sqrt(E / rho). Solids are far more elastic than gases and their particles are closely packed and strongly linked, so a disturbance is passed on very quickly. The much greater elasticity of solids more than makes up for their greater density.

mcqs.q: How are beats useful in tuning a musical instrument?
options: The instrument is adjusted until the beats become as fast as possible
Its note is sounded with a standard note and adjusted until the beats slow down and disappear, showing the frequencies are equal
Beats tell the player the amplitude of the note
Beats amplify the standard note so it can be heard
mcqs.why: When two notes of nearly the same frequency sound together, beats are heard at a rate equal to the difference of the frequencies. The instrument's note is sounded with a standard note, such as a tuning fork, and the tension or length is adjusted until the beats slow down and finally disappear, which shows the two frequencies are equal.

mcqs.q: Two notes of frequencies f1 and f2 are sounded together, with f1 > f2. The frequency of the beats formed is:
mcqs.why: The beat frequency is the difference between the two frequencies. Since f1 is greater than f2, the number of beats per second is f1 - f2, as stated in the notes.

mcqs.q: After a distant explosion, an observer senses a ground tremor before hearing the explosion. Why?
options: Because sound is reflected by clouds and takes a longer path
Because the tremor is carried by seismic waves through the Earth, which travel much faster than sound through the air
Because the observer's ears react more slowly than the sense of touch
Because light from the explosion delays the sound
mcqs.why: The ground tremor is carried by seismic waves travelling through the Earth, which move much faster than sound waves travelling through the air. The observer therefore feels the tremor before the sound arrives, the time difference being due to the different speeds of the two kinds of wave over the same distance.

mcqs.q: Why does sound travel faster in warm air than in cold air?
options: Because warm air is less dense at the surface only
Because the speed increases by about 0.61 ms^-1 for every degree Celsius rise in temperature, v being proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature
Because warm air molecules are larger
Because cold air absorbs high frequencies
mcqs.why: The speed of sound in a gas increases with temperature, v being proportional to the square root of the absolute temperature. In warm air the molecules move faster and collide more often, handing the disturbance on more quickly; the speed is v = v0 + 0.61 t, rising by about 0.61 ms^-1 per degree Celsius.

mcqs.q: How should a sound source move with respect to an observer so that the frequency of its sound does not change?
options: Directly towards the observer at constant speed
At right angles to the line joining source and observer, so there is no relative motion along that line
In a circle around the observer at high speed towards him
mcqs.why: The Doppler change in frequency depends on the component of the relative motion along the line joining the source and the observer. If the source moves at right angles to that line, or moves with exactly the same velocity as the observer, there is no approach or recession along the line and the apparent frequency does not change.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
8.1. The wavelength of the signals from a radio transmitter is 1500 m and the frequency is 200 kHz. What is the wavelength for a transmitter operating at 1000 kHz and with what speed the radio waves travel?

Step 1: Speed of the radio waves: v = f lambda = 200 x 10^3 x 1500 = 3.0 x 10^8 m s^-1.

Step 2: Radio waves all travel at the same speed, so for the second transmitter, wavelength = v / f = 3.0 x 10^8 / (1000 x 10^3) = 300 m.

Answer: 300 m, 3 x 10^8 ms^-1 (as printed in the book).

8.2. Two speakers are arranged as shown in Fig. 8.24. The distance between them is 3 m and they emit a constant tone of 344 Hz. A microphone P is moved along a line parallel to and 4.00 m from the line connecting the two speakers. It is found that tone of maximum loudness is heard and displayed on the CRO when microphone is on the centre of the line and directly opposite each speakers. Calculate the speed of sound.

Step 1: At the centre of the line the microphone is equidistant from the two speakers, so the path difference is zero, the first maximum.

Step 2: Directly opposite one speaker, the distance to that speaker is 4.00 m, and to the other speaker it is sqrt(4.00^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(25) = 5.00 m.

Step 3: The path difference there is 5.00 - 4.00 = 1.00 m. Since this is also a maximum, the path difference equals one wavelength: lambda = 1.00 m.

Step 4: Speed of sound v = f lambda = 344 x 1.00 = 344 m s^-1.

Answer: 344 ms^-1 (as printed in the book).

8.3. A stationary wave is established in a string which is 120 cm long and fixed at both ends. The string vibrates in four segments, at a frequency of 120 Hz. Determine its wavelength and the fundamental frequency?

Step 1: Each segment is half a wavelength long. Four segments fill the string, so 120 cm = 2 wavelengths.

Step 2: Wavelength lambda = 120 / 2 = 60 cm = 0.60 m.

Step 3: Speed of the wave v = f lambda = 120 x 0.60 = 72 m s^-1.

Step 4: Fundamental frequency f1 = v / (2 L) = 72 / (2 x 1.20) = 72 / 2.40 = 30 Hz. The given vibration at 120 Hz is the fourth harmonic.

Answer: 0.6 m, 30 Hz (as printed in the book).

8.4. The frequency of the note emitted by a stretched string is 300 Hz. What will be the frequency of this note when; (a) the length of the wave is reduced by one-third without changing the tension. (b) the tension is increased by one-third without changing the length of the wire.

Step 1: (a) Frequency is inversely proportional to length: f is proportional to 1 / L. The new length is L - L/3 = (2/3) L.

Step 2: New frequency = 300 x L / [(2/3) L] = 300 x 3 / 2 = 450 Hz.

Step 3: (b) Frequency is proportional to the square root of tension: f is proportional to sqrt(T). The new tension is T + T/3 = (4/3) T.

Step 4: New frequency = 300 x sqrt(4/3) = 300 x 1.155 = 346 Hz.

Answer: 450 Hz, 346 Hz (as printed in the book).

8.5. An organ pipe has a length of 50 cm. Find the frequency of its fundamental note and the next harmonic when it is (a) open at both ends. (b) closed at one end. (Speed of sound = 350 ms^-1.)

Step 1: (a) Open at both ends: fundamental f1 = v / (2 L) = 350 / (2 x 0.50) = 350 Hz. The next harmonic is the second harmonic, 2 f1 = 700 Hz.

Step 2: (b) Closed at one end: fundamental f1 = v / (4 L) = 350 / (4 x 0.50) = 175 Hz. The next harmonic is the third harmonic, 3 f1 = 525 Hz.

Answer: (a) 350 Hz, 700 Hz, (b) 175 Hz, 525 Hz (as printed in the book).

8.6. A church organ consists of pipes, each open at one end, of different lengths. The minimum length is 30 mm and the longest is 4 m. Calculate the frequency range of the fundamental notes. (Speed of sound = 340 ms^-1.)

Step 1: Each pipe is closed at one end, so its fundamental is f1 = v / (4 L).

Step 2: Longest pipe, L = 4 m: f1 = 340 / (4 x 4) = 340 / 16 = 21.25 Hz, about 21 Hz.

Step 3: Shortest pipe, L = 30 mm = 0.030 m: f1 = 340 / (4 x 0.030) = 340 / 0.12 = 2833 Hz.

Answer: 21 Hz to 2833 Hz (as printed in the book).

8.7. Two tuning forks exhibit beats at a beat frequency of 3 Hz. The frequency of one fork is 256 Hz. Its frequency is then lowered slightly by adding a bit of wax to one of its prong. The two forks then exhibit a beat frequency of 1 Hz. Determine the frequency of the second tuning fork.

Step 1: The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies, so the second fork is either 256 + 3 = 259 Hz or 256 - 3 = 253 Hz.

Step 2: Wax is added to the 256 Hz fork, lowering its frequency slightly. If the second fork were 259 Hz, lowering the first fork would increase the difference, and the beat frequency would grow, not fall.

Step 3: Since the beat frequency instead falls from 3 Hz to 1 Hz, the second fork must be below 256 Hz, so that lowering the first fork brings the two frequencies closer together.

Answer: 253 Hz (as printed in the book).

8.8. Two cars P and Q are travelling along a motorway in the same direction. The leading car P travels at a steady speed of 12 ms^-1; the other car Q, travelling at a steady speed of 20 ms^-1, sound its horn to emit a steady note which P's driver estimates, has a frequency of 830 Hz. What frequency does Q's own driver hear? (Speed of sound = 340 ms^-1.)

Step 1: Q's driver travels with the source, so he hears the true frequency f of the horn. P is the moving observer.

Step 2: Q is behind P and moving faster, so Q approaches P, while P moves away from Q. The Doppler formula gives f' = f x (v - v_observer) / (v - v_source) = f x (340 - 12) / (340 - 20).

Step 3: 830 = f x 328 / 320, so f = 830 x 320 / 328 = 809.8 Hz, about 810 Hz.

Answer: 810 Hz (as printed in the book).

8.9. A train sounds its horn before it sets off from the station and an observer waiting on the platform estimates its frequency at 1200 Hz. The train then moves on and accelerates steadily. Fifty seconds after departure, the driver sounds the horn again and the platform observer estimates the frequency at 1140 Hz. Calculate the train speed 50 s after departure. How far from the station is the train after 50 s? (Speed of sound = 340 ms^-1.)

Step 1: At rest the observer hears the true frequency, f = 1200 Hz.

Step 2: For a source receding from a stationary observer, f' = f x v / (v + v_source). So 1140 = 1200 x 340 / (340 + v_source).

Step 3: 340 + v_source = 1200 x 340 / 1140 = 357.9, so v_source = 17.9 m s^-1.

Step 4: The train started from rest with steady acceleration, so its acceleration is a = v / t = 17.9 / 50 = 0.358 m s^-2.

Step 5: Distance from the station: s = (1/2) a t^2 = (1/2) x 0.358 x 50^2 = 0.179 x 2500 = 447.5 m, about 448 m.

Answer: 17.9 ms^-1, 448 m (as printed in the book).

8.10. The absorption spectrum of faint galaxy is measured and the wavelength of one of the lines identified as the Calcium alpha line is found to be 478 nm. The same line has a wavelength of 397 nm when measured in a laboratory. (a) Is the galaxy moving towards or away from the Earth? (b) Calculate the speed of the galaxy relative to Earth. (Speed of light = 3.0 x 10^8 ms^-1.)

Step 1: (a) The observed wavelength, 478 nm, is longer than the laboratory wavelength, 397 nm. The light is shifted towards the red end of the spectrum, a red shift, which means the galaxy is moving away from the Earth.

Step 2: (b) For speeds much less than the speed of light, the fractional shift equals v / c: (delta lambda) / lambda = v / c.

Step 3: Change in wavelength = 478 - 397 = 81 nm. So v = c x 81 / 397 = 3.0 x 10^8 x 0.204 = 6.12 x 10^7 m s^-1.

Answer: (a) away from the Earth, (b) 6.1 x 10^7 ms^-1 (as printed in the book).

mcqs.q: The signals from a radio transmitter have wavelength 1500 m and frequency 200 kHz. The wavelength for a transmitter operating at 1000 kHz is:
mcqs.why: Working: speed of the radio waves v = f lambda = 200 x 10^3 x 1500 = 3.0 x 10^8 ms^-1. All radio waves travel at this speed, so at 1000 kHz the wavelength = v / f = 3.0 x 10^8 / (1000 x 10^3) = 300 m.

mcqs.q: Two speakers 3 m apart emit a tone of 344 Hz. A microphone moved along a line 4.00 m away hears maximum loudness at the centre and again directly opposite one speaker, where the path difference is one wavelength. The speed of sound is:
mcqs.why: Working: opposite one speaker the distances are 4.00 m and sqrt(16 + 9) = 5.00 m, so the path difference = 5.00 - 4.00 = 1.00 m. This is also a maximum, so lambda = 1.00 m. Speed v = f lambda = 344 x 1.00 = 344 ms^-1.

mcqs.q: A string 120 cm long, fixed at both ends, vibrates in four segments at 120 Hz. Its fundamental frequency is:
mcqs.why: Working: each segment is half a wavelength, so four segments make 2 wavelengths in 120 cm and lambda = 120 / 2 = 60 cm = 0.60 m. Wave speed v = f lambda = 120 x 0.60 = 72 ms^-1. Fundamental frequency f1 = v / (2 L) = 72 / 2.40 = 30 Hz; the 120 Hz vibration is the fourth harmonic.

mcqs.q: A stretched string emits a note of 300 Hz. If the length of the wire is reduced by one-third without changing the tension, the new frequency is:
mcqs.why: Working: frequency is inversely proportional to length. The new length is (2/3) L, so the new frequency = 300 x 3 / 2 = 450 Hz. (If instead the tension were increased by one-third at fixed length, the frequency would become 300 x sqrt(4/3) = 346 Hz.)

mcqs.q: An organ pipe of length 50 cm is closed at one end (speed of sound 350 ms^-1). Its fundamental frequency is:
mcqs.why: Working: for a pipe closed at one end the fundamental is f1 = v / (4 L) = 350 / (4 x 0.50) = 175 Hz, and the next harmonic is the third, 3 f1 = 525 Hz. Open at both ends the same pipe would give f1 = v / (2 L) = 350 Hz with next harmonic 700 Hz.

mcqs.q: A church organ's pipes are open at one end, the longest being 4 m (speed of sound 340 ms^-1). The lowest fundamental frequency is about:
mcqs.why: Working: each pipe is closed at one end, so f1 = v / (4 L). For the longest pipe, L = 4 m: f1 = 340 / 16 = 21.25 Hz, about 21 Hz. The shortest pipe, 30 mm long, gives 340 / 0.12 = 2833 Hz, so the range of fundamentals runs from 21 Hz to 2833 Hz.

mcqs.q: Two tuning forks give beats of 3 Hz. One fork is 256 Hz; when wax is added to it, lowering its frequency slightly, the beats fall to 1 Hz. The frequency of the second fork is:
mcqs.why: The beat frequency is the difference of the two frequencies, so the second fork is either 256 + 3 = 259 Hz or 256 - 3 = 253 Hz. Adding wax lowers the 256 Hz fork; if the second fork were 259 Hz the difference would grow, not fall. Since the beats fall from 3 Hz to 1 Hz, the second fork must be below 256 Hz: 253 Hz.

mcqs.q: Car Q travels at 20 ms^-1 behind car P travelling at 12 ms^-1 in the same direction. Q sounds its horn; P's driver estimates its frequency at 830 Hz (speed of sound 340 ms^-1). The true frequency heard by Q's own driver is:
mcqs.why: Working: Q's driver travels with the source and hears the true frequency f. P is a moving observer receding from the approaching source: 830 = f x (340 - 12) / (340 - 20) = f x 328 / 320. So f = 830 x 320 / 328 = 809.8 Hz, about 810 Hz.

mcqs.q: A train's horn has a true frequency of 1200 Hz. After departure with steady acceleration, a platform observer estimates the receding horn at 1140 Hz fifty seconds later (speed of sound 340 ms^-1). The train's speed then is:
mcqs.why: Working: for a receding source, 1140 = 1200 x 340 / (340 + v). So 340 + v = 1200 x 340 / 1140 = 357.9, giving v = 357.9 - 340 = 17.9 ms^-1. The train is then about 448 m from the station.

mcqs.q: A galaxy's calcium line is observed at 478 nm against its laboratory wavelength of 397 nm. The speed of the galaxy relative to Earth is:
options: 6.1 x 10^7 ms^-1, moving away from Earth
mcqs.why: Working: the observed wavelength is longer than the laboratory one, a red shift, so the galaxy is moving away. Change in wavelength = 478 - 397 = 81 nm. Then v = c x 81 / 397 = 3.0 x 10^8 x 0.204 = 6.12 x 10^7 ms^-1, about 6.1 x 10^7 ms^-1.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.notes_html:
9.1. Under what conditions two or more sources of light behave as coherent sources?

Two or more sources of light behave as coherent sources when they emit waves of the same frequency and wavelength with a constant phase difference between them, so that the interference pattern does not shift with time. In practice this is achieved by dividing the light from a single source, for example by Young's double slit or by a biprism, because two independent sources change their relative phase randomly and cannot give a steady pattern.

9.2. How is the distance between interference fringes affected by the separation between the slits of Young's experiment? Can fringes disappear?

The distance between adjacent fringes is delta y = L lambda / d, where L is the slit-to-screen distance, lambda the wavelength and d the slit separation. The fringe spacing is therefore inversely proportional to the slit separation: increasing d makes the fringes closer together. Yes, the fringes can disappear: when d becomes so large that the fringes are too fine to be resolved by the eye, or so large that the two slits no longer act as coherent sources, the pattern washes out into uniform illumination.

9.3. Can visible light produce interference fringes? Explain.

Yes. Visible light produces interference fringes whenever coherent beams overlap, as in Young's double-slit experiment, where a screen shows alternate bright and dark fringes. Thin films also show it: soap bubbles and oil films on water display coloured fringes, and Newton's rings are interference fringes formed in the thin air film between a lens and a glass plate. The fringes are visible because the wavelength of light is small and the slit separation or film thickness is comparable with it.

9.4. In the Young's experiment, one of the slits is covered with blue filter and other with red filter. What would be the pattern of light intensity on the screen?

No interference pattern would appear. Light passing through the blue filter has a different wavelength from light passing through the red filter, so the two beams are not coherent and cannot interfere. The screen would show only the sum of the two separate single-slit diffraction patterns, a uniform overlapping wash of blue and red light with no bright and dark interference fringes.

9.5. Explain whether the Young's experiment is an experiment for studying interference or diffraction effects of light.

Young's experiment is an experiment for studying interference. The pattern of bright and dark fringes on the screen is produced by the superposition of the two coherent waves coming from the two slits. Diffraction is also involved, because each narrow slit diffracts the light, spreading it out so that the two beams overlap on the screen, but the fringe pattern itself is an interference effect.

9.6. An oil film spreading over a wet footpath shows colours. Explain how does it happen?

The oil forms a very thin film on the water. White light is reflected partly from the top surface of the film and partly from the bottom surface, and the two reflected beams interfere. The path difference between them depends on the thickness of the film, which varies as the oil spreads. For each thickness, some wavelengths interfere constructively and appear bright, while others interfere destructively and are missing, so the film shows different colours at different places.

9.7. Could you obtain Newton's rings with transmitted light? If yes, would the pattern be different from that obtained with reflected light?

Yes, Newton's rings can also be obtained with transmitted light, because the light transmitted through the thin air film also interferes. The pattern is, however, different from the reflected-light pattern: it is complementary, with a bright centre instead of a dark centre, and the rings are much fainter, because the two transmitted beams have very unequal intensities, so the contrast is poor.

9.8. In the white light spectrum obtained with a diffraction grating, the third order image of a wavelength coincides with the fourth order image of a second wavelength. Calculate the ratio of the two wavelengths.

For a diffraction grating, d sin(theta) = n lambda. The third order image of one wavelength and the fourth order image of the second wavelength appear at the same angle, so 3 lambda1 = 4 lambda2, since d and sin(theta) are the same for both. The ratio of the two wavelengths is therefore lambda1 : lambda2 = 4 : 3.

9.9. How would you manage to get more orders of spectra using a diffraction grating?

The maximum order obtainable is n = d / lambda, since sin(theta) cannot exceed 1. To get more orders, increase the grating spacing d, that is, use a coarser grating with fewer lines per centimetre, or use light of shorter wavelength. A finer grating spreads the orders wider apart and improves resolution, but it reduces the number of orders, so the two aims must be balanced.

9.10. Why the polaroid sunglasses are better than ordinary sunglasses?

Ordinary sunglasses only darken the view by absorbing a fraction of all the light. Polaroid sunglasses do more: light reflected from a road or water surface is largely polarized in the horizontal plane, and the polaroid lens is oriented to block that horizontally polarized glare, while letting through the vertically polarized part of the light. They therefore cut the dazzling glare much more effectively than ordinary dark glasses, without making the whole scene equally dark.

9.11. How would you distinguish between un-polarized and plane-polarized lights?

Pass the light through a polarizer, such as a polaroid sheet, and rotate the polarizer. For unpolarized light the transmitted intensity stays the same at every orientation, because it contains vibrations in all directions. For plane-polarized light the transmitted intensity varies: it is maximum when the polarizer's axis is parallel to the direction of polarization, and falls to zero (minimum) when the axis is at right angles to it.

9.12. Fill in the blanks. (i) According to ______ principle, each point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary ______. (ii) In Young's experiment, the distance between two adjacent bright fringes for violet light is ______ than that for green light. (iii) The distance between bright fringes in the interference pattern ______ as the wavelength of light used increases. (iv) A diffraction grating is used to make a diffraction pattern for yellow light and then for red light. The distances between the red spots will be ______ than that for yellow light. (v) The phenomenon of polarization of light reveals that light waves are ______ waves. (vi) A polaroid is a commercial ______. (vii) A polaroid glass ______ glare of light produced at a road surface.

(i) According to Huygen's principle, each point on a wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets. (ii) In Young's experiment, the distance between two adjacent bright fringes for violet light is less than that for green light. (iii) The distance between bright fringes in the interference pattern increases as the wavelength of light used increases. (iv) A diffraction grating is used to make a diffraction pattern for yellow light and then for red light. The distances between the red spots will be greater than that for yellow light. (v) The phenomenon of polarization of light reveals that light waves are transverse waves. (vi) A polaroid is a commercial polarizer. (vii) A polaroid glass reduces glare of light produced at a road surface.

mcqs.q: Under what conditions do two sources of light behave as coherent sources?
options: When they have the same brightness
When they emit waves of the same frequency and wavelength with a constant phase difference between them
When they are placed very close together
When they are two independent lamps of the same colour
mcqs.why: Two sources are coherent when they emit waves of the same frequency and wavelength with a constant phase difference, so the interference pattern does not shift with time. In practice this is achieved by dividing light from a single source, as in Young's double slit, because two independent sources change their relative phase randomly.

mcqs.q: In Young's experiment the fringe spacing is delta y = L lambda / d. How is the spacing affected by the separation d between the slits?
options: Increasing d makes the fringes wider apart
Increasing d makes the fringes closer together, the spacing being inversely proportional to d
The spacing does not depend on d
The spacing is proportional to the square of d
mcqs.why: The distance between adjacent fringes is delta y = L lambda / d, where L is the slit-to-screen distance, lambda the wavelength and d the slit separation. The spacing is inversely proportional to d, so increasing the slit separation makes the fringes closer together; if d becomes too large the fringes wash out.

mcqs.q: In Young's experiment one slit is covered with a blue filter and the other with a red filter. What appears on the screen?
options: Fringes of a mixed purple colour
No interference pattern, only a uniform overlapping wash of blue and red light
Fringes from the blue light only
mcqs.why: No interference pattern appears. Light through the blue filter has a different wavelength from light through the red filter, so the two beams are not coherent and cannot interfere. The screen shows only the sum of the two separate single-slit diffraction patterns.

mcqs.q: Young's double-slit experiment is an experiment for studying which effect of light?
options: Interference; the fringes come from superposition of the two coherent waves, diffraction only spreading the beams so they overlap
mcqs.why: Young's experiment studies interference: the bright and dark fringes are produced by the superposition of the two coherent waves from the two slits. Diffraction is also involved, because each narrow slit diffracts the light and spreads it out so the two beams overlap, but the fringe pattern itself is an interference effect.

mcqs.q: An oil film spreading over a wet footpath shows colours. How does this happen?
options: The oil absorbs all colours except the one seen
Light reflected from the top and bottom surfaces of the thin film interferes; for each thickness some wavelengths reinforce and others cancel
The water beneath disperses the light like a prism
The oil emits coloured light of its own
mcqs.why: The oil forms a very thin film on the water. White light reflects partly from the top surface and partly from the bottom surface, and the two reflected beams interfere. The path difference depends on the film thickness, which varies as the oil spreads, so different colours appear bright at different places.

mcqs.q: Could Newton's rings be obtained with transmitted light, and how would the pattern differ?
options: Yes, but the pattern is identical to the reflected one
Yes; the pattern is complementary, with a bright centre instead of a dark one, and much fainter
Yes; the rings become wider and brighter
mcqs.why: Yes, the light transmitted through the thin air film also interferes. The pattern is complementary to the reflected-light pattern: it has a bright centre instead of a dark centre, and the rings are much fainter because the two transmitted beams have very unequal intensities, so the contrast is poor.

mcqs.q: With a diffraction grating, the third order image of one wavelength coincides with the fourth order image of a second wavelength. The ratio of the two wavelengths lambda1 : lambda2 is:
mcqs.why: Working: for a grating, d sin(theta) = n lambda. Both images appear at the same angle, with the same d, so 3 lambda1 = 4 lambda2. Hence the ratio lambda1 : lambda2 = 4 : 3.

mcqs.q: How would you manage to get more orders of spectra using a diffraction grating?
options: Use a finer grating with more lines per centimetre
Increase the grating spacing d, or use light of shorter wavelength, since the maximum order is n = d / lambda
mcqs.why: The maximum order obtainable is n = d / lambda, since sin(theta) cannot exceed 1. To get more orders, increase the grating spacing d, that is, use a coarser grating with fewer lines per centimetre, or use light of shorter wavelength. A finer grating spreads the orders wider but reduces their number.

mcqs.q: Why are polaroid sunglasses better than ordinary sunglasses?
options: They are darker than ordinary sunglasses
They block the horizontally polarized glare reflected from roads and water, while ordinary sunglasses only darken the whole view
mcqs.why: Ordinary sunglasses only darken the view by absorbing a fraction of all the light. Light reflected from a road or water surface is largely polarized horizontally, and the polaroid lens is oriented to block that horizontally polarized glare while letting the vertically polarized part through, cutting the dazzle much more effectively.

mcqs.q: How would you distinguish between unpolarized and plane-polarized light?
options: By passing it through a coloured filter
By rotating a polarizer in the beam: unpolarized light keeps the same transmitted intensity, while plane-polarized light varies and falls to zero at one orientation
By splitting it with a prism
mcqs.why: Pass the light through a polarizer, such as a polaroid sheet, and rotate it. For unpolarized light the transmitted intensity stays the same at every orientation. For plane-polarized light the intensity varies: maximum when the polarizer's axis is parallel to the direction of polarization and zero when it is at right angles to it.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
9.1. Light of wavelength 546 nm is allowed to illuminate the slits of Young's experiment. The separation between the slits is 0.10 mm and the distance of the screen from the slits where interference effects are observed is 20 cm. At what angle the first minimum will fall? What will be the linear distance on the screen between adjacent maxima?

Step 1: First minimum: d sin(theta) = (m + 1/2) lambda with m = 0, so sin(theta) = lambda / (2 d) = 546 x 10^-9 / (2 x 0.10 x 10^-3) = 546 x 10^-9 / (2.0 x 10^-4) = 2.73 x 10^-3.

Step 2: For such a small angle, theta in radians is about sin(theta) = 2.73 x 10^-3 rad = 2.73 x 10^-3 x (180 / pi) degrees = 0.156 degrees, about 0.16 degrees.

Step 3: Linear distance between adjacent maxima (fringe spacing) = L lambda / d = 0.20 x 546 x 10^-9 / (0.10 x 10^-3) = 1.092 x 10^-3 m = 1.09 mm, about 1.1 mm.

Answer: 0.16 degrees, 1.1 mm (as printed in the book).

9.2. Calculate the wavelength of light, which illuminates two slits 0.5 mm apart and produces an interference pattern on a screen placed 200 cm away from the slits. The first bright fringe is observed at a distance of 2.40 mm from the central bright image.

Step 1: For a bright fringe, y = m L lambda / d, with m = 1 for the first bright fringe.

Step 2: So lambda = y d / L = (2.40 x 10^-3 x 0.5 x 10^-3) / 2.00.

Step 3: lambda = 1.20 x 10^-6 / 2.00 = 6.0 x 10^-7 m = 600 nm.

Answer: 600 nm (as printed in the book).

9.3. In a double slit experiment the second order maximum occurs at theta = 0.25 degrees. The wavelength is 650 nm. Determine the slit separation.

Step 1: For a bright fringe, d sin(theta) = m lambda, with m = 2.

Step 2: d = m lambda / sin(theta) = 2 x 650 x 10^-9 / sin(0.25 degrees).

Step 3: sin(0.25 degrees) = 0.004363, so d = 1300 x 10^-9 / 0.004363 = 2.98 x 10^-4 m = 0.30 mm.

Answer: 0.30 mm (as printed in the book).

9.4. A monochromatic light of lambda = 588 nm is allowed to fall on the half silvered glass plate G1, in the Michelson Interferometer. If mirror M1 is moved through 0.233 mm, how many fringes will be observed to shift?

Step 1: When the mirror moves a distance L, the path difference changes by 2 L, and one fringe shifts for each wavelength of path change: number of fringes m = 2 L / lambda.

Step 2: m = 2 x 0.233 x 10^-3 / (588 x 10^-9) = 466 x 10^-6 / (588 x 10^-9) = 792.5.

Step 3: About 792 fringes shift.

Answer: 792 (as printed in the book; the unrounded value is 792.5).

9.5. A second order spectrum is formed at an angle of 38.0 degrees when light falls normally on a diffraction grating having 5400 lines per centimetre. Determine wavelength of the light used.

Step 1: Grating spacing d = 1 cm / 5400 = 1.852 x 10^-6 m.

Step 2: For a grating, d sin(theta) = n lambda, with n = 2.

Step 3: lambda = d sin(theta) / n = 1.852 x 10^-6 x sin(38.0 degrees) / 2 = 1.852 x 10^-6 x 0.6157 / 2 = 5.70 x 10^-7 m = 570 nm.

Answer: 570 nm (as printed in the book).

9.6. A light is incident normally on a grating which has 2500 lines per centimetre. Compute the wavelength of a spectral line for which the deviation in second order is 15.0 degrees.

Step 1: Grating spacing d = 1 cm / 2500 = 4.0 x 10^-6 m.

Step 2: d sin(theta) = n lambda, with n = 2, so lambda = d sin(theta) / 2 = 4.0 x 10^-6 x sin(15.0 degrees) / 2.

Step 3: sin(15.0 degrees) = 0.2588, so lambda = 4.0 x 10^-6 x 0.2588 / 2 = 5.18 x 10^-7 m = 518 nm.

Answer: 518 nm (as printed in the book).

9.7. Sodium light (lambda = 589 nm) is incident normally on a grating having 3000 lines per centimetre. What is the highest order of the spectrum obtained with this grating?

Step 1: Grating spacing d = 1 cm / 3000 = 3.333 x 10^-6 m.

Step 2: The highest order is reached when sin(theta) = 1: n_max = d / lambda = 3.333 x 10^-6 / (589 x 10^-9) = 5.66.

Step 3: Only whole orders occur, so the highest order actually obtained is the 5th order.

Answer: 5th (as printed in the book).

9.8. Blue light of wavelength 480 nm illuminates a diffraction grating. The second order image is formed at an angle of 30 degrees from the central image. How many lines in a centimetre of the grating have been ruled?

Step 1: Grating spacing from d sin(theta) = n lambda: d = n lambda / sin(theta) = 2 x 480 x 10^-9 / sin(30 degrees) = 960 x 10^-9 / 0.5 = 1.92 x 10^-6 m.

Step 2: In centimetres, d = 1.92 x 10^-4 cm.

Step 3: Lines per centimetre = 1 / d = 1 / (1.92 x 10^-4) = 5208, about 5.2 x 10^3 lines per cm.

Answer: 5.2 x 10^3 lines per cm (as printed in the book).

9.9. X-rays of wavelength 0.150 nm are observed to undergo a first order reflection at a Bragg angle of 13.3 degrees from a quartz (SiO2) crystal. What is the interplanar spacing of the reflecting planes in the crystal?

Step 1: Bragg's law: 2 d sin(theta) = n lambda, with n = 1.

Step 2: d = n lambda / (2 sin(theta)) = 0.150 / (2 x sin(13.3 degrees)).

Step 3: sin(13.3 degrees) = 0.2300, so d = 0.150 / 0.460 = 0.326 nm.

Answer: 0.326 nm (as printed in the book).

9.10. An X-ray beam of wavelength lambda undergoes a first order reflection from a crystal when its angle of incidence to a crystal face is 26.5 degrees, and an X-ray beam of wavelength 0.097 nm undergoes a third order reflection when its angle of incidence to that face is 60.0 degrees. Assuming that the two beams reflect from the same family of planes, calculate (a) the interplanar spacing of the planes and (b) the wavelength lambda.

Step 1: (a) For the second beam, Bragg's law gives 2 d sin(theta) = n lambda: 2 d sin(60.0 degrees) = 3 x 0.097 = 0.291 nm.

Step 2: d = 0.291 / (2 x 0.8660) = 0.291 / 1.732 = 0.168 nm.

Step 3: (b) For the first beam, 2 d sin(theta) = lambda, with n = 1: lambda = 2 x 0.168 x sin(26.5 degrees) = 0.336 x 0.4462 = 0.150 nm.

Answer: (a) 0.168 nm (b) 0.150 nm (as printed in the book).

mcqs.q: In Young's experiment (lambda = 546 nm, slit separation 0.10 mm, screen 20 cm away), the linear distance between adjacent maxima is:
mcqs.why: Working: fringe spacing = L lambda / d = 0.20 x 546 x 10^-9 / (0.10 x 10^-3) = 1.092 x 10^-3 m = 1.09 mm, about 1.1 mm. The first minimum falls at an angle of about 0.16 degrees.

mcqs.q: Two slits 0.5 mm apart produce an interference pattern on a screen 200 cm away, with the first bright fringe 2.40 mm from the central bright image. The wavelength of the light is:
mcqs.why: Working: for the first bright fringe, lambda = y d / L = (2.40 x 10^-3 x 0.5 x 10^-3) / 2.00. The numerator is 1.20 x 10^-6, so lambda = 1.20 x 10^-6 / 2.00 = 6.0 x 10^-7 m = 600 nm.

mcqs.q: In a double-slit experiment the second order maximum occurs at theta = 0.25 degrees with lambda = 650 nm. The slit separation is:
mcqs.why: Working: d = m lambda / sin(theta) = 2 x 650 x 10^-9 / sin(0.25 degrees). With sin(0.25 degrees) = 0.004363: d = 1300 x 10^-9 / 0.004363 = 2.98 x 10^-4 m = 0.30 mm.

mcqs.q: In a Michelson interferometer using light of lambda = 588 nm, mirror M1 is moved through 0.233 mm. How many fringes shift past the reference point?
mcqs.why: Working: moving the mirror by L changes the path difference by 2 L, and one fringe shifts for each wavelength of path change. Path change = 0.466 mm, which is 466000 nm. Number of fringes = 466000 / 588 = 792.5, so about 792 fringes shift.

mcqs.q: A second order spectrum is formed at 38.0 degrees with a grating of 5400 lines per centimetre. The wavelength of the light is:
mcqs.why: Working: grating spacing d = 1 / 5400 cm = 1.852 x 10^-6 m. Then lambda = d sin(theta) / n = 1.852 x 10^-6 x 0.6157 / 2. The product 1.852 x 10^-6 x 0.6157 = 1.140 x 10^-6, and dividing by 2 gives 5.70 x 10^-7 m = 570 nm.

mcqs.q: Light falls normally on a grating of 2500 lines per centimetre and a spectral line is deviated by 15.0 degrees in second order. Its wavelength is:
mcqs.why: Working: grating spacing d = 1 / 2500 cm = 4.0 x 10^-6 m. lambda = d sin(theta) / n = 4.0 x 10^-6 x 0.2588 / 2. The product 4.0 x 10^-6 x 0.2588 = 1.035 x 10^-6, and dividing by 2 gives 5.18 x 10^-7 m = 518 nm.

mcqs.q: Sodium light (lambda = 589 nm) falls normally on a grating of 3000 lines per centimetre. The highest order of spectrum obtained is:
mcqs.why: Working: grating spacing d = 1 / 3000 cm = 3.333 x 10^-6 m. The highest order is reached at sin(theta) = 1: n_max = d / lambda = 3.333 x 10^-6 / (589 x 10^-9) = 5.66. Only whole orders occur, so the highest order actually obtained is the 5th.

mcqs.q: Blue light of wavelength 480 nm gives a second order image at 30 degrees from the central image of a grating. How many lines per centimetre does the grating have?
mcqs.why: Working: d = n lambda / sin(theta) = 2 x 480 x 10^-9 / 0.5 = 1.92 x 10^-6 m = 1.92 x 10^-4 cm. Lines per centimetre = 1 / d = 1 / (1.92 x 10^-4) = 5208, about 5.2 x 10^3 lines per cm.

mcqs.q: X-rays of wavelength 0.150 nm undergo first order Bragg reflection at 13.3 degrees from a quartz crystal. The interplanar spacing is:
mcqs.why: Working: Bragg's law 2 d sin(theta) = n lambda with n = 1 gives d = 0.150 / (2 x sin(13.3 degrees)). With sin(13.3 degrees) = 0.2300: d = 0.150 / 0.460 = 0.326 nm.

mcqs.q: An X-ray beam of wavelength 0.097 nm undergoes third order reflection at 60.0 degrees from a family of crystal planes. The interplanar spacing is:
mcqs.why: Working: Bragg's law: 2 d sin(60.0 degrees) = 3 x 0.097 = 0.291 nm. With sin(60.0 degrees) = 0.8660: d = 0.291 / 1.732 = 0.168 nm. The companion first-order beam at 26.5 degrees then has wavelength 2 x 0.168 x 0.4462 = 0.150 nm.

lessons.title: Questions
lessons.notes_html:
10.1. What do you understand by linear magnification and angular magnification? Explain how a convex lens is used as a magnifier?

Linear magnification is the ratio of the size of the image to the size of the object, m = size of image / size of object = image distance / object distance. Angular magnification, or magnifying power, is the ratio of the angle subtended at the eye by the image formed with the instrument to the angle subtended at the unaided eye by the object placed at the least distance of distinct vision, 25 cm. A convex lens is used as a magnifier by placing the object within its focal length. The lens then forms an erect, virtual and magnified image on the same side as the object, at the near point or at infinity, and the eye sees the object under a larger angle than it would unaided.

10.2. Explain the difference between angular magnification and resolving power of an optical instrument. What limits the magnification of an optical instrument?

Angular magnification tells how much larger an object appears, that is, how many times bigger the angle subtended at the eye becomes. Resolving power tells how much detail can be seen, that is, the smallest separation between two close points that can still be distinguished as two separate points. The magnification of an optical instrument is limited by its resolving power: magnifying beyond it only enlarges a blurred image without revealing new detail, a condition called empty magnification. It is also limited by the aberrations of the lenses and by the loss of brightness as magnification increases.

10.3. Why would it be advantageous to use blue light with a compound microscope?

The resolving power of a microscope improves as the wavelength of the light used decreases, since the smallest distance that can be resolved is proportional to the wavelength. Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red light or the average wavelength of white light, so a microscope used with blue light can resolve finer detail and show smaller structures distinctly.

10.4. One can buy a cheap microscope for use by the children. The images seen in such a microscope have coloured edges. Why is this so?

Because of chromatic aberration. A cheap microscope uses simple, uncorrected lenses, and the refractive index of glass is different for different colours, so each colour is brought to a focus at a slightly different place. The image of a white object is therefore fringed with colours at its edges. Good microscopes use achromatic combinations of lenses that correct this defect.

10.5. Describe with the help of diagrams, how (a) a single biconvex lens can be used as a magnifying glass. (b) biconvex lenses can be arranged to form a microscope.

(a) A single biconvex lens as a magnifying glass: the object is placed within the focal length of the lens. A ray from the top of the object parallel to the axis is refracted through the far focus, and a ray through the centre of the lens passes undeviated. On the eye side these rays diverge, and their back-projections meet at an erect, virtual, magnified image on the same side of the lens as the object. (b) A microscope from two biconvex lenses: the objective, of very short focal length, is placed close to the object and forms a real, inverted, magnified intermediate image just inside the focal length of the eyepiece. The eyepiece then acts as a magnifying glass, forming a final virtual, magnified image at the least distance of distinct vision.

10.6. If a person was looking through a telescope at the full moon, how would the appearance of the moon be changed by covering half of the objective lens.

The appearance of the moon would not be changed in shape or size, only dimmed. Every part of the image is formed by light passing through the whole of the objective lens, so covering half of the objective only cuts off half the light. The full moon would still be seen complete, but fainter.

10.7. A magnifying glass gives a five times enlarged image at a distance of 25 cm from the lens. Find, by ray diagram, the focal length of the lens.

The magnifying power with the image at the near point is M = 1 + d / f, where d = 25 cm. So 5 = 1 + 25 / f, giving 25 / f = 4, and f = 25 / 4 = 6.25 cm. By the ray diagram, the object is placed 5 cm from the lens: with the virtual image at 25 cm, the lens formula gives an object distance of 5.0 cm, and the image is five times as large as the object.

10.8. Identify the correct answer. (i) The resolving power of a compound microscope depends on; a. Length of the microscope. b. The diameter of the objective lens. c. The diameter of the eyepiece. d. The position of an observer's eye with regard to the eye lens. (ii) The resolving power of an astronomical telescope depends on: a. The focal length of the objective lens. b. The least distance of distinct vision of the observer. c. The focal length of the eye lens. d. The diameter of the objective lens.

(i) b. The diameter of the objective lens. The resolving power of a microscope depends on the aperture of its objective, which gathers the light and fixes the smallest distance that can be resolved; it does not depend on the length of the microscope, the eyepiece, or the position of the eye. (ii) d. The diameter of the objective lens. The resolving power of an astronomical telescope is proportional to the diameter of its objective, since a larger objective collects more light and resolves smaller angles.

10.9. Draw sketches showing the different light paths through a single-mode and a multi mode fibre. Why is the single-mode fibre preferred in telecommunications?

In a single-mode fibre the light travels along essentially one path, straight down the centre of the core, so all parts of a pulse arrive together. In a multi-mode fibre the light travels along many paths at different angles, bouncing off the core-cladding boundary, so the parts of a pulse that take steeper paths arrive later than those that take straighter paths. The single-mode fibre is preferred in telecommunications because it has no such modal dispersion: pulses stay sharp over long distances, so signals can be sent faster and with less distortion.

10.10. How the light signal is transmitted through the optical fibre?

Light is transmitted through an optical fibre by total internal reflection. A ray entering the core strikes the boundary between the core, of higher refractive index, and the cladding, of lower refractive index, at an angle greater than the critical angle, and is reflected back into the core instead of escaping. It is reflected again and again along the fibre, zig-zagging its way to the far end with very little loss.

10.11. How the power is lost in optical fibre through dispersion? Explain.

Power is lost in an optical fibre through dispersion in two ways. In modal dispersion, different modes travel different path lengths and arrive at different times, so a pulse spreads out. In material (chromatic) dispersion, different wavelengths travel at different speeds in the glass, so a pulse containing several wavelengths also spreads out. As the pulse spreads, its peak power falls and neighbouring pulses begin to overlap, so the signal becomes weaker and harder to read. Absorption and scattering in the glass add further loss of power.

mcqs.q: What is meant by angular magnification (magnifying power) of an optical instrument?
options: The ratio of the size of the image to the size of the object
The ratio of the angle subtended at the eye by the image formed with the instrument to the angle subtended at the unaided eye by the object at the least distance of distinct vision, 25 cm
The ratio of the image distance to the object distance
The smallest separation that can be distinguished as two points
mcqs.why: Angular magnification is the ratio of the angle subtended at the eye by the image formed with the instrument to the angle subtended at the unaided eye by the object placed at the least distance of distinct vision, 25 cm. Linear magnification, by contrast, is the ratio of image size to object size.

mcqs.q: How is a convex lens used as a magnifier?
options: The object is placed beyond the focal length and a real image is viewed
The object is placed within the focal length, so the lens forms an erect, virtual and magnified image on the same side as the object
The object is placed exactly at the centre of curvature
Two convex lenses are always needed
mcqs.why: A convex lens is used as a magnifier by placing the object within its focal length. The lens then forms an erect, virtual and magnified image on the same side as the object, at the near point or at infinity, and the eye sees the object under a larger angle than it would unaided.

mcqs.q: What limits the magnification of an optical instrument?
options: The length of the instrument's tube
The brightness of the object only
Its resolving power: magnifying beyond it only enlarges a blurred image without revealing new detail (empty magnification)
The focal length of the eyepiece only
mcqs.why: Angular magnification tells how much larger an object appears; resolving power tells how much detail can be seen. The magnification is limited by the resolving power: magnifying beyond it gives empty magnification, an enlarged blur with no new detail. Aberrations and loss of brightness also limit it.

mcqs.q: Why would it be advantageous to use blue light with a compound microscope?
options: Blue light is brighter than white light
Blue light has a shorter wavelength, and the smallest distance that can be resolved is proportional to the wavelength, so finer detail can be resolved
Blue light passes through glass without refraction
mcqs.why: The resolving power of a microscope improves as the wavelength of the light decreases, since the smallest resolvable distance is proportional to the wavelength. Blue light has a shorter wavelength than red light or average white light, so the microscope can resolve finer detail with it.

mcqs.q: The images seen in a cheap children's microscope have coloured edges. Why is this so?
options: Because of chromatic aberration: the simple uncorrected lenses focus different colours at slightly different places
Because the objects themselves are coloured
Because the light source is coloured
Because of spherical aberration of the mirror
mcqs.why: Because of chromatic aberration. A cheap microscope uses simple, uncorrected lenses, and the refractive index of glass differs for different colours, so each colour is brought to a focus at a slightly different place and the image of a white object is fringed with colours. Good microscopes use achromatic combinations to correct this.

mcqs.q: A person looks through a telescope at the full moon and half of the objective lens is covered. How does the appearance of the moon change?
options: Only half of the moon remains visible
The moon appears the same in shape and size, only dimmer
mcqs.why: Every part of the image is formed by light passing through the whole of the objective lens, so covering half of the objective only cuts off half the light. The full moon is still seen complete, in the same shape and size, but fainter.

mcqs.q: A magnifying glass gives a five times enlarged image at a distance of 25 cm from the lens. The focal length of the lens is:
mcqs.why: Working: the magnifying power with the image at the near point is M = 1 + d / f, with d = 25 cm. So 25 / f = 4, giving f = 25 / 4 = 6.25 cm. The ray diagram confirms this: the object is placed 5 cm from the lens and the virtual image at 25 cm is five times as large.

mcqs.q: The resolving power of a compound microscope depends on:
options: The position of the observer's eye
The diameter of the objective lens
mcqs.why: The resolving power of a microscope depends on the aperture (diameter) of its objective, which gathers the light and fixes the smallest distance that can be resolved. It does not depend on the length of the microscope, the eyepiece, or the position of the eye.

mcqs.q: Why is a single-mode fibre preferred in telecommunications over a multi-mode fibre?
options: Light travels along essentially one path, so there is no modal dispersion and pulses stay sharp over long distances
It can carry more colours of light
It does not need total internal reflection
mcqs.why: In a single-mode fibre the light travels along essentially one path down the centre of the core, so all parts of a pulse arrive together. In a multi-mode fibre the many paths arrive at different times and pulses spread out. With no modal dispersion, single-mode signals can be sent faster and with less distortion over long distances.

mcqs.q: How is a light signal transmitted through an optical fibre?
options: By refraction at the core-cladding boundary
By total internal reflection: the ray strikes the core-cladding boundary at an angle greater than the critical angle and is reflected back into the core again and again
By diffraction along the fibre axis
mcqs.why: Light is transmitted by total internal reflection. A ray entering the core strikes the boundary with the cladding (of lower refractive index) at an angle greater than the critical angle and is reflected back into the core instead of escaping, zig-zagging its way to the far end with very little loss.

lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
10.1. A converging lens of focal length 5.0 cm is used as a magnifying glass. If the near point of the observer is 25 cm and the lens is held close to the eye, calculate (i) the distance of the object from the lens (ii) the angular magnification. What is the angular magnification when the final image is formed at infinity?

Step 1: The final image is at the near point, 25 cm from the lens, and virtual, so with the lens formula, 1 / f = 1 / v - 1 / u, with v = -25 cm and f = 5.0 cm: 1 / 5.0 = -1 / 25 - 1 / u.

Step 2: So 1 / u = -1 / 25 - 1 / 5.0 = -(1 + 5) / 25 = -6 / 25, giving u = -4.17 cm. (i) The object is 4.2 cm from the lens.

Step 3: (ii) Angular magnification with the image at the near point: M = 1 + d / f = 1 + 25 / 5.0 = 6.0.

Step 4: With the final image at infinity, M = d / f = 25 / 5.0 = 5.0.

Answer: (i) 4.2 cm (ii) 6.0 ; 5.0 (as printed in the book).

10.2. A telescope objective has focal length 96 cm and diameter 12 cm. Calculate the focal length and minimum diameter of a simple eye piece lens for use with the telescope, if the linear magnification required is 24 times and all the light transmitted by the objective from a distant point on the telescope axis is to fall on the eye piece.

Step 1: Magnifying power of the telescope M = f_objective / f_eyepiece = 24, so f_eyepiece = 96 / 24 = 4.0 cm.

Step 2: For all the light from the objective to fall on the eyepiece, the diameter of the eyepiece must be at least the diameter of the beam, which is reduced by the magnification: diameter of eyepiece = diameter of objective / M = 12 / 24 = 0.50 cm.

Answer: f_e = 4.0 cm, dia = 0.50 cm (as printed in the book).

10.3. A telescope is made of an objective of focal length 20 cm and an eye piece of 5.0 cm, both convex lenses. Find the angular magnification.

Step 1: Angular magnification of a telescope in normal adjustment: M = f_objective / f_eyepiece.

Step 2: M = 20 / 5.0 = 4.0.

Answer: 4.0 (as printed in the book).

10.4. A simple astronomical telescope in normal adjustment has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eye piece of focal length 5.0 cm. (i) Where is the final image formed? (ii) Calculate the angular magnification.

Step 1: (i) In normal adjustment the intermediate image formed by the objective lies at the focal point of the eyepiece, so the eyepiece forms the final image at infinity, for relaxed viewing.

Step 2: (ii) Angular magnification M = f_objective / f_eyepiece = 100 / 5.0 = 20.

Answer: (i) infinity (ii) 20 (as printed in the book).

10.5. A point object is placed on the axis of and 3.6 cm from a thin convex lens of focal length 3.0 cm. A second thin convex lens of focal length 16.0 cm is placed coaxial with the first and 26.0 cm from it on the side away from the object. Find the position of the final image produced by the two lenses.

Step 1: Image by the first lens: 1 / v1 = 1 / f1 + 1 / u1 in magnitudes, 1 / v1 = 1 / 3.0 - 1 / 3.6 = 0.3333 - 0.2778 = 0.0556, so v1 = 18 cm. The first lens forms a real image 18 cm beyond it.

Step 2: The second lens is 26.0 cm from the first, so this image is 26.0 - 18 = 8.0 cm in front of the second lens and acts as its object.

Step 3: Image by the second lens: 1 / v2 = 1 / f2 - 1 / u2 = 1 / 16.0 - 1 / 8.0 = 0.0625 - 0.125 = -0.0625, so v2 = -16 cm.

Step 4: The negative sign means the final image is virtual, 16 cm in front of the second lens, on the side from which the light comes.

Answer: 16 cm from second lens (as printed in the book).

10.6. A compound microscope has lenses of focal length 1.0 cm and 3.0 cm. An object is placed 1.2 cm from the object lens. If a virtual image is formed, 25 cm from the eye, calculate the separation of the lenses and the magnification of the instrument.

Step 1: Image by the objective: 1 / v = 1 / f_o - 1 / u = 1 / 1.0 - 1 / 1.2 = 1 - 0.8333 = 0.1667, so v = 6.0 cm. The objective forms a real image 6.0 cm beyond it, with linear magnification 6.0 / 1.2 = 5.

Step 2: The eyepiece forms the final virtual image at 25 cm: 1 / u_e = -1 / 25 - 1 / f_e = -0.04 - 0.3333 = -0.3733, so the intermediate image is 2.68 cm in front of the eyepiece.

Step 3: Separation of the lenses = 6.0 + 2.68 = 8.68 cm, about 8.7 cm.

Step 4: Magnifying power of the eyepiece = 1 + d / f_e = 1 + 25 / 3.0 = 9.33. Total magnification = 5 x 9.33 = 46.7, about 47.

Answer: 8.7 cm, 47 (as printed in the book).

10.7. Sodium light of wavelength 589 nm is used to view an object under a microscope. If the aperture of the objective is 0.90 cm, (i) find the limiting angle of resolution, (ii) using visible light of any wavelength, what is the maximum limit of resolution for this microscope.

Step 1: (i) Limiting angle of resolution theta = 1.22 lambda / D = 1.22 x 589 x 10^-9 / 0.0090 = 7.99 x 10^-5 rad, about 8.0 x 10^-5 rad.

Step 2: (ii) The best resolution comes from the shortest visible wavelength, violet light, about 400 nm: theta = 1.22 x 400 x 10^-9 / 0.0090 = 5.42 x 10^-5 rad, about 5.4 x 10^-5 rad.

Answer: (i) 8.0 x 10^-5 rad, (ii) 5.4 x 10^-5 rad (as printed in the book).

10.8. An astronomical telescope having magnifying power of 5 consist of two thin lenses 24 cm apart. Find the focal lengths of the lenses.

Step 1: In normal adjustment the separation of the lenses equals the sum of the focal lengths: f_o + f_e = 24 cm. The magnifying power is M = f_o / f_e = 5, so f_o = 5 f_e.

Step 2: Substituting: 5 f_e + f_e = 24, so 6 f_e = 24, f_e = 4 cm and f_o = 20 cm.

Answer: 20 cm, 4 cm (as printed in the book).

10.9. A glass light pipe in air will totally internally reflect a light ray if its angle of incidence is at least 39 degrees. What is the minimum angle for total internal reflection if pipe is in water? (Refractive Index of water = 1.33.)

Step 1: In air, the critical angle is 39 degrees, so the refractive index of the glass is n = 1 / sin(39 degrees) = 1 / 0.6293 = 1.589.

Step 2: In water, sin(critical angle) = n_water / n_glass = 1.33 / 1.589 = 0.8370.

Step 3: Critical angle = sin^-1(0.8370) = 56.9 degrees, about 57 degrees.

Answer: 57 degrees (as printed in the book).

10.10. The refractive index of the core and cladding of an optical fibre are 1.6 and 1.4 respectively. Calculate (i) the critical angle for the interface (ii) the maximum angle of incidence in the air of a ray which enters the fibre and is incident at the critical angle on the interface.

Step 1: (i) Critical angle at the core-cladding interface: sin(c) = n_cladding / n_core = 1.4 / 1.6 = 0.875, so c = sin^-1(0.875) = 61.0 degrees, about 61 degrees.

Step 2: (ii) At the entrance face, the ray in the core makes an angle of (90 degrees - 61 degrees) = 29 degrees with the normal to the entrance face. By Snell's law at the entrance, sin(theta) = n_core x sin(29 degrees) = 1.6 x 0.4848 = 0.7757.

Step 3: theta = sin^-1(0.7757) = 50.9 degrees, about 51 degrees.

Answer: (i) 61 degrees, (ii) 51 degrees (as printed in the book).

mcqs.q: A converging lens of focal length 5.0 cm is used as a magnifying glass, the near point being 25 cm. The angular magnification with the final image at the near point is:
mcqs.why: Working: with the image at the near point, M = 1 + d / f = 1 + 25 / 5.0. Now 25 / 5.0 = 5.0, so M = 1 + 5.0 = 6.0. The object sits 4.2 cm from the lens. With the final image at infinity instead, M = d / f = 5.0.

mcqs.q: A telescope objective has focal length 96 cm. For a linear magnification of 24 times, the focal length of the eyepiece must be:
mcqs.why: Working: magnifying power M = f_objective / f_eyepiece = 24, so f_eyepiece = 96 / 24 = 4.0 cm. For all the light from the 12 cm objective to fall on the eyepiece, its minimum diameter is 12 / 24 = 0.50 cm.

mcqs.q: A telescope is made of an objective of focal length 20 cm and an eyepiece of 5.0 cm. Its angular magnification is:
mcqs.why: Working: the angular magnification of a telescope in normal adjustment is M = f_objective / f_eyepiece = 20 / 5.0 = 4.0.

mcqs.q: A simple astronomical telescope in normal adjustment has an objective of focal length 100 cm and an eyepiece of 5.0 cm. Its angular magnification is:
options: 20, with the final image at infinity
5, with the final image at the near point
mcqs.why: Working: in normal adjustment the intermediate image lies at the focal point of the eyepiece, so the final image is formed at infinity for relaxed viewing. Angular magnification M = f_objective / f_eyepiece = 100 / 5.0 = 20.

mcqs.q: A point object 3.6 cm from a convex lens (f = 3.0 cm) is imaged by a second convex lens (f = 16.0 cm) placed 26.0 cm beyond the first. The final image is:
options: Real, 16 cm beyond the second lens
Virtual, 16 cm in front of the second lens
Real, 18 cm beyond the first lens only
mcqs.why: Working: the first lens forms a real image at v1 where 1 / v1 = 1 / 3.0 - 1 / 3.6 = 0.0556, so v1 = 18 cm beyond it. This image is 26.0 - 18 = 8.0 cm in front of the second lens. For the second lens, 1 / v2 = 1 / 16.0 - 1 / 8.0 = -0.0625, so v2 = -16 cm: a virtual image 16 cm in front of the second lens.

mcqs.q: A compound microscope has lenses of focal length 1.0 cm (objective) and 3.0 cm (eyepiece); the object is 1.2 cm from the objective and the final virtual image is 25 cm from the eye. The magnification of the instrument is about:
mcqs.why: Working: the objective forms an image at v where 1 / v = 1 / 1.0 - 1 / 1.2 = 0.1667, so v = 6.0 cm, with linear magnification 6.0 / 1.2 = 5. The eyepiece magnifies by 1 + 25 / 3.0 = 9.33. Total magnification = 5 x 9.33 = 46.7, about 47. The lens separation is 8.7 cm.

mcqs.q: Sodium light (589 nm) is used under a microscope whose objective aperture is 0.90 cm. The limiting angle of resolution is:
mcqs.why: Working: limiting angle theta = 1.22 lambda / D = 1.22 x 589 x 10^-9 / 0.0090 = 7.99 x 10^-5 rad, about 8.0 x 10^-5 rad. With the shortest visible wavelength (violet, 400 nm) the best possible value for this microscope is 5.4 x 10^-5 rad.

mcqs.q: An astronomical telescope of magnifying power 5 has its two thin lenses 24 cm apart in normal adjustment. The focal length of the objective is:
mcqs.why: Working: in normal adjustment f_o + f_e = 24 cm and M = f_o / f_e = 5, so f_o = 5 f_e. Substituting: 6 f_e = 24, so f_e = 24 / 6 = 4 cm and f_o = 5 x 4 = 20 cm.

mcqs.q: A glass light pipe in air totally internally reflects a ray if its angle of incidence is at least 39 degrees. If the pipe is placed in water (refractive index 1.33), the minimum angle for total internal reflection becomes:
mcqs.why: Working: in air the critical angle is 39 degrees, so the refractive index of the glass is n = 1 / sin(39 degrees) = 1 / 0.6293 = 1.589. In water, sin(critical angle) = 1.33 / 1.589 = 0.8370, so the critical angle = 56.9 degrees, about 57 degrees.

mcqs.q: The refractive indices of the core and cladding of an optical fibre are 1.6 and 1.4. The critical angle at the core-cladding interface is:
mcqs.why: Working: sin(critical angle) = n_cladding / n_core = 1.4 / 1.6 = 0.875, so the critical angle = 61.0 degrees, about 61 degrees. The maximum angle of incidence in air for a ray entering the fibre and striking the interface at this angle is about 51 degrees.

lessons.notes_html:
11.1. Why is the average velocity of the molecules in a gas zero but the average of the square of velocities is not zero?

The molecules of a gas move in all directions with equal probability, so their vector velocities cancel one another on average and the mean velocity is zero. The square of a velocity, however, is always positive, whether the molecule moves to the left or to the right, so the squares do not cancel, and the average of the squares, <v^2>, is not zero. Its square root is the root mean square speed of the molecules.

11.2. Why does the pressure of a gas in a car tyre increase when it is driven through some distance?

When a car is driven, the tyre is repeatedly flexed and friction acts between the tyre and the road, so work is done on the tyre and the air inside it, and the temperature of the air rises. The volume of the tyre is almost constant, and at constant volume the pressure of a gas is proportional to its absolute temperature, so the pressure in the tyre increases.

11.3. A system undergoes from state P1 V1 to state P2 V2 as shown in Fig. 11.12. What will be the change in internal energy?

Zero. The curve in Fig. 11.12 is marked 'Constant Temperature', so the change from state P1 V1 to state P2 V2 is an isothermal change: the pressure falls from 4 x 10^5 Pa to 1 x 10^5 Pa while the volume rises from 1 cm^3 to 4 cm^3, keeping P V constant. The internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, so when the temperature does not change, the change in internal energy is zero.

11.4. Variation of volume by pressure is given in Fig 11.13. A gas is taken along the paths ABCDA, ABCA and A to A. What will be the change in internal energy?

Zero in every case. Internal energy is a state function: its change depends only on the initial and final states of the system, not on the path taken. In Fig. 11.13(a) the gas goes round the cycle ABCDA, in (b) along ABCA, and in (c) round the closed loop, so in each case it returns to its starting state A. The change in internal energy is therefore zero for all three paths, even though the work done and the heat exchanged differ from path to path.

11.5. Specific heat of a gas at constant pressure is greater than specific heat at constant volume. Why?

At constant volume, all the heat supplied goes into raising the internal energy, and hence the temperature, of the gas. At constant pressure, the gas expands as it is heated and does work against the outside pressure, so extra heat must be supplied to do that work as well as to raise the temperature. The specific heat at constant pressure is therefore greater than at constant volume, and for one mole of an ideal gas, Cp - Cv = R.

11.6. Give an example of a process in which no heat is transferred to or from the system but the temperature of the system changes.

An adiabatic process, in which no heat is transferred to or from the system, but the temperature still changes. For example, when air is compressed rapidly in a bicycle pump, no appreciable heat escapes during the quick compression, yet the air and the pump become warm, because the work done on the air increases its internal energy. Conversely, a gas escaping rapidly from a spray can cools, because it does work at the expense of its internal energy.

11.7. Is it possible to convert internal energy into mechanical energy? Explain with an example.

Yes. A heat engine converts internal energy into mechanical energy: in a steam engine, heat from the boiler turns water into steam, and the expanding steam pushes a piston and does work. In a petrol engine, the hot gases produced by burning fuel expand and drive the piston. Only part of the heat can be converted into work; the rest must be rejected to a cold sink.

11.8. Is it possible to construct a heat engine that will not expel heat into the atmosphere?

No. By the second law of thermodynamics, no heat engine can convert all the heat it absorbs into work; some heat must always be rejected to a colder reservoir. An engine that expelled no heat into the atmosphere would be 100 percent efficient, which is impossible, and would be a perpetual motion machine of the second kind.

11.9. A thermos flask containing milk as a system is shaken rapidly. Does the temperature of milk rise?

Yes, very slightly. Shaking the flask does work on the milk, and since the thermos is insulated, almost no heat escapes, so the work done increases the internal energy of the milk and its temperature rises a little. The rise is tiny, because the work done by shaking is small compared with the heat capacity of the milk.

11.10. What happens to the temperature of the room, when an airconditioner is left running on a table in the middle of the room?

The temperature of the room will rise, not fall. An air conditioner pumps heat from the cold side to the hot side, but it also consumes electrical energy, which ends up as heat as well. With both the cooling unit and the heat-rejecting unit inside the same room, all the heat taken from the room air is dumped back into the room, together with the heat from the motor, so the room as a whole warms up. An air conditioner cools a room only when its hot side rejects heat outside the room.

11.11. Can the mechanical energy be converted completely into heat energy? If so give an example.

Yes. Mechanical energy can be converted completely into heat energy. For example, when a moving car brakes to a stop, all of its kinetic energy is converted into heat in the brakes and tyres; rubbing the hands together converts the work done against friction into heat. The reverse is not possible: heat energy cannot be converted completely into mechanical energy.

11.12. Does entropy of a system increase or decrease due to friction?

It increases. Friction converts ordered mechanical energy into disordered thermal energy, that is, into random molecular motion. The disorder of the system and its surroundings therefore grows, and by the second law of thermodynamics the total entropy increases as a result of any natural process involving friction.

11.13. Give an example of a natural process that involves an increase in entropy.

Many natural processes involve an increase in entropy, for example the melting of ice at room temperature, the mixing of two gases, the flow of heat from a hot body to a cold body, the spreading of perfume through a room by diffusion, or the dissolving of salt in water. In each case the system becomes more disordered and its entropy increases.

11.14. An adiabatic change is the one in which a. No heat is added to or taken out of a system b. No change of temperature takes place c. Boyle's law is applicable d. Pressure and volume remains constant

a. No heat is added to or taken out of a system. An adiabatic change is defined by zero heat transfer. Option (b), no change of temperature, describes an isothermal change; option (c), Boyle's law, also applies to isothermal changes; and option (d) is false, since pressure and volume both change in an adiabatic change.

11.15. Which one of the following process is irreversible? a. Slow compressions of an elastic spring b. Slow evaporation of a substance in an isolated vessel c. Slow compression of a gas d. A chemical explosion

d. A chemical explosion. An explosion is a fast, violent, dissipative process that cannot be made to retrace its steps. The other three processes are slow and quasi-static, a slow compression of a spring, a slow evaporation in an isolated vessel, and a slow compression of a gas, and can be reversed approximately, so they are nearly reversible.

11.16. An ideal reversible heat engine has a. 100% efficiency b. Highest efficiency c. An efficiency which depends on the nature of working substance d. None of these

b. Highest efficiency. An ideal reversible (Carnot) engine has the highest possible efficiency for working between two given temperatures, equal to 1 - T2 / T1, where T1 and T2 are the absolute temperatures of the source and sink. It is not 100 percent efficient, since T2 is never zero, and its efficiency does not depend on the nature of the working substance.

options: Because the molecules are all at rest on average
Because the molecules move in all directions with equal probability, so their vector velocities cancel, but the squares are always positive and do not cancel
Because velocity is a scalar quantity
Because the gas is in a closed container

Zero, because the internal energy of an ideal gas depends only on its temperature, which does not change
