lessons.title: Numerical Problems — Worked in Full
lessons.notes_html:
11.1. Estimate the average speed of nitrogen molecules in air under standard conditions of pressure and temperature.

Step 1: For a gas molecule, the mean square speed is given by <v^2> = 3 k T / m = 3 R T / M, where M is the molar mass.

Step 2: For nitrogen, M = 28 g per mole = 0.028 kg per mole. At standard temperature T = 273 K and R = 8.31 J per mole per K.

Step 3: Root mean square speed = sqrt(3 R T / M) = sqrt(3 x 8.31 x 273 / 0.028) = sqrt(6808 / 0.028) = sqrt(243,143) = 493 m s^-1.

Answer: 493 ms^-1 (as printed in the book; this is the root mean square speed, which the chapter uses as the average molecular speed).

11.2. Show that ratio of the root mean square speeds of molecules of two different gases at a certain temperature is equal to the square root of the inverse ratio of their masses.

Step 1: The root mean square speed of a gas is v_rms = sqrt(3 k T / m), where k is Boltzmann's constant, T the absolute temperature and m the mass of one molecule.

Step 2: For two gases at the same temperature T, v1 = sqrt(3 k T / m1) and v2 = sqrt(3 k T / m2).

Step 3: Dividing: v1 / v2 = sqrt(3 k T / m1) / sqrt(3 k T / m2) = sqrt(m2 / m1).

Step 4: The ratio of the root mean square speeds is therefore the square root of the inverse ratio of the molecular masses, as required.

11.3. A sample of gas is compressed to one half of its initial volume at constant pressure of 1.25 x 10^5 Nm^-2. During the compression, 100 J of work is done on the gas. Determine the final volume of the gas.

Step 1: At constant pressure, the work done on the gas is W = P x (change in volume) = P x (V1 - V2).

Step 2: The final volume is half the initial volume: V2 = V1 / 2, so the change in volume is V1 - V2 = V1 / 2.

Step 3: So 100 = 1.25 x 10^5 x (V1 / 2), giving V1 / 2 = 100 / (1.25 x 10^5) = 8.0 x 10^-4 m^3.

Step 4: The final volume is V2 = V1 / 2 = 8.0 x 10^-4 m^3.

Answer: 8 x 10^-4 m^3 (as printed in the book).

11.4. A thermodynamic system undergoes a process in which its internal energy decreases by 300 J. If at the same time 120 J of work is done on the system, find the heat lost by the system.

Step 1: First law of thermodynamics: change in internal energy = heat supplied - work done by the system, delta U = Q - W.

Step 2: Here delta U = -300 J (a decrease). Work done on the system is 120 J, so work done by the system is W = -120 J.

Step 3: Substituting: -300 = Q - (-120) = Q + 120, so Q = -300 - 120 = -420 J.

Step 4: The negative sign means heat is lost by the system: heat lost = 420 J.

Answer: -420 J (as printed in the book).

11.5. A carnot engine utilises an ideal gas. The source temperature is 227 degrees C and the sink temperature is 127 degrees C. Find the efficiency of the engine. Also find the heat input from the source and heat rejected to the sink when 10000 J of work is done.

Step 1: Convert to absolute temperatures: source T1 = 227 + 273 = 500 K, sink T2 = 127 + 273 = 400 K.

Step 2: Efficiency of a Carnot engine = 1 - T2 / T1 = 1 - 400 / 500 = 1 - 0.80 = 0.20 = 20%.

Step 3: Efficiency = work done / heat input, so heat input Q1 = W / efficiency = 10000 / 0.20 = 50,000 J = 5.00 x 10^4 J.

Step 4: Heat rejected to the sink Q2 = Q1 - W = 50,000 - 10,000 = 40,000 J = 4.00 x 10^4 J.

Answer: 20%, 5.00 x 10^4 J, 4.00 x 10^4 J (as printed in the book).

11.6. A reversible engine works between two temperatures whose difference is 100 degrees C. If it absorbs 746 J of heat from the source and rejects 546 J to the sink, calculate the temperature of the source and the sink.

Step 1: For a reversible engine, Q1 / Q2 = T1 / T2, where Q1 = 746 J is absorbed from the source and Q2 = 546 J is rejected to the sink.

Step 2: So T1 / T2 = 746 / 546 = 1.366. Also T1 - T2 = 100 K (a difference of 100 degrees C equals 100 K).

Step 3: Substituting T1 = 1.366 T2: 1.366 T2 - T2 = 100, so 0.366 T2 = 100, giving T2 = 273 K.

Step 4: T1 = 273 + 100 = 373 K. In Celsius: source 100 degrees C, sink 0 degrees C.

Answer: 100 degrees C, 0 degrees C (as printed in the book).

11.7. A mechanical engineer develops an engine, working between 327 degrees C and 27 degrees C and claims to have an efficiency of 52%. Does he claim correctly? Explain.

Step 1: Convert to absolute temperatures: source T1 = 327 + 273 = 600 K, sink T2 = 27 + 273 = 300 K.

Step 2: The maximum possible efficiency between these temperatures is the Carnot efficiency: 1 - T2 / T1 = 1 - 300 / 600 = 1 - 0.50 = 50%.

Step 3: No real or ideal engine working between these temperatures can exceed 50% efficiency.

Step 4: The claimed efficiency of 52% is greater than the maximum possible, so the claim is incorrect.

Answer: No (as printed in the book).

11.8. A heat engine performs 100 J of work and at the same time rejects 400 J of heat energy to the cold reservoirs. What is the efficiency of the engine?

Step 1: Heat input from the source Q1 = work done + heat rejected = 100 + 400 = 500 J.

Step 2: Efficiency = work done / heat input = 100 / 500 = 0.20 = 20%.

Answer: 20% (as printed in the book).

11.9. A Carnot engine whose low temperature reservoir is at 7 degrees C has an efficiency of 50%. It is desired to increase the efficiency to 70%. By how many degrees the temperature of the source be increased?

Step 1: Sink temperature T2 = 7 + 273 = 280 K. With efficiency 50%: 0.50 = 1 - T2 / T1, so T1 = 280 / 0.50 = 560 K = 287 degrees C.

Step 2: For efficiency 70%: 0.70 = 1 - 280 / T1', so T1' = 280 / 0.30 = 933 K = 660 degrees C.

Step 3: Increase in source temperature = 660 - 287 = 373 degrees C (the same in kelvin).

Answer: 373 degrees C (as printed in the book).

11.10. A steam engine has a boiler that operates at 450 K. The heat changes water to steam, which drives the piston. The exhaust temperature of the outside air is about 300 K. What is maximum efficiency of this steam engine?

Step 1: Maximum efficiency is the Carnot efficiency between the boiler temperature and the exhaust temperature: efficiency = 1 - T2 / T1.

Step 2: Efficiency = 1 - 300 / 450 = 1 - 0.667 = 0.333 = 33.3%.

Answer: 33% (as printed in the book).

11.11. 336 J of energy is required to melt 1 g of ice at 0 degrees C. What is the change in entropy of 30 g of water at 0 degrees C as it is changed to ice at 0 degrees C by a refrigerator?

Step 1: Heat released when 30 g of water freezes at 0 degrees C: Q = 30 x 336 = 10,080 J.

Step 2: The temperature is 0 degrees C = 273 K. Entropy change = heat transferred / absolute temperature, with a negative sign because heat leaves the water: delta S = -Q / T = -10,080 / 273.

Step 3: delta S = -36.9 J K^-1.

Answer: -36.8 J K^-1 (as printed in the book; the direct value is -36.9 J K^-1, the small difference being rounding of the temperature and latent heat).

mcqs.q: Estimate the root mean square speed of nitrogen molecules under standard conditions (M = 0.028 kg per mole, T = 273 K, R = 8.31 J per mole per K).
mcqs.why: Working: v_rms = sqrt(3 R T / M) = sqrt(3 x 8.31 x 273 / 0.028). The numerator 3 x 8.31 x 273 = 6808, and 6808 / 0.028 = 243143. Then v_rms = sqrt(243143) = 493 ms^-1, the value the chapter uses as the average molecular speed.

mcqs.q: A gas is compressed to one half of its initial volume at a constant pressure of 1.25 x 10^5 N m^-2, and 100 J of work is done on the gas. The final volume is:
mcqs.why: Working: at constant pressure the work done on the gas is W = P x (V1 - V2), and the volume change is V1 / 2 since the gas is halved. So V1 / 2 = 100 / (1.25 x 10^5) = 8.0 x 10^-4 m^3. The final volume is V2 = V1 / 2 = 8 x 10^-4 m^3.

mcqs.q: A system's internal energy decreases by 300 J while 120 J of work is done on the system. The heat lost by the system is:
mcqs.why: Working: first law, delta U = Q - W, with delta U = -300 J. Work done on the system is 120 J, so work done by the system is W = -120 J. Then -300 = Q + 120, giving Q = -300 - 120 = -420 J. The negative sign means 420 J of heat is lost by the system.

mcqs.q: A Carnot engine uses an ideal gas with source at 227 degrees C and sink at 127 degrees C. Its efficiency is:
mcqs.why: Working: absolute temperatures: T1 = 227 + 273 = 500 K and T2 = 127 + 273 = 400 K. Efficiency = 1 - T2 / T1 = 1 - 400 / 500 = 1 - 0.80 = 0.20, that is 20 percent. For 10000 J of work the heat input is 5.00 x 10^4 J and the heat rejected is 4.00 x 10^4 J.

mcqs.q: A reversible engine works between two temperatures differing by 100 degrees C, absorbing 746 J from the source and rejecting 546 J to the sink. The source and sink temperatures are:
options: Source 100 degrees C, sink 0 degrees C
Source 373 degrees C, sink 273 degrees C
Source 200 degrees C, sink 100 degrees C
Source 546 degrees C, sink 446 degrees C
mcqs.why: Working: for a reversible engine T1 / T2 = Q1 / Q2 = 746 / 546 = 1.366, and T1 - T2 = 100 K. Substituting T1 = 1.366 T2 gives 0.366 T2 = 100, so T2 = 273 K and T1 = 373 K: source 100 degrees C, sink 0 degrees C.

mcqs.q: An engineer claims an efficiency of 52 percent for an engine working between 327 degrees C and 27 degrees C. Is the claim correct?
options: No, because the maximum (Carnot) efficiency between these temperatures is 50 percent
Yes, because real engines can exceed the Carnot efficiency
No, because no engine can exceed 40 percent
Yes, because 52 percent is less than the temperature ratio
mcqs.why: Working: T1 = 327 + 273 = 600 K and T2 = 27 + 273 = 300 K. Maximum efficiency = 1 - T2 / T1 = 1 - 300 / 600 = 0.50, that is 50 percent. The claimed 52 percent exceeds the maximum possible, so the claim is incorrect.

mcqs.q: A heat engine performs 100 J of work and rejects 400 J of heat to the cold reservoir. Its efficiency is:
mcqs.why: Working: heat input Q1 = work done + heat rejected = 100 + 400 = 500 J. Efficiency = work done / heat input = 100 / 500 = 0.20, that is 20 percent.

mcqs.q: A Carnot engine with its sink at 7 degrees C has an efficiency of 50 percent. To raise the efficiency to 70 percent, the temperature of the source must be increased by:
mcqs.why: Working: sink T2 = 7 + 273 = 280 K. At 50 percent efficiency, T1 = 280 / 0.50 = 560 K = 287 degrees C. At 70 percent, T1 = 280 / 0.30 = 933 K = 660 degrees C. Increase = 660 - 287 = 373 degrees C.

mcqs.q: A steam engine's boiler operates at 450 K and the exhaust temperature is about 300 K. The maximum efficiency of the engine is:
mcqs.why: Working: the maximum efficiency is the Carnot value between the boiler and exhaust temperatures: efficiency = 1 - T2 / T1 = 1 - 300 / 450 = 1 - 0.667 = 0.333, about 33 percent.

mcqs.q: 336 J of energy is required to melt 1 g of ice at 0 degrees C. The change in entropy when 30 g of water at 0 degrees C is changed to ice at 0 degrees C is:
options: -36.9 J K^-1 (the book prints -36.8 J K^-1 with its rounding)
Zero, because the temperature does not change
mcqs.why: Working: heat released on freezing = 30 x 336 = 10080 J. The temperature is 0 degrees C = 273 K. Entropy change = -Q / T = -10080 / 273 = -36.9 J K^-1, negative because heat leaves the water. The book prints -36.8 J K^-1, the small difference being rounding of the temperature and latent heat.
